sourceDefinition: is a quasi-inf. n. of A^atama in the last of the senses explained above. (Msb.) [Thus it signifies A staying, remaining, dwelling, or abiding, in a place. But it more commonly signifies] The assembling of women [and of men also] in a case of rejoicing and of mourning. (Har p. 234.) ― -b2- It is also a noun of time from the same. (Msb.) [Thus it signifies A time of staying or remaining, &c.] ― -b3- And it is also a noun of place from the same. (Msb.) [And thus it signifies A place of staying or remaining, &c. But it more commonly signifies] A place of assembling of women [and of men also] in a case of rejoicing and of mourning: from A^atima , aor. , accord. to Khálid Ibn-Yezeed. (T.) ― -b4- And hence, tropically, (Msb,) (tropical:) Women assembling together (T, S, M, Mgh, Msb, K) in a case of rejoicing and of mourning, (T, M, Mgh, K,) or in a case of good and of evil: (S, Msb:) or any assembly, (M, K,) of men and of women, (M,) in a case of mourning or of rejoicing: (M, K:) or particularly of young women; (M, K,) accord. to some; but it is not so: and some assert that the word is derived from A^atomN , in the first of the senses explained in this art.; and from A^atuwmN , as an epithet applied to a woman; because it signifies women coming together, and meeting face to face, in a case of good and of evil: (M:) the pl. is maA=timu . (S, Mgh.) Abu-l-'Atà Es-Sindee says, Ea$iy~apa qaAma Aln~aAy^iHaAtu wa $uq~iqato juyuwbN biA^ayodiY maA^otamK wa xuduwdu [ In the evening when arose the wailing women to wail, and openings at the necks and bosoms of garments were rent with the hands of assembled mourning women, and cheeks also were lacerated]: (S, M, Mgh:) i. e., biA^ayodiY nisaA='K . (S.) And another says, Hat~aY taraAhun~a ladayohi quy~amaA kamaA taraY Hawola AlA^amiyri AlmA^otamaA [ So that thou seest them (referring to women) standing in his presence, or at, or by, it, like as thou seest the assembly of men around the prince, or commander ]: AlmA^tm here necessarily denoting men. (M.) ― -b5- IKt says, (Msb,) it is used by the vulgar to denote An affliction, or evil accident; (S, Mgh, Msb;) [and Mtr adds,] and a wailing: (Mgh:) they say, kun~aA fiY maA_otami falaAnK [meaning We were present at the affliction of such a one ]: (S, Msb:) or kun~aA fiY maA^otami baniy fulalnK [meaning, We were present at the affliction, and wailing, of the sons of such a one ]: (Mgh:) but the correct word in this case, (S, Mgh,) or the better, (Msb,) is manaAHap : (S, Mgh, Msb:) so says IAmb. (Mgh.) But accord. to IB, nothing forbids that it may occur in the sense of A place of wailing; and in the sense of mourning, and wailing, and weeping; for therefore do women assemble: and thus it may be in the saying of Et-Teymee, respecting Mansoor Ibn-Ziyád, wa Aln~aAsu maA^otamuhumo Ealayohi waAHidN fiY kl~i daArK ran~apN wa zafiyru [ The people's mourning, &c., for him was one: in every house was a moaning, and a sighting ]: and in the saying of another, A^aDoHaY banaAtu Als~ubiY~i A_i*o qutiluwA fiY maA^otamK waAls~ibaAEu fiY Eurusi i. e. [ The daughters of the captives, when they were slain, became, in the early part of the day, ] in a state mourning; and the beasts of prey, in a state of rejoicing. (TA.)

definition: One who walks quickly, and runs, in this and that manner.
sourceDefinition: One who walks quickly, and runs, in this and that manner. (K, * TA.) ― -b2- yaA^ojuwju and ↓ maA^ojuwju , (S, Msb, K,) imperfectly decl., (S,) [ Gog and Magog; ] two tribes of God's creatures; (TA;) or two great nations; (Msb;) or two tribes of the children of Japheth the son of Noah: or, as some say, the former, of the Turks; and the latter, of the Jeel [meaning Jeel-Jeelán, said in the TA in art. jyl , on the authority of ISd, to be a people beyond the Deylem; and on the authority of Az, to be believers in a plurality of gods; ( the Geli and Gelœ of Ptolemy and Strabo, as observed by Sale, in a note on ch. xviii. v. 93 of the Kur, on the authority of Golius in Alfrag. p. 207;)]: (Bd in xviii. 93:) [said by the Arabs to be Scythians of the furthest East; particularly those on the north of the Chinese: (Golius:) or, as some say, the descendants of Japheth, and all the nations inhabiting the north of Asia and of Europe: (Freytag:)] said in a rad., (TA,) on the authority of I' Ab, (Msb,) to compose nine tenths of mankind: (Msb, TA:) or yA^jwj is the name of the males, and mA^jwj is that of the females: (Msb:) he who pronounces them thus, and makes the A^ a radical letter, says that the former is of the measure yafoEuwlu , and the latter of the measure mafoEuwlu ; as though from A^ajayju Aln~aAri ; (Akh, S, Msb; *) or from maA='N A^ujaAjN ; (TA;) or from A^aj~a said of an ostrich; and imperfectly decl. as being determinate and fem.: (Bd ubi suprà:) he who pronounces them without ' , making the A in each an augmentative letter, says that the former is from yajajotu , and the latter from majajotu : (Akh, S, K:) this is the case if they be Arabic: (TA:) but some say that they are foreign names; (Msb, TA;) their being imperfectly decl. is said to indicate this; (Bd ubi suprà;) and if so, the A in them is similar to that in haAruwt and maAruwt and daAwuwd and the like; and the ' , anomalous, as that in EaA^olimN and the like; and their measure is faAEuwlu . (Msb.) Ru-beh used to read ↓ A=juwju and maAjuwju [in the CK mA^juwj ]; and Aboo-Mo'ádh, yamojuwju . (K.)

sourceDefinition: [ The earth; ] that whereon are mankind: (TA:) [and earth, as opposed to heaven: and the ground, as meaning the surface of the earth, on which we tread and sit and lie; and the floor: without Al signifying a land, or country: and a piece of land or ground: and land, or soil, or ground, considered in relation to its quality: ] it is fem.: (S, A, Msb, K:) and is a coll. gen. n.; (S, A, K;) of which the n. un. should be A^aroDapN , but this they did not say: (S:) or a pl. having no sing.; (A, K;) for A^aroDapN has not been heard: (K:) its pl. is A^araDaAtN , (S, K,) in [some of] the copies of the K A^aroDaAtN , (TA,) for they sometimes form the pl. of a word which has not the fem. p with A and t , as in the instance of EurusaAtN ; (S;) and A^araDuwna , [which is more common,] (AZ, AHn, S, Mgh, Msb, K,) with fet-h to the r , (AZ, AHn, Mgh, Msb,) and with w and n , though a fem. has not its pl. formed [regularly] with w and n unless it is of the defective kind, like vubapN and ZubapN , but they have made the w and n [in this instance] a substitute for the A and t which they have elided [from A^araDaAtN ], and have left the fet-hah of the r as it was; (S;) but they also said A^aroDuwna , (AZ, AHn, S,) sometimes, making the r quiescent; (S;) and A^uruwDN (AZ, AHn, Msb, K) is sometimes used as a pl., as in the saying maA A^akovara A^uruwDa baniY fulaAnK [ How many are the lands of the sons of such a one! ]; (TA;) and another [and very common] pl. is [ A^araADK , with the article written] AlA^araADiY , contr. to rule, (S, Msb, K,) as though they had formed a pl. from A=ruDN ; (S;) thus written in all the copies of the S; [accord. to SM; but in one copy of the S, I find kaA^an~ahumo jamaEuwA AArADFA ; and in another, ArDFA ;] and in one copy [is added], “ thus it is found in his [J's] handwriting; ” but IB says that correctly he should have said A^aroDaY , like A^aroTaY ; for as to A=ruDN , its regular pl. would be A^awaAriDu ; and [SM says] I have found it observed in a marginal note to the S that the pl. of A=ruDN would be A^aA=riDu , like as A^akaAlibu is pl. of A^akolubN ; and wherefore did he not say that AlArADY is a pl. of an unused sing., like layaAlK and A^ahaAlK , so that it is as though it were pl. of A^aroDaApN , like as layaAlK is pl. of layolaApN ? yet if any one should propose the plea that it may be formed by transposition from A^aA=riDu , he would not say what is improbable; its measure being in this case A^aEaAlifu ; the word being A^araADiy^u , and the ' being changed into Y : (TA:) accord. to Abu-l-Khattáb, (S,) A=raADN is also a pl. of A^aroDN , (S, K,) like as A=haAlN is a pl. of A^aholN ; (S;) but IB says that, in the opinion of the critics, the truth with respect to what is related on the authority of Abu-l-Khattáb is, that from A^aroDN and A^aholN are formed A^araADK and A^ahaAlK , as though they were pls. of A^aroDaApN and A^aholaApN ; like as they said layolapN and layaAl , as though this were pl. of layolaApN . (TA.) It is said in proverbs, A^ajomaEu mina AlA^aroDi [ More comprehensive than the earth ]: (TA:) and A=manu mina AlA^aroDi [ More trustworthy than the earth, in which treasures are securely buried]: and A^a$ad~u mina AlA^aroDi [ Harder than the earth, or ground ]: (A, TA:) and A^a*al~u mina AlA^aroDi [ More vile, or more submissive, than the earth, or ground ]. (TA.) And you say, mano A^aTaAEaniY kunotu lahu A^aroDaA (tropical:) [ Whoso obeyeth me, I will be to him as ground whereon one treads]; denoting submissiveness. (A, TA.) And fulaAnN A_inN Duriba faA^aroDN (tropical:) [ Such one, if he be beaten, is like ground ]; i. e. he cares not for beating. (A, TA.) One says also, laA A^aroDa laka [ Mayest thou have no land, or country! or thou hast no land, or country ]; like as one says, laA A^um~a laka . (S, K,) ― -b2- [And hence,] huwa Abonu A^aroDK He is a stranger, (A, K, TA,) of whom neither father nor mother is known. (TA.) ― -b3- Aibonu AlA^aroDi [with the art. Al prefixed to the latter word] is A certain plant, (AHn, K,) which comes forth upon the summits of the [ hills called ] A=kaAm , having a stem ( A^aSol ), but not growing tall, (AHn,) which resembles hair, and is eaten, (AHn, K,) and quickly dries up; (AHn;) a species of baqol , as also binotu AlA^aroDi : (S in art. bnY :) and banaAtu AlA^aroDi plants: (M in art. bsr :) and the places which are concealed from the pastor. (S in that art.) Also The pool that is left by a torrent: (T in art. bnY :) and banaAtu AlA^aroDi pools in which are remains of water: (IAar in TA art. bsr :) and rivulets. (T in art. bnY .) ― -b4- A^aroDN is also used to signify (assumed tropical:) A carpet; or anything that is spread: and in this sense, in poetry, it is sometimes made masc. (Msb.) ― -b5- And (assumed tropical:) Anything that is low. (S, K.) And (tropical:) The lower, or lowest, part of the legs of a horse or the like: (S, K:) or the legs of a camel or of a horse or the like: and the part that is next to the ground thereof. (TA.) You say baEiyrN $adiydu AlA^aroDi (tropical:) A camel strong in the legs. (TA.) And farasN baEiydN maA bayoma A^aroDihi wasamaAy^ihi (tropical:) A horse that is large and tall. (A, TA.) ― -b6- Also, of a man, (tropical:) The knees and what is beneath, or below, (lit. after, ) them. (TA.) ― -b7- And of a sandal, (assumed tropical:) [The lower surface of the sole; ] the part that touches the ground. (TA.) -A2- A febrile shivering; a tremor: (S, K:) or vertigo: or it signifies also vertigo arising from a relaxed state, and occasioning a defluxion from the nose and eyes. (TA.) I'Ab is related to have said, on the occasion of an earthquake, A^azulozilati AlA^aroDu A^amo biY A^aroDN , (S,) i. e. [ Hath the earth been made to quake, or is there in me ] a tremor? or a vertigo? (TA.) [ A^aholu AlA^aroDi signifies A certain class of the jinn, or genii; by whom human beings are believed to be possessed, and affected by an involuntary tremor; whence it seems that this appellation may perhaps be from A^aroDN as signifying “ a tremor. ” See maA^oruwDN : and see xabalN , as explained in the S.] ― -b2- Also Rheum; syn. zukaAmN : (S, K:) in this sense masc.; or, accord. to Kr, fem., on the authority of Ibn-Ahmar. (TA.) -A3- See also maA^oruwDN .

definition: [The wood-fretter;
sourceDefinition: [The wood-fretter; ] a certain insect that eats wood, (S A, Msb, K,) well known; (A, K;) it is a white worm, resembling the ant, appearing in the days of the [ season called ] rabiyE : (TA:) there are two kinds: one kind is small, like the large of the *ar~ [or grubs of ants ]; and this is the bane of wood in particular: (AHn, TA:) or this kind is the bane of wood and of other things, and is a white worm with a black head, not having wings, and it penetrates into the earth, and builds for itself a habitation of clay, or soil; and this is said to be that which ate the staff of Solomon [as is related in the Kur xxxiv. 13, where it is called daAb~apu AlA^aroDi , as is said in the A]: (TA:) the other kind [ is the termite, or white ant; termes fatale of Linn.; called by Forskål (in his Descr. Animalium &c., p. 96,) termes arda, destructor; and this ] is like a large common ant, having wings; it is the bane of everything that is of wood, and of plants; except that it does not attack what is moist, or succulent; and it has legs: (AHn, TA:) the pl. is ↓ A^araDN (AHn, Msb, TA) and A^araDaAtN ; (Msb;) or, as some [more properly] say, A^araDN is a quasi-pl. [or coll. gen.] n. (AHn, TA.) It is said in a prov., A=kalu mina AlA^araDapi [ More consuming than the wood-fretter, or the termite ]. (TA.) And in another, A^afosadu mina AlA^araDapi [ More marring, or injuring, or destructive, than the wood-fretter, or the termite. ] (A, TA.)

definition: The lower, or lowest, part of a thing;
sourceDefinition: The lower, or lowest, part of a thing; [i. e. its root, bottom, or foot; ] (M, Msb, K;) as also ↓ yaA^oSuwlN : (M, K:) so of a mountain: and of a wall; (TA;) i. e. its foundation, or base: (Msb:) and of a tree [or plant]; (TA;) i. e. [its stem, or trunk, or stock, or] the part from which the branches are broken off: (TA in art. ksr :) [and also its root, or foot; for] the saAq of a tree is said to be the part between its A^aSol and the place where its branches shoot out: (TA in art. swq :) [and a stump of a tree: and hence, a block of wood: (see exs. voce naqiyrN :)] pl. A^uSuwlN (S, M, Msb, K) and [pl. of pauc.] A=SulN : (AHn, K:) [ISd says that] the former is its only pl.: (M:) [but] the latter pl. occurs in a verse of Lebeed, (which see below,) as cited by AHn. (TA.) You say, qaEada fiY A^aSoli jabali He sat upon, or at, the lowest part [&c.] of the mountain; and fiY A^aSoli AlHaAy^iTi at the lowest part [&c.] of the wall. (TA.) And qalaEahu mino A^aSolihi [ He pulled it up, or out, or off, from its root, or foundation, or lowest part ]; and bA^uSuwlihi [ with its roots, or foundations, or lowest parts; both meaning, utterly, entirely, or altogether ]. (TA in explanation of AstA^Slhu , q. v.) And qalaEa A^aSola Al$~ajarapi He pulled up, or out, the lowest part, [or stem or stock or root or foot or stump, ] of the tree. (TA.) definition: [ Having root, or a foundation;
sourceDefinition: [ Having root, or a foundation; and consequently, having rootedness, fixedness, immobility, stability, or permanence; rooted, fixed, immoveable, stable, or permanent ]. You say, A_in~a Aln~axola fiY A^aroDinaA laA^aSiylN Verily the palm-trees in our land remain permanently, not perishing. (A, TA.) ― -b2- A man having A^aSol , (K, TA,) i. e., lincage, or pedigree: (TA:) or established in his A^aSol : (Abu-l-BaKà, TA:) or noble, or generous. (Msb.) ― -b3- A man firm of judgment, and intelligent. (M, K.* [Accord. to the copies of the latter, the signification is EaAqibN vaAbitu Alr~aA^oYi : but I think that the right reading of the first word is EaAqilN , as in the M, in which this word occupies the last place in the explanation.]) And A^aSiylu Alr~aA^oYi A man firm, or sound, of judgment. (S.) And raA^oYN A^aSiylN Judgment having A^aSol [i. e. firmness ]. (M.) And majodN A^aSiylN Glory, honour, dignity, or nobility, having a firm root or foundation. (S.) And $ar~N A^aSiylN Vehement evil or mischief. (Ibn-'Abbád.) -A2- See also A^aSilN , in two places. ― -b2- [Hence, app.,] AlA^aSiylu Destruction: and death: as also, in both senses, ↓ AlA^aSiylapu . (K.) -A3- [The evening; or] i. q. Ea$iY~N ; (M, K, Msb, TA;) i. e. (Msb, TA) the time from the EaSor , (S, TA,) from the prayer of the ESr , (Msb,) to sunset; (Sudot;, Msb, TA;) as also ↓ A^aSiylapN : (R, TA:) the pl. is A^uSulN , (S, M, R, Msb, K,) or ↓ this is a sing., (TA,) or it may be a sing., (M,) for it is used as such, (M, TA,) and A^uSolaAnN , (S, M, K,) and A=SaAlN , (S, M, Sgh, K,) [a pl. of pauc.,] or, accord. to Es- Saláh Es-Safadee, this is a pl. of A^uSulN , the sing., not the pl., (TA,) or it is pl. of A^uSulN , (Zj, M,) which may be a pl. or a sing., (M,) and A^aSaAy^ilu , (S, M, K,) as though pl. of A^aSiylapN , (S,) or it is pl. of this last word. (R, TA.) You say, laqiytuhu A^aSiylFA and ↓ A^uSulFA , i. e. [ I met him in the evening, ] Ea$iy~FA . (A, TA.) From the pl. A^uSolaAnu is formed the dim. ↓ A^uSayolaAnN , (S, M, K,) which is extr., (M, K,) because the dim. of a pl. is [regularly] formed only from a pl. of pauc., which ASlAn is not; or, if ASlAn be a sing., like rum~aAnN and qurobaAnN , this dim. is regular: (M:) sometimes, (K,) one says also ↓ A^uSayolaAlN , (S, M, K,) substituting l for the [final] n (S, M.*) You say, ↓ laqiytuhu A^uSayolaAnFA and ↓ A^uSayolaAlFA , meaning, as above, Ea$iy~FA : (A, TA:) and Lh mentions ↓ lqyth A^uSay~aAlFA . (So in two copies of the S.)

definition: , (S, M, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, M, K,) aor. yaA^oniY , (S,) inf. n. A_inNY (S, M, K) and A^anoYN and A^anaA='N , (M, K,) or, accord. to [some of the copies of] the M, A^anFY , (TA, [in which this is said to be the right form,]) or A^anFA , (as written in the CK,) said of a thing, Its time came; or it was, or became, or drew, near; syn. A^ataY waqotuhu , and jaA='a A^anaAhu ; (Bd lvii. 15 [in explanation of a passage cited voce A^ano ];) or HaAna : (S, M, K:) or A^anaY , aor. yaA^oniY , inf. n. A^anoYN , signifies it was, or became, or drew, near; and it was, or became, present. (Msb.) You say, A^anaY laka A^ano tafoEala , aor. yaA^oniY ; and A=na , aor. yay^iynu ; and naAla lk , aor. yaniylu ; and A^anaAla ; all meaning HaAna laka [ The time has come, or has drawn near, for thee that thou shouldst do such a thing: or the time of thy doing such a thing has come to thee: or thy doing such a thing has drawn near ]: so says Zj; and Fr says the like: but the best of these is A^anaY laka . (T.) And A^anaY Alr~aHiylu The time of departure came, or drew near; syn. HaAna waqotuhu . (TA, from a trad.) ― -b2- It came, or attained, to its time; to its full, or final, time or state; to maturity, or ripeness; it became mature, or ripe; (T, S, M, IAmb, * Msb, * K;) or, accord. to some, only when said of a plant; (M, K;) [or it signifies also] it became thoroughly cooked. (T, Msb. *) Hence, in the Kur [xxxiii. 53], gayoranaAZiriyna A_inaAhu Not waiting, or watching, for its becoming thoroughly cooked; or for its cooking becoming finished. (T, S, * M.) [See also A_inFY , below.] You say also, A^anaY AlHamiymu , (inf. n. A^anoYN , TA,) The hot water became heated to the utmost degree. (S, K.) And A^anaY AlmaA='u The water became hot to the utmost degree. (M.) -A2- A^anaY , aor. A^uniY~N , inf. n. A^anoYN , It (a thing) was, or became, behind, or after, its time: (Lth, T:) or A^anaY , inf. n. A^uniY~N , it, or he, (a man, TA,) was, or became, behind, backward, or late; it, or he, delayed, or held back; (M, K;) as also A^aniYa , aor. yaA^onaY , inf. n.

definition: He acted deliberately, or leisurely, not hastily;
sourceDefinition: He acted deliberately, or leisurely, not hastily; as also ↓ AstA^nY ; and ↓ A^aniYa , (M, K,) aor. yaA^onaY , (K,) inf. n. A^noYN : (TA:) he acted with moderation, gently, deliberately, or leisurely; without haste; and with gravity, staidness, sedateness, or calmness; fiY AlA^amori in the affair; as also ↓ AstA^nY : (Mgh:) or he acted gently; (IAar, T, TA;) as also ↓ A^aniYa , aor. and inf. n. as above: (TA:) or he acted gently, and waited; fiY AlA^amori in the affair: (S:) or he waited, or was patient, or waited with patience, (T, Msb,) and did not hasten, in an affair. (Msb.) Alt~aA^at~iY and Alt~aA^an~iY are nearly syn.: you say, tA^n~Y lahu He acted gently with him, [or to him, ] and did not hasten in his affair. (Mgh.) And bihi HawolFA ↓ Ausotuw^oniYa [ He was waited patiently with for a year ]. (S.) And fiY A^amorika ↓ AisotaA^oni Hasten not in thine affair. (Lth, T.) And fiY AlT~aEaAmi ↓ AisotaA^onayotu I waited for the food to become perfectly prepared or cooked. (Har p. 67.) And taA^an~ayotu Alr~ajula (and Ealayohi , M and K in art. nZr , [see AinotaZarahu ,]) I waited for the man; as also bihi ↓ AisotaA^onayotu : whence, biAlojiraAHaAti ↓ yusotaA^naY One should wait for the issues, or consequences, or results, of wounds. (Mgh.) And taA^n~ayotuka Hat~aY laA A^anaApa biY [ I have waited patiently for thee until there is no disposition to wait patiently in me ]. (S.)

sourceDefinition: Moderation; gentleness; deliberateness; a leisurely manner of proceeding, or of deportment, &c.; patience, as meaning contr. of hastiness: and gravity; staidness; sedateness; calmness: a subst. from taA^an~aY ; (S, Msb;) syn. tuw^adapN ; (T;) and rifoqN ; (Ham p. 317;) and HilomN and waqaArN ; (M, Mgh, K;) as also ↓ A^nFY . (M, K, TA. [In the CK, kAlAanoYi is erroneously put for kaAlA^anaY .]) ― -b2- Also Hope: [in this sense, accord. to the TA, written with kesr; but this is doubtless a mistake, probably occasioned by a mistranscription:] so in the charge of 'Orweh to his sons; yaA baniY~a A_i*aA raA^ayotumo xal~apF raAy^iEapF mino rajulK falaA taqoTaEuwA A^anaAtakumo mitohu waA_ino kaAna Einoda Aln~aAsi rajula saw^o'K [ O my sons, when ye see a quality exciting admiration and approval, in a man, cut not ye off your hope of him, though he be in the estimation of the people a bad man ]. (M.) -A2- A woman in whom is a languor on the occasion of rising, or standing up; (T, S, K;) and a gentle, or grave, deportment: (S:) or in whom is a languor impeding from rising, or standing up: (As:) and wahonaAnapN signifies the like: (T:) Sb says that it is originally wanaApN , like as A^aHadN is originally waHadN ; from AlwanaY : (S:) the people of El-Koofeh say that it is only wanaApN : so says Lth: and he says that A^anaApN signifies, as applied to a woman, blessed, prospered, or abounding in good, as it is explained also by ADk, and forbearing, gentle, grave, staid, sedate, or calm, and compliant, or agreeing with another in mind or opinion: and the pl. is A^anawAtN : or, as some say, it signifies a grave, staid, sedate, or calm, woman, who does not clamour, nor utter foul language. (T.)

sourceDefinition: a word expressive of disapproval, and of deeming a thing remote or improbable: Sb relates that it was said to an Arab of the desert, who had taken up his abode in a town, or place, “Wilt thou go forth when the desert shall have become plentiful in herbage?” and he said, A^aA^anaA A_iniyho [ What, I, indeed? ], meaning “Do ye say this to me when I am know to do thus?” as though he disapproved of their questioning him: but there is much diversity of opinion respecting this word: (TA:) [accord. to some,] it is composed of the redundant A_ino and the meddeh denoting disapproval [followed by the h of silence]. (Mughnee voce A_inN .) [See what is said of the redundant Ano in the present work.]

definition: signifies Whence? syn.
sourceDefinition: signifies Whence? syn. mino A^ayona ; (T, S, M;) being an interrogative respecting the direction, or quarter, from which a thing is: (Msb:) and whence [used to denote a condition]: (TA:) and where? and where [used to denote a condition]; syn. A^ayona : (T, K: [in which latter the first signification is not mentioned:]) and as one of the adverbial nouns used to denote a condition, whencesoever; from whatever direction or quarter: (S:) and wherever; wheresoever: (Lth, T:) and when? and when [used to den a condition]; syn. mataY : (T, K: [but in the latter of these, in art. An , in the place of mataY we find Hayovu , which I regard as a mistake:]) and how? syn. kayofa : (Lth, T, S, M, K:) and however. (Lth, TA.) sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. buruwdapN ; (S, M, Mgh, Msb, K;) and barada , aor. , (M, Msb, K,) inf. n. barodN ; (M, Msb;) It (a thing, S, Msb, and the latter said of water, Msb) was, or became, cold, chill, or cool; [see barodN below;] (S, M;) its heat became allayed. (Msb.) The latter verb is also used transitively, as will be shown below. (Msb.) ― -b2- [Hence,] baruda maDojaEahu [lit. His bed, or place of sleep, became cold; meaning] (tropical:) he went on a journey. (A.) ― -b3- barada also signifies (tropical:) He died; (As, T, S, A, K;) because death is the non-existence of the heat of the soul; (L;) or it is allusive to the extinction of the natural heat; or to the cessation of motion. (MF.) For ― -b4- barada , (MF,) aor. , (Mgh,) inf. n. barodN , (MF,) likewise signifies (assumed tropical:) It was, or became, still, quiet, or motionless; (Mgh, MF;) for instance, a slaughtered sheep or goat [&c.]. (Mgh.) And (assumed tropical:) It (beverage of the kind called nabiy* ) became still, and without briskness. (TA, from a trad.) You say, ruEiba fabarada makaAnahu [(assumed tropical:) He became frightened, and remained motionless in his place; makaAnahu meaning fiY makaAnahu : and hence,] (tropical:) he became amazed, or stupified. (A.) And baradato Eayonuhu (assumed tropical:) The pain in his eye became allayed, or stilled. (L.) And barada A^amorunaA (assumed tropical:) Our affair, or case, became easy. (TA, from a trad. [See also baAridN .]) ― -b5- Also, inf. n. barod , [which see below,] (assumed tropical:) He slept. (T.) ― -b6- And hence, (tropical:) It remained, or became permanent, or fixed, or settled. (T.) So in the saying, lamo yaborudo biyadiY minohu $ayo'N (tropical:) There did not remain, or become permanent or fixed or settled, in my hand, thereof, anything. (T, L. *) You say also, barada A^asiyrFA fiY A^ayodiyohimo (tropical:) He remained safely a captive in their hands. (A.) And barada fiY A^ayodiyhmo salomFA (tropical:) He became a permanent captive, remaining in their hands, not to be ransomed nor liberated nor demanded. (L.) And barada Almawoti EalaYmuSoTalaAhu (tropical:) Death fixed, or settled, [ upon his face and extremities, or] upon his limbs, or upon his arms and legs and face and every prominent part, which become cold at the time of death, and which are warmed at the fire. (AHeyth, L.) And barada Almawoti Ealayohi [(tropical:) Death became impressed upon him; ] the marks, or signs, of death became apparent upon him. (A.) ― -b7- [And hence, app.,] (tropical:) It (a right, or due,) became incumbent, or obligatory, (M, K, TA,) and established. (TA.) You say, barada liY Haq~iY EalaY fulaAnK (tropical:) My right, or due, became incumbent, or obligatory, on such a one, and established against him. (M, * A, * TA.) And maA barada laka EalaY fulaAnK (tropical:) What hath become incumbent, or obligatory, to thee, on such a one, and established against him? or what hath become owed, or due, to thee, by, or from, such a one? as also maA *aAba laka Ealayohi . (S.) And barada liY Ealayohi ka*aA mina AlmaAli (tropical:) Such an amount of the property, or of property, became incumbent, or obligatory, to me, on him, and established against him; or became owed, or due, to me, by, or from, him. (S.) ― -b8- Also, (K,) aor. , inf. n. barodN , (TA, [but see the next sentence,]) (assumed tropical:) He (a man) was, or became, weak; and so burida , a verb like EuniYa . (K.) And, inf. n. buraAdN and buruwdN , (M, K,) (assumed tropical:) He was, or became, languid, (K,) or weak and languid, from leanness or disease: (M:) or weak in the legs, from hunger or fatigue. (Ibn-Buzurj, T.) And barada mux~uhu , (A, K,) aor. , inf. n. barodN , (TA,) (tropical:) He was, or became, lean, or emaciated; (A, K;) and so baradato EiZaAmuhu . (A, TA.) ― -b9- (assumed tropical:) It (a sword [or the like]) was, or became, blunt. (M, K.) -A2- baradahu , (S, Msb, K,) aor. , (Msb,) inf. n. barodN ; (K;) and ↓ br~dhu , (S, M, Msb, K,) inf. n. taboriydN ; (S;) He made it, or rendered it, (for ex., water, M, Msb, K,) cold, chill, or cool: (S, &c.:) but the latter has an intensive signification [ he made it, or rendered it, very cold, or very cool ]: (Msb:) or both signify, (K,) or the former signifies, (M, TA,) he mixed it with snow: (M, K:) one does not say ↓ Abrdhu , except in a bad dialect. (S.) bar~idiyhi , being used by a poet for balo ridiyhi , has been erroneously supposed to mean “Make thou it hot.” (M.) You say, baradanaA All~ayolu , (aor. and inf. n. as above, M,) and barada EalayonaA , The night affected us with its cold. (M, K.) And saqayotuhu $arobapF baradato fuw^aAdahu , (S, M, *) aor. and inf. n. as above, (S,) I gave him to drink a draught that cooled his heart: (S, M:) or baradotu bihaA fuw^aAdahu [ with which I cooled his heart ]. (So in the T.) And fuw^aAdaka bi$arobapK ↓ bar~ido Cool thy heart by a draught. (A.) And AisoqiniY sawiyqFA A^aborudo bihi kabidiY [ Give thou me to drink swyq with which I may cool my liver ]. (T.) And barada Eayonuhu biAlokuHoli , (A'Obeyd, T, M,) or biAlobaruwdi , (S, Msb, K,) aor. and inf. n. as above, (M,) [ He cooled his eye with the collyrium, or] he applied the cooling collyrium to his eye, (T, * S, M, * Msb, K, *) and allayed its pain. (M.) The following words, cited by IAar, baraduwA gawaAriba A^ayonuqK Hudobi [lit. They cooled the fore parts of the humps, or the backs, of humped she-camels ], mean (tropical:) they put off from them their saddles, that their backs might become cool. (M.) You say also, ↓ bar~ido Zahora farasika saAEapF (tropical:) Relieve thy horse from riding [lit. cool his back ] awhile. (A.) And ↓ laA tubar~ido Eano fulaAnK (tropical:) Do not thou alleviate the punishment [ in the world to come ] due to the offence of such a one by thy reviling him, or cursing him, when he has acted injuriously to thee. definition: He entered upon a cold, or cool, time: (Mgh, Msb:) he entered upon the last part of the day: (M, K:) he entered upon the time when the sun had declined: (Mohammad Ibn-Kaab, T:) and he entered upon the cool season, at the end of the summer.
sourceDefinition: He entered upon a cold, or cool, time: (Mgh, Msb:) he entered upon the last part of the day: (M, K:) he entered upon the time when the sun had declined: (Mohammad Ibn-Kaab, T:) and he entered upon the cool season, at the end of the summer. (M, and L in art. fyH .) ― -b2- Abrdlahu He gave him to drink what was cold, or cool. (M, K.) You say also, saqayotuhu faA^aboradotu lahu , meaning I gave him to drink what was cold, or cool. definition: A kind of garment;
sourceDefinition: A kind of garment; (S;) a kind of striped garment: (M, K:) accord. to some, of the description termed wa$oYN [or variegated ]: (M:) or particular kinds thereof are distinguished by such terms as burodu EaSobK and burodu wa $oYK : (Msb:) also, (as a coll. gen. n., TA,) garments of the kind called A^akosiyapN , [pl. of kisaA='N ,] which are wrapped round the body; (K;) one of which is called ↓ burodapN : (M, K:) or, as Lth says, the burod is [ a ] well-known [ garment ], of the kind called buruwdu AlEaSobi and buruwdu Alwa$oYi ; (T;) but the ↓ burodapN is a garment of the kind called kisaA='N , four-sided, black, and somewhat small, worn by the Arabs of the desert: (T, S, Mgh, * Msb, * TA:) or this latter (the brdp ) is a striped garment of the kind called $amolapN : (T:) or it is an oblong piece of woollen cloth, fringed: (M:) Sh says, I saw an Arab of the desert wearing a piece of woollen cloth resembling a napkin, wrapped round the body like an apron; and on my saying to him, What dost thou call it? he answered, burodap : (T:) [the modern brdp , in every case in which I have seen it, I have observed to be an oblong piece of thick woollen cloth, generally brown or of a dark or ashy dust-colour, and either plain, or having stripes so narrow and near together as to appear, at a little distance, of one colour; used both to envelop the person by day and as a night-covering: the brdp of Mohammad is described as about seven feet and a half in length, and four and a half in width, and in colour either A^axoDar or A^aHomar , i. e. of a dark or ashy dust-colour or brown; for such are the significations of these two epithets when applied to a garment of this kind, and in some other cases:] the pl. of burodN is A^aborudN (M, K) and A^aboraAdN [both pls. of pauc.] and buruwdN (S, M, K) and buradN , (IAar, T,) or this last is pl. of burodapN , (S, M,) and biraAdN , like as qiraATN is pl. of quroTN , or this, also, is pl. of burodapN , like as biraAmN is pl. of buromapN . (M.) ― -b2- *uwburodK , as opposed to *uw kisaA='i , means (assumed tropical:) A rich man. (S in art. Ej .) ― -b3- waqaEa bayonuhumaA qad~u buruwdK yumonapK , (so in copies of the K, in the TA yumanapK ,) or buruwdK vamiynapK , (so in a copy of the A,) (tropical:) [ There happened between them two the rending of buruwd of the fabric of El-Yemen, accord. to the reading in the K, or of costly buruwd , accord. to the reading in the A,] means they arrived at a great, or severe, state of affairs; (K;) or is said of two men who have contended together in vehement altercation so that they have rent each other's garments; (A;) [accord. to the reading in the K,] because yumanN , [in the CK yumon ,] which are buruwd of El-Yemen, are not rent save on account of some great, or severe, thing, or affair. (K.) ― -b4- ↓ humaA fiY burodapi A^axomaAsK means (assumed tropical:) They two do one deed; or act alike; (IAar, M, K;) and resemble each other, as though they were in one burodap : (IAar, M:) or they two have become near together, and in a state of agreement. (K in art. xms , q. v.) ― -b5- And ↓ salaba AlS~ahobaA='a burodatahaA (tropical:) He, or it, deprived the wine of its colour. definition: A well-known kind of plant, (S, M, * K,) of which the kind of paper termed qiroTaAs is made;
sourceDefinition: A well-known kind of plant, (S, M, * K,) of which the kind of paper termed qiroTaAs is made; (TA in art. qrTs , q. v. ;) [namely, papyrus; and] of which mats are made; (Msb;) [app. meaning rushes in general: but the former is generally meant by it in the present day, and is probably the proper signification: anciently, mats, as well as ropes and sails &c., were made of the rind of the papyrus; and even small boats were constructed of its stalks bound together; and of such, probably, was the ark in which the infant Moses was exposed: it is a coll. gen. n.:] n. un. barodiy~apN . (M, TA.) Hence, qaTonu AlbarodiY~ The cotton of the papyrus, which, resembling wool, is gathered from the stalk, and, mixed with lime, composes a very tenacious kind of cement. (Golius, from Ibn-Maaroof.) ― -b2- [Also, a rel. n. from the same, meaning Of, or belonging to, or resembling, the plant so called. Hence the saying,] lahaA saAqN barodiy~apN [ She has a shank like a papyrus-stalk ]. (A.)

definition: -A2- Also A mule appointed [ for the conveyance of messengers ] in a ribaAT [or public building for the accommodation of travellers and their beasts, or in a sik~ap , which is a house or the like...
sourceDefinition: : see baruwdN . -A2- Also A mule appointed [ for the conveyance of messengers ] in a ribaAT [or public building for the accommodation of travellers and their beasts, or in a sik~ap , which is a house or the like specially appropriated to messengers and the beasts that carry them: thus it signifies a postmule: afterwards, it was applied also to a posthorse, and any beast appointed for the conveyance of messengers ]: (Mgh:) [this is what is meant by the words in the S and K, Albariydu Almurat~abu :] it is a word of Persian origin, (Z in the Fáïk,) arabicized, from buriydaho dumo , (Z in the Fáïk, and Mgh,) i. e. “docked,” or “having the tail cut off;” for the post-mules ( bigaAlu Albariydi ) had their tails cut off in order that they might be known: (Z in the Fáïk:) [or perhaps it is from the Hebrew פֶּרֶד “a mule:”] or it is applied to the beast appointed for the conveyance of messengers ( daAb~apu Albariydi ) because he traverses the space called bariyd [defined below: but the reason before given for this appellation is more probable: it is like the Lat. “veredus”]: (T, Msb:) pl. burudN (Z, Mgh, Msb) and burodN , which is a contraction of the former, like as rusolN is of rusulN . (Z.) You say, Humila fulaAnN EalaY Albariyid [ Such a one was borne on the postmule or post-horse ]. (S.) Imra-el-Keys speaks of a bryd of the horses of Barbar. (S.) ― -b2- Having been originally used in the sense first explained above, it was afterwards applied to A messenger borne on a post-mule [or post-horse ]: (Z in the Fáïk, and Mgh:) or messengers on beasts of the post: (M, K:) or a messenger that journeys with haste: (A:) or [simply] a messenger: (S, Msb, K:) pl. as above. (M, * Z.) Hence the saying, AlHum~aY bariydu Almawoti Fever is the messenger of death: (T, Msb:) because it gives warning thereof. (T.) Hence also Albariydu applied to The animal called AlfuraAniqu , (said to be the jackal, but some say otherwise, TA,) because he gives warning before [the approach of] the lion. (T, S, K.) And SaAHibu Albariyid [ The master of the messengers that journey on post-mules or post-horses ]. (S.) [And xayolN Albariyid , occurring in many histories &c., The post-horses, that carry messengers and others. ] ― -b3- Also, having been applied to a messenger on a post-mule [or post-horse], it then became applied to The space, or distance, traversed by the messenger thus called; (Mgh, Msb; *) the space, or distance, between each sik~ap and the sik~ap next to it; the sk~p being a structure of either of the kinds called bayot and qub~ap , or a ribaAT [explained above], in which the appointed messengers lodge; (Z in the Fáïk;) the space, or distance, between two stations, or places of alighting; or two parasangs, or leagues; (M, K;) [ six miles; ] each parasang, or league, being three miles, and each mile being four thousand cubits: (TA:) or twelve miles; (S, A, Msb, K;) i. e. four parasangs, or leagues: (Mgh, TA:) [for] the space, or distance, between each station termed sik~ap and the next to it is either two parasangs or four: (Z in the Fáïk:) the distance of twelve miles is [also] termed sik~apu Albariyid : (T:) the pl. is as above. (T, Z.) A journey of four burud , or forty-eight miles, renders it allowable to shorten prayers; which miles are of the Háshimee measure, such as are measured on the road to Mekkeh. (T.) ― -b4- Also The course, or pace, of a camel along the space thus called: so in the following verse of Muzarrid, in praise of 'Arábeh El-Owsee: fadatoka EaraAba Alyawoma A^um~iY wa xaAlatiY wa naAqatiYa Aln~aAjiY A_ilayoka bariyduhaA [ May my mother, and my maternal aunt, and my she-camel that is swift in her course to thee from one station to another, be ransoms for thee, O 'Arábeh, (the name being contracted,) this day! ]. (S.)

rawSourceText: : see baruwdN . -A2- Also A mule appointed [ for the conveyance of messengers ] in a ribaAT [or public building for the accommodation of travellers and their beasts, or in a sik~ap , which is a house or the like specially appropriated to messengers and the beasts that carry them: thus it signifies a postmule: afterwards, it was applied also to a posthorse, and any beast appointed for the conveyance of messengers ]: (Mgh:) [this is what is meant by the words in the S and K, Albariydu Almurat~abu :] it is a word of Persian origin, (Z in the Fáïk,) arabicized, from buriydaho dumo , (Z in the Fáïk, and Mgh,) i. e. “docked,” or “having the tail cut off;” for the post-mules ( bigaAlu Albariydi ) had their tails cut off in order that they might be known: (Z in the Fáïk:) [or perhaps it is from the Hebrew פֶּרֶד “a mule:”] or it is applied to the beast appointed for the conveyance of messengers ( daAb~apu Albariydi ) because he traverses the space called bariyd [defined below: but the reason before given for this appellation is more probable: it is like the Lat. “veredus”]: (T, Msb:) pl. burudN (Z, Mgh, Msb) and burodN , which is a contraction of the former, like as rusolN is of rusulN . (Z.) You say, Humila fulaAnN EalaY Albariyid [ Such a one was borne on the postmule or post-horse ]. (S.) Imra-el-Keys speaks of a bryd of the horses of Barbar. (S.) ― -b2- Having been originally used in the sense first explained above, it was afterwards applied to A messenger borne on a post-mule [or post-horse ]: (Z in the Fáïk, and Mgh:) or messengers on beasts of the post: (M, K:) or a messenger that journeys with haste: (A:) or [simply] a messenger: (S, Msb, K:) pl. as above. (M, * Z.) Hence the saying, AlHum~aY bariydu Almawoti Fever is the messenger of death: (T, Msb:) because it gives warning thereof. (T.) Hence also Albariydu applied to The animal called AlfuraAniqu , (said to be the jackal, but some say otherwise, TA,) because he gives warning before [the approach of] the lion. (T, S, K.) And SaAHibu Albariyid [ The master of the messengers that journey on post-mules or post-horses ]. (S.) [And xayolN Albariyid , occurring in many histories &c., The post-horses, that carry messengers and others. ] ― -b3- Also, having been applied to a messenger on a post-mule [or post-horse], it then became applied to The space, or distance, traversed by the messenger thus called; (Mgh, Msb; *) the space, or distance, between each sik~ap and the sik~ap next to it; the sk~p being a structure of either of the kinds called bayot and qub~ap , or a ribaAT [explained above], in which the appointed messengers lodge; (Z in the Fáïk;) the space, or distance, between two stations, or places of alighting; or two parasangs, or leagues; (M, K;) [ six miles; ] each parasang, or league, being three miles, and each mile being four thousand cubits: (TA:) or twelve miles; (S, A, Msb, K;) i. e. four parasangs, or leagues: (Mgh, TA:) [for] the space, or distance, between each station termed sik~ap and the next to it is either two parasangs or four: (Z in the Fáïk:) the distance of twelve miles is [also] termed sik~apu Albariyid : (T:) the pl. is as above. sourceDefinition: , [inf. n. baEovarapN ,] He took, drew, or pulled, a thing out, or forth, and uncovered it, laid it open, or exposed it; (S, K;) as also baHovara : (S:) he raised what was in a thing, (S, K,) and caused it to come forth. (S.) Hence, in the Kur [c. 9], A_i*aA buEovira maA fiY A@loqubuwri When that which is in the graves is raised, and caused to come forth: (AO, S:) [see also baHovara :] or the meaning is, when the dust, or earth, in the graves is turned over, and the dead in them are raised: (Zj:) or when what is in the graves, of gold and silver, comes forth; after which the dead are to come forth. (Fr.) ― -b2- Also He examined; he searched. (K.) ― -b3- He searched for, or after, or into, news, or tidings. (TA.) ― -b4- He scattered, or dispersed, a thing, and turned it over, one part upon another: (K:) he scattered, or dispersed, his household goods, or his commodities, (Fr, S,) and turned them over, one upon another; (Fr, Zj, S;) as also baHovara , (Fr, S,) and bagovara . (Yaakoob.) ― -b5- He demolished a watering-trough or tank, and turned it upside-down. (AO, S, K.)

sourceDefinition: and baAqilaA='N , (JK, S, Mgh, Msb, K,) the former with teshdeed and the latter without tesh-deed, (S, Mgh, Msb,) and baAqlFY , (K,) [every one with tenween when it has not the article Al , for] the n. un. is with p , (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) i. e. baAqil~aApN and baqilaA='apN (S, Mgh, Msb) [and baqilaApN ] or the sing. and pl. are alike, (El-Ahmar, K,) [and if so, the word may be fem., as Ibn-Buzurj, cited in the TA voce hinodabN , asserts baqilaA=' to be, and therefore in every case without tenween,] i. q. fuwlN [ Beans; or the bean; faba sativa of Jussieu; vicia faba of Linnæus]; (JK, K;) a name of the dial. of the Sawád [of El-'Irák]; its produce is called Aljirojiru ; (TA; [but see jarojiyrN ; and see turomusN ;]) [or it is applied to the plant and to its produce;] a certain well-known Hab~ [or grain ]: (Mgh:) the eating of it produces exhalations (K) of a gross kind, (TA,) and bad dreams, and sadar , (K,) i. e. vertigo, (TA,) and anxiety, and gross humours; but it is good for the cough, and for rendering the body fruitful ( taxoSiyb Albadan ); when properly qualified [app. by seasoning or by some admixture ] ( A_i*aA A^uSoliHa ), it preserves the health; and in its green state, together with ginger, it has the utmost effect in strengthening the venereal faculty: (K:) the pl. is bawaAqilu : and the dim. of bAq~lY is ↓ buwayoqilapN and ↓ buwayoqiloyapN , the latter with the l quiescent because kesreh is disapproved in so long a word; [both forms indicating that bAql~Y is held to be fem.;] and that of bAqlA=' is buwayoqilaA=' [with or without tenween accord. as it is held to be masc. or fem.], or, if one will, he [who holds bAqlA=' to be fem.] may say ↓ buwayoqlapN , suppressing the augmentative meddeh, and adding p to indicate the fem. gender; and that of bAql~Ap is ↓ buwayoqilaApN . (TA.) ― -b2- AlbaAqil~aY AlqboTiY~u [app. the same as AlbAq~lY AlmiSoriY~u mentioned in the K voce turomusN , &c., i. e. The Egyptian bean; an appellation said to be applied by some in the present day to the colocasia; but what it properly denotes is doubtful;] a certain plant, the grain of which is smaller than the fuwl [or bean ]: (K:) the people of Egypt know it by the name of AljaAmisap , with jym , and with the unpointed syn : he who says that it is the turomus is in error. (Ibn-Beytár, cited by De Sacy in his “ Relation de l'Égypte par Abd-allatif, ” q. v., p. 97.)

definition: , originally bawabN , (M, Msb,) A door;
sourceDefinition: , originally bawabN , (M, Msb,) A door; a gate; a place of entrance: and the thing with which a place of entrance, such as a door or gate, is closed; of wood &c.: (MF, TA:) pl. A^abowaAbN (S, M, Msb, K) and biybaAnN (M, K) and A^abowibapN , (S, M, K,) [a pl. of pauc., said to be] only used for conformity with another word mentioned therewith, as in the saying (of Ibn-Mukbil, so in a copy of the S), hat~aAku A^axobiyapK wa l~aAju A^abowibapK [ A frequent render of tents, a frequent enterer of doors ], (S, M,) not being allowable when occurring alone; (S;) but IAar and Lh assert that it is a pl. of bAb without its being used for conformity with another word; (M;) and this is extr.; (M, K;) for bAb is of the measure faEalN , and a word of this measure has not a pl. of the measure A^afoEilapN [by rule]. (M.) You say, baAbN Ald~aAri [ The door of the house ]; and baAbu Albayoti [ the door of the house, and of the chamber, and of the tent ]; (Msb;) and baAbu Albaladi [ the gate of the town or city ]. (The Lexicons &c. passim.) And Bishr Ibn-Abee-Házim assigns a bAb to a grave; calling the latter a bayot . (M.) It is also applied to an opening, or a channel, made for water, to irrigate seed-produce: pl. A^abowaAbN . (Mgh.) [And in Egypt, it is applied also to A sepulchral chamber, grotto, or cave, hewn in a mountain; from the Coptic βηβ : pl. biybaAnN only.] ― -b2- Hence, i. e. in a secondary application, the primary signification being “ a place of entrance, ” it is used as meaning (tropical:) A means of access, or of attainment, to a thing: (B, Kull, TK:) as in the saying, h`*aA AlEilomu baAbN A_ilaY Eilomi ka*aA (tropical:) This science is a means of attainment to such a science. (B, TK.) ― -b3- [And hence, (assumed tropical:) An expedient, a trick, a stratagem, or a process, by which something is to be effected pl. A^abowaAbN : as in A^abowaAbu AlHarobi the expedients. &c. of war, battle, or fight; and baAbN mina Aln~ujuwmi a process of the science of the stars, meaning astrology or astronomy; and baAbN mina Als~iHori a process of enchantment; see an ex. voce siHorN . Compare Matt. xvi. 18, πύλαι ᾅδου οὐ κατισχύσουσιν αύτης , probably meaning “ the stratagems of Hell shall not prevail against it. ”] ― -b4- [Also (assumed tropical:) A mode, kind, sort, class, or category. ] Suweyd Ibn-Kuráa uses metaphorically the pl. A^abowaAb in relation to rhymes; saying, A^atayotu biA^abowaAbi AlqawaAfiY kaA^an~amaA A^a*uwdu bihaA sirobFA mina AlwaHo$i nuz~aEaA (tropical:) [ I gave utterance to the various kinds of rhymes as though I were driving with them a herd of wild animals desirous of the males, or of their wonted places of pasture ]. (M, L.) [You say also, huwa mino h`*aA AlbaAbi (assumed tropical:) It is of this mode, kind, sort, class, or category: a phrase of frequent occurrence in lexicons &c. See also baAbapN .] ― -b5- [Also (assumed tropical:) A chapter; and sometimes a section, or subdivision, of a chapter; of a book or writing;] conventionally, (assumed tropical:) a piece consisting of words relating to matters of one kind; and sometimes, to matters of one species: (Kull:) pl. A^abowaAbN . (A.) See also baAbapN . ― -b6- [Also (assumed tropical:) A head, or class of items or articles, in an account, or a reckoning; as in the saying,] bay~anotu lahu HisaAbahu baAbFA baAbFA (assumed tropical:) [ I explained, or made clear, to him his account, or reckoning, head by head, or each class of items or articles by itself ]; a phrase mentioned by Sb: (M:) [or, sometimes,] baAbN (M, K) and ↓ baAbapN (T, M, K) are used in relation to Huduwd [which here means the punishments so termed], and to an account, or a reckoning, (T, M, K,) and the like, (T, M,) as signifying the extreme term or limit; syn. gaAyapN ; (M, K;) but IDrd hesitated respecting this, and therefore it is not mentioned in the S. (TA.)

definition: (assumed tropical:) A mode, or manner;
sourceDefinition: (assumed tropical:) A mode, or manner; syn. wajohN : (ISk, K:) pl. baAbaAtN . (K.) [See also baAbN , which has a similar, and perhaps the same, signification.] Hence, h`*aA mino baAbatiY means (assumed tropical:) This is of the mode, or manner, that I desire; (TA;) this is suitable to me: (IAmb, TA:) and h`*aA $aYo'N mino baAbatika , (S,) or h`*aA baAbatuka , (A,) (assumed tropical:) this is a thing suitable to thee: (S, A:) and h`*aA baAbatuhu (assumed tropical:) this is suitable to him. (K.) Accord. to most of the critics, it is tropical. (TA.) (TA.)

sourceDefinition: [The fox; canis vulpes of Linn.: but in the dial. of Egypt, the jackal; canis aureus of Linn.: the former animal being there called A^abuw AlHuSayoni , as it often is by the Arabs of other countries:] a certain beast of prey; (TA;) well known: (S, K:) applied to the male and the female; so that one says vaEolabN *akarN and vaEolabN A^unovaY ; but if one would designate the male by a single word applying to it only, he says ↓ vuEolubaAnN , with damm to the v and l : (IAmb, Msb:) or the former applies to the female: (K:) or the female is called ↓ vaEolabapN ; (Ks, S, Msb, K;) and the male, ↓ vuEolubaAnN (Ks, S, K) and vaEolabN , (K,) [accord. to some,] like as one says EaqorabapN [and EuqorubaAnN ] and EaqorabN : (Msb:) or vaEolabN is the male; and the female is called ↓ vuEaAlapu : (Az, TA: [but see this word is art. vEl :]) the pl. of vElb is vaEaAlibu and vaEaAlK , (K,) accord. to Lh: but ISd disapproves of this [latter pl.]; and Sb does not allow it except in poetry. (TA.) F charges J with error in citing, as a proof that ↓ vuEolubaAnN signifies the male, the following verse: A^arab~N yabuwlu Alv~uEolubaAnu biraA^osihi laqado *al~a mano baAlato Ealayohi Alv~aEaAlibu [ Is he a Lord, upon whose head the he-fox makes water? (the b in brA^sh being syn. with EalaY : so in the Mughnee, in art. b :) Vile indeed is he upon whom the foxes make water! ] said by a man who was keeper of an idol, on seeing a he-fox make water upon it: but in this, F opposes also Ks and others; and it is asserted by several authorities that the correct reading of the word vElbAn in a trad. whereby F attempts to establish his charge against J is not vaEolabaAni , dual. of vaEolabN , as he pronounces it to be, but vuEolabaAni , which is said to be the masc. of vaEolabN , like as A^ufoEuwaAnN and EuqorubaAnN are mascs. of A^afoEFY and EaqorabN . (TA.) ― -b2- daA='u Alv~aEolabi [for which Golius seems to have found in a copy of the K dawaA='u Alv~aEolabi ] A well-known disease, [namely, alopecia, ] (S, K,) in consequence of which the hair falls off. (S.) ― -b3- Einabu Alv~aEolabi [ Fox-grape: rendered by Golius “ uvæ vulpinæ, i. e. solanum: ” but now applied by some to the gooseberry: and the solanum nigrum, or gardennightshade, is now commonly called Einabu Al*~iy^obi :] a certain astringent, cooling plant: seven (or, as in one copy of the K, nine ) Hab~aAt [which here seems to mean berries] thereof, swallowed, are a cure for the jaundice ( AlyaraqaAn ), and stop pregnancy, (K, TA,) like the berries of the xirowaE [or castor-oil-plant], for the year, or, as some say, absolutely. (TA.) -A2- A hole, or aperture, ( juHor ,) whence rain-water flows. (TA.) [And particularly,] The outlet, hole, or aperture, ( maxoraj , S and Msb, or juHor , K, or vaqob , TA,) whence the rain-water flows from the place where dates are dried. (S, Msb, K, TA.) And The place whence the water flows forth (L, K) from, (L, TA,) or to, (K, [probably a mistake,]) a watering-trough or tank. (L, K.) -A3- The upper extremity of a spear-shaft that enters into the head thereof. (S, K.) ― -b2- The lowest part of a palm-shoot when it is cut from [the root of] the mother-tree: or the lowest part of a [shoot such as is termed ] rAkuwb , on the trunk of a palm-tree. (AA, K.)

(TA.) ― -b6- vulija fuw^aAduhu (tropical:) He was, or became, stupid, dull, wanting in intelligence: (IAar, A, TA:) his heart, or his mind, or intellect, quitted him. definition: The mounting a fornicator, or an adulterer, upon an ass, and turning his face towards the tail;
sourceDefinition: The mounting a fornicator, or an adulterer, upon an ass, and turning his face towards the tail; whence the trad. of the Jews respecting the adulterer, yuHum~amu wayujab~ahu wyujoladu [ He shall have his face blackened with charcoal, and be mounted on an ass with his face towards the tail, and be flogged ]: (Mgh:) or the mounting two fornicators, or adulterers, upon an ass, and turning the backs of their heads towards each other, (JK, Mgh,) and parading them round about; thus accord. to the Tekmileh: (Mgh:) or the blackening [with charcoal] the faces of two fornicators, or adulterers, ( A^ano yuHam~ara in the K being a mistake for A^ano yuHum~ama , i. e. yusaw~ada , TA,) and mounting them upon a camel or an ass, and turning their faces in contrary directions: accord. to analogy, it should mean turning their faces towards each other; for it is from Aljabotapu : tajobiyhN also signifies the bending, inclining, lowering, or hanging down, the head towards the ground: and it may be hence; (i. e. it may be hence that it is applied to him who is mounted on a beast in the manner described above; TA;) because he to whom this is done bends down his head in shame and confusion: or it may be from jabahahu meaning "he did to him a thing disliked, or hated." (K.)

definition: [The forehead; ] the part of the face which is the place of prostration: (As, Msb, K:) or the even part that is between the eyebrows and the naASiyap [or place where the hair grows in the fore part...
sourceDefinition: [The forehead; ] the part of the face which is the place of prostration: (As, Msb, K:) or the even part that is between the eyebrows and the naASiyap [or place where the hair grows in the fore part of the head ]: (Kh, JK, Msb, K:) so of a man, (S, Msb,) and of others: (S:) [or,] of a horse, the part that is below the ears and above the eyes: (TA:) pl. jibaAhN . (Msb, TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] Aljabohapu (assumed tropical:) A certain Mansion of the Moon; [the Tenth Mansion; ] (S, K, Kzw;) consisting of four stars; (S;) the four stars [ ζ , γ , η , and α,] in the neck and heart of Leo; [regarded by the Arabs as the fore-part, or forehead, of Leo; ] (Kzw in his descr. of Leo;) between each of which and the next to it is the space of a whip's length; the northernmost of them called by astrologers AlA^asadu . (Kzw in his descr. of the Mansions of the Moon.) ― -b3- Also (assumed tropical:) The moon (K, TA) itself: but [it rather seems to mean the upper part of the disc of the moon; for] it is said in the M that a certain unknown poet has metaphorically assigned a jbhp to the moon. (TA.) ― -b4- Also jabohapN , (tropical:) The chief of a people, or company of men; (JK, Mgh, K, TA;) like as one says the wajoh thereof. (Mgh, TA.) ― -b5- (tropical:) The generous and manly, or manly and noble, persons of a people, or company of men: or men exerting themselves in the case of a bloodwit or a debt or other obligation, (K, TA,) or in repairing the condition of a poor man, (TA,) and who come not to any one but he is ashamed to turn them back, (K, TA,) or who are seldom or never turned back by anyone: so, accord. to Aboo-Sa'eed, in a trad. in which it is said that there shall be no poor-rate in the case of the jbhp . (TA.) ― -b6- (tropical:) A company, or collected number, of men, (JK, S, Msb,) and of horses: (JK, Msb:) or, of horses, the best: (TA:) and [simply] horses; (Lth, S, M, Mgh, K;) a word having no sing., or n. un.: (M, K:) accord. to Lth, (TA,) having this last meaning in the trad. above mentioned; (S, Mgh, TA;) because horses are the best of beasts. (Mgh.) -A2- (tropical:) Abjectness, or ignominy; (JK, M, K, TA;) and a state of annoyance, or molestation: (Z, TA:) thought by ISd to be from jabahahu meaning “ he encountered him with that which he disliked or hated, ” or “ he accused him thereof to his face; ” because the doing this causes one to experience abjectness, or ignominy. (TA.) It is said to have this meaning in a trad., in which it is said, faA_in~a A@ll~`ha qado A^araAHakumo mina Aljabohapi wAls~aj~api wAlbaj~api , i. e. For God hath relieved you from abjectness, or ignominy, &c., and milk diluted with water, and blood drawn from a vein [ of a camel ], which the Arabs used to eat: or in this trad., (TA,) Aljabotahapu is the name of a certain idol (ISd, K, TA) that was worshipped in the Time of Ignorance: (TA:) and Alsj~p and Albj~p were two idols. (S and K in art. sj .)

definition: Drought, barrenness, or dearth;
sourceDefinition: Drought, barrenness, or dearth; contr. of xiSobN ; (S;) i. q. maHolN , (A, Msb, K,) i. e. drought, or suspension of rain, and dryness of the earth; (Msb;) dryness and barrenness of the earth: (Har p. 576:) and ↓ jidab~N is a name, or subst., for AljadobN , (K, TA,) meaning AlmaHolu ; as in the saying of the rájiz, cited by Sb, laqado xa$iytu A^ano A^araY jidab~aA fiY EaAminaA baEoda maA A^axoSab~aA [ Verily I feared to see drought, or barrenness, &c., in this our year, after it had been abundant in herbage ]; jidab~aA being used for AljadobaA ; or, accord. to one reading, it is ↓ jadobab~aA , with a doubled b added; the change being made for the sake of the metre. (M, TA. [Respecting A^axoSab~aA , see 4 in art. xSb .]) ― -b2- Also A place, (S, A, K,) or a country, or region, (Msb,) affected with drought, barrenness, or dearth; or with drought, and dryness of the earth; and so ↓ jadiybN (S, A, Msb, K) and ↓ jaduwbN and ↓ majoduwbN , (K,) the last derived from judiba though this verb has not been used, (TA,) and ↓ mujodibN , (M, A,) of which the pl. is majaAdiybu . (A.) You say also A^aroDN jadobN [in which jdb is an inf. n. (though app. obsolete as such) and therefore applicable to a fem. subst.] (ISd, TA) and jadobapN (S, A, Msb, K) and ↓ jadibapN (A, Msb) and ↓ jadiybN (Msb) and ↓ jaduwbN (Lh, M, Msb) and ↓ mujodibapN , of which last the pl. is majaAdiybu , (Msb,) A land affected with drought, &c.: (S, M, A, &c.:) and A^aroDuwna juduwbN , (S, K,) as though to each part were applied the term jadobN [used as a subst.] from which is formed the pl. juduwbN , (TA,) and jadobN , (K,) which is here an inf. n. used as an epithet [and therefore applicable to a pl. subst.], (TA,) lands affected with drought, &c. (S, K.) And ↓ falaApN jadobaA='u [fem. of A^ajodabu ] (M, K) A desert affected with drought, &c.; (K;) in which is neither little nor much, neither pasture nor herbage. (M, TA.) And ↓ fulaAnN jadiybu AljanaAbi Such a one is environed by a tract affected with drought, &c. (S. [But this phrase is generally used tropically, as meaning (assumed tropical:) Such a one is ungenerous or illiberal or inhospitable. See art. jnb .]) And sanapN jadobapN (K in art. jrz ) and EaAmN ↓ jaduwbN (M, TA) [ A year of drought, &c.]. See also A^ajaAdibu , in two places. -A2- Also i. q. EayobN [ A vice, fault, defect, &c.]; (S, A, K;) a signification which may be either proper or tropical. (Er-Rághib, MF.)

definition: A place of seed-produce;
sourceDefinition: A place of seed-produce; (S, K;) as also ↓ jariybN : (K:) and a tract of land such as is termed qaraAH [i. e. a field, or land, sown or for sowing, without any building or trees in it; or land cleared for sowing and planting; or a separate piece of land in which palm-trees &c. grow; &c.]: (K:) metaphorically applied by Imra-el-Keys to [ a grove of] palm-trees, where he says kajirobapi naxolK A^awo kajan~api yavoriba [ Like a grove of palm-trees, or like the plantation of Yethrib ]: (AHn, TA:) or land prepared for sowing or planting: (AHn, K:) or a piece of land differing in condition from the land adjoining it, [i. e. a patch of land, ] producing good plants or herbage: (Lth, TA:) the pl. [or rather coll. gen. n.] is ↓ jirobN , (Lth, AHn,) like as tibonN is of tibonapN , and sidorN of sidorapN : (AHn:) or jirobN signifies a qaraAH ; and its pl. is jirabapN . (IAar, TA.) ― -b2- A skin, or a mat, which is placed upon the brink of a well, lest the water should be scattered into the well [app. in falling from the bucket into the channel of the tank or cistern &c.]: or ( a skin, TA,) that is placed in a rivulet or streamlet jadowal [which is applied in the present day to an artificial streamlet for irrigation, in the form of a trench or gutter,]) that the water may flow down over it [app. from the well to the tank or cistern &c.]. (M, K.)

(MF, TA.) For the pl., see what follows. ― -b2- Hence, (Mgh,) (assumed tropical:) A certain quantity of land; (S, Mgh, Msb;) as much as is sown with the measure of seed so called; (A, Mgh;) like as mules and the space that they travel are termed bariydN : (A, Mgh: *) it is sixty cubits by sixty cubits; accord. to Kudámeh, the extent termed A^a$ol multiplied by itself; the A$l being sixty cubits; the cubit being six qabaDaAt ; and the qaboDap , four A^aSaAbiE : the tenth part of the jryb is called qfyz , and the tenth of the qfyz is called E$yr ; so that the qfyz is ten AE$rA' : (Mgh:) it is a distinct portion of land, differing according to the different conventional usages of the people of different provinces: it is said that the width of six moderate-sized barleycorns is called A_iSobaEN ; the qbDp is four ASAbE ; the *iraAE is six qbDAt ; ten A^a*oruE are called qaSabapN ; ten qaSabaAt are called A$l ; and the jryb is the extent termed A$l multiplied by itself: the A$l multiplied by the qSbp is called qfyz ; and the A$l multiplied by the *rAE is called E$yr : so the jiryb is ten thousand cubits: or, accord. to Kudámeh the Scribe, it is three thousand and six hundred cubits: (Msb:) pl. [of pauc.] A^ajoribapN and [of mult.] jurobaAnN (S, Msb, K) and juruwbN . (R, TA.) sourceDefinition: A man who has his camels affected with what is termed jarab [i. e. the mange, or scab ]: whence the prov., laA A_ilaAha limujoribK [ There is no god to one who has his camels affected with the mange ]; as though he renounced his god by frequently swearing falsely by him that he had no pitch when it was demanded of him [for the purpose of curing other camels]: (A:) or laA A^aliy~apa limojoribK [ There is no oath to one who has his camels affected with the mange; for the reason above mentioned, or because he is likely to deny that he has mangy camels lest his camels should be prevented from coming to water: and hence also,] A^akodabu mino mujoribK [ More lying than one who has his camels affected with the mange ]; another prov. (Meyd. [See Freytag's Arab. Prov., ii. 382.])

definition: One who has been tried, or proved, in affairs, and whose qualities have become known: (T, TA:) or one who has been tried, or proved, and strengthened by experience in affairs: (S:) [ experienced, or...
sourceDefinition: One who has been tried, or proved, in affairs, and whose qualities have become known: (T, TA:) or one who has been tried, or proved, and strengthened by experience in affairs: (S:) [ experienced, or expert, in affairs: ] or one whose qualities have been tried, or proved. (K, TA.) And ↓ mujar~ibN One having experience in affairs. (K, TA.) In general, but not always, (MF,) the Arabs used the former of these two epithets [which are virtually synonymous]. (S, MF.) ― -b2- daraAhimu mujar~abapN Weighed money. (Kr, K.) ― -b3- Almujar~abu The lion. (Sgh, K.) -A2- [It is also employed as an inf. n. of 2, in accordance with a usage of which there are many other instances; as in the saying,] A^anota EalaY Almujar~abi [ Thou art about to have the proof, or experience ]: a prov., mentioned by AZ: said to him who asks respecting a thing which he is about to know of himself: originally said by a woman to a man who asked her an indecent question which he was himself about to resolve. (TA.)

definition: (S, M, MA, Mgh, K) and juwaAliqN (IAar, M, K) and jiwaAliqN (K) A sack;
sourceDefinition: (S, M, MA, Mgh, K) and juwaAliqN (IAar, M, K) and jiwaAliqN (K) A sack; in Pers. juwaAlo ; (MA, PS;) [not so well rendered in the KL by xurojiyno , which means a saddle-bag or a pair of saddle-bags, like the Arabic xurojN ;] a certain kind of wiEaA='i [or receptacle ], (S, M, K,) [ for corn &c., ] well known: (M, K:) it has a loop, into which is inserted a stick, or piece of wood, called $iZaAZN , (S and K in art. $Z ,) this being also inserted into the loop of another jwAlq , when they are bound upon the camel: (K * and TA in that art.:) or it has two loops, one of which is inserted into the other, (S and K voce qaTaba ,) [ and then the stick is put through, ] on the occasion of putting it on a camel: (TA ibid.:) the word is arabicized; (M, TA;) said to be from kwAlh , (TA,) or kwAlk , (KL,) but correctly from JwAlh , which is Pers.: (TA:) the pl. is jawaAliqu (S, MA, Mgh, K) and jawaAliyqu , (Sb, S, MA, Mgh, K,) the latter occurring in poetry, (TA,) and juwaAliqaAtN (S, K) was sometimes used, (S,) but this is disallowed by Sb. (S, M.) The saying [of a rájiz], cited by Th, A^uHib~u maAwiy~apa Hub~FA SaAdiqaA Hub~a A^abiY AljuwaAliqi AljuwaAliqaA [ I love Máweeyeh with a true love; with the love of the owner (lit. father ) of the sack for the sack; ] means that the speaker had a vehement love for the food, or wheat, that was in his jwAlq . (M.) definition: (S, K) and ↓ jum~ayozaY (K) [The sycamorefig: and the sycamore fig-tree: ficus sycomorus;
sourceDefinition: (S, K) and ↓ jum~ayozaY (K) [The sycamorefig: and the sycamore fig-tree: ficus sycomorus; also called the Egyptian fig: ] the male fig; (K, TA;) which is found in the Ghowr, or Ghór, [here meaning the Valley of the Jordan, ] (TA,) and is sweet: (K, TA:) this is the yellow: the black makes the mouth bleed: (TA:) it is of various colours, or kinds, ( A^alowaAn ,) (K, * TA;) abundant in Syria and in Egypt: n. un. jum~ayozapN : (TA:) [ a fruit ] resembling the tiyn [or common fig ]: (S:) AHn says, of the kinds of fig is the fig of the jum~ayoz , a sweet, moist fig, which has long fruit-stalks, and which is dried in the sun: and there is another species of the jm~yz , the fruit of which is like the fig in make, but its leaves are smaller than those of the fig, and its figs are yellow, of a small size, and black: it is found in the Ghowr, or Ghór, and is called the male fig: the yellow is sweet: the black makes the mouth bleed: and its fig has no stalk, but cleaves to the wood. ('Abd-el-Lateef, Account of Egypt: White's ed., entitled Abdollatiphi Historiæ Aegypti Compendium: p. 22. See also De Sacy's notes to his transl. of that work, pp. 82—86.) ― -b2- [ Aljum~ayozapu also signifies (assumed tropical:) The pudendum muliebre: opposed to Alt~iynapu as meaning “ the anus. ”]

definition: The air: (K:) or [the atmosphere;
sourceDefinition: The air: (K:) or [the atmosphere; i. e.] what is between the heaven, or sky, and the earth; (S, Mgh;) the air [or the region ] between the heaven, or sky, and the earth: pl. A^ajowaA='N . (TA.) fiY jaw~i Als~amaA='i , in the Kur [xvi. 81], means In the air between the heaven, or sky, and the earth: (Jel:) or in the middle of the sky: (Katádeh, TA:) or in the air that is remote from the earth. (Bd.) ― -b2- A low, or depressed, part of the ground; (M, K;) as also ↓ jaw~apN : (K:) or a wide part of a valley: (S, Msb:) pl. (in the latter sense, Msb, or in the former, K, TA) jiwaA='N (Msb, K) and [of pauc.] A^ajowiyapN . (TA.) It has the latter meaning in the saying of Tarafeh, [addressing a lark,] xalaA laki Aljaw~u fabiyDiY waA@SofiriY [ The wide part of the valley has become vacant for thee; so lay thine eggs, and whistle ]. (AA, S.) Az says, I entered, with an Arab of the desert, a [hollow place in which water collected, termed a] daHol , in El-Khalsà, and when we came to the water, he said, h`*aA jaw~N mina AlmaA'i laA yuwqafu EalaY A^aqoSaAhu [ This is an abyss of water: one knows not the utmost extent of it ]. (TA.) ― -b3- A vacant, void, or desolate, place, in which is no one to cheer by his company. (Ham p. 293.) ― -b4- The inside, or interior, of a house or tent; (K;) and of anything; of the dial. of Syria; also termed ↓ jaw~apN , (TA,) and ↓ jaw~aAniY~N ; (K; [in the CK A is erroneously put for n ;]) in which last, the A and A^uriydu jaw~FA wayuriydu bar~FA are augmentatives for the purpose of corroboration. (TA.) ― -b5- [Hence,] jaw~apN I desire concealment, or secrecy, and he desires publicity. (A in art. br .)

sourceDefinition: , inf. n. mujaAwarapN and jiwaArN (S, Msb, K) and ↓ juwaArN , (S, M, and some copies of the K,) or the last is a simple subst., (Msb,) and ↓ jawaArN , (M, and so in some copies of the K instead of juwaArN ,) of which forms the second ( jiwaArN ) is more chaste than the third (S, TA) and than the fourth, as relating to the verb in the sense here following, though some disapprove of it, and assert the third and the fourth to be more chaste; (TA;) He became his jAr [or neighbour ]; (K;) he lived in his neighbourhood, or near to him: (Msb, TA:) or he lived in a dwelling contiguous to his. (Msb.) ― -b2- Also jAwrhu , (TA,) inf. n. jiwaArN , (K,) and ↓ juwaArN is said to be a quasi-inf. n., and more chaste than jiwaArN as relating to the verb in the sense here following; (TA;) He bound himself to him by a covenant to protect him. (K, TA.) ― -b3- And jAwr ban~Y fulaAnK , and fiY bnY flAn , inf. n. majaAwarapN and jiwaArN , He protected himself by a covenant with the sons of such a one; from mujaAwarapN signifying the “ living near. ” (TA.) ― -b4- And jAwr , inf. n. mujaAwarapN , i. q. AiEotakafa fiY masojidK [ He confined himself in a mosque, or place of worship, during a period of days and nights, or at least during one whole day, fasting from daybreak to sunset, and occupying himself in prayer and religious meditation, without any interruption by affairs distracting the mind from devotion and not pressing ]. (S, K.) But jAwr bimak~apa , and biAlmadiynapi , signifies absolutely He abode in Mekkeh, and El-Medeeneh; not necessarily implying conformity with the conditions of AiEotikaAf required by the law [though generally meaning for the purpose of study: and so in the neighbourhood of the great collegiate mosque called the Azhar, in Cairo: so that the term ↓ mujaAwirN means a student of Mekkeh &c.]. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, A, &c.,) inf. n. A_ijaArapN (Mgh, K) and ↓ jaArapN , (Kr, K,) [or the latter is rather a quasi-inf. n., like TaAEapN from A^aTaAEahu ,] He protected him; granted him refuge; (K;) preserved, saved, rescued, or liberated, him; (S, A, Msb, K;) from ( mino ) wrongful, unjust, injurious, or tyrannical, treatment; (S, K;) from punishment; (S, A;) or from what he feared: (Msb:) he aided him; succoured him; delivered him from evil: the A^a having a privative effect. (Mgh.) It is said of God, yujiyru walaA yujaAru Ealayohi He protects, but none is protected against him. (TA.) And in the Kur [lxxii. 22], qulo A_in~iY lano yujiyraniY mina A@ll~`hi A^aHadN Verily none will protect me against God. (TA.) ― -b2- AjAr AlmataAEa He put the household-goods, or commodities, into the repository, (K, TA,) and so preserved them from being lost. (TA.) ― -b3- It is said [of God] in a trad., yujiyru bayona AlbuHuwri He makes a division between the seas, and prevents one from mixing with another and encroaching upon it. (TA.)

definition: A neighbour; one who lives near to another; (S, Mgh, Msb, K;) one who lives in the next tent or house: (IAar, Th, T, Msb:) pl. [of mult.] jiyraAnN (Msb, K) [and jiwaArN (a pl. not of unfrequent...
sourceDefinition: A neighbour; one who lives near to another; (S, Mgh, Msb, K;) one who lives in the next tent or house: (IAar, Th, T, Msb:) pl. [of mult.] jiyraAnN (Msb, K) [and jiwaArN (a pl. not of unfrequent occurrence, and mentioned by Freytag as used by El-Mutanebbee,)] and [of pauc.] jiyrapN and A^ajowaArN ; (K;) like qaAEN , pl. qiyEaAnN and qiyEapN and A^aqowaAEN , the only similar instance: (TA:) fem. with p . (Mgh.) AljaAru *uw AlqurobaY [in the Kur iv. 40] is The relation, or kinsman, who is abiding in one's neighbourhood: or who is abiding in one town or district or the like while thou art in another, and who has that title to respect which belongs to nearness of relationship: (TA:) or the near neighbour: (Bd, Jel:) or the near relation: (Jel:) or he who is near, and connected, by relationship or religion. (Bd.) jaAru Aljanobi : and AljaAru Aljunubu and jaAru Aljunubi : see art. jnb . jaArN nif~iyjN A stranger [ who has become one's neighbour ]. (TA.) ― -b2- A person whom one protects from wrongful, unjust, injurious, or tyrannical, treatment. (S, Mgh, Msb, K.) ― -b3- One who seeks, or asks, protection (Msb, K) of another: jaAruka signifying he who seeks thy protection. (TA.) ― -b4- A protector; (A, Mgh, Msb, K;) one who protects another from that which he fears; (Msb;) one who grants refuge, or protects, or preserves. (AHeyth.) mino *`lika AlA^amori ↓ humo jaArapN They are protectors from that thing, is a phrase mentioned by Th, respecting which ISd says, I know not how this is, unless the sing. be supposed to be originally jaAy^irN , so as to have a pl. of the measure faEalapN [as jaArapN is originally jawarapN ]. (TA.) ― -b5- An aider, or assister. (IAar, Msb, K.) ― -b6- A confederate. (IAar, Msb, K.) ― -b7- A woman's husband. (Msb, K.) ― -b8- A man's wife; (Msb;) as also ↓ jaArapN : (S, M, A, Mgh, Msb, K:) or the latter, the object of his love: (M:) and the latter also, a woman's fellow-wife; (Mgh, Msb, TA;) so called because the term Dar~apN is disliked, (Mgh, Msb,) as being of evil omen. (Mgh.) ― -b9- A partner who has not divided with his partner: so in the trad. AljaAru A^aHaq~u biSaqabihi [explained in art. Sqb ]; as is shown by another trad. (Az, Msb.) ― -b10- A partner, or sharer, (Msb, K,) in immoveable property, such as land and houses, (Msb, TA,) and in merchandise, (K, TA,) whether he divide the property with the other or not, (Msb,) or whether he be partner in the whole or only in part. (TA.) ― -b11- One who divides with another. (IAar, K.) ― -b12- (tropical:) The froj [or pudendum ] of a woman: and (tropical:) The anus; as also ↓ jaArapN . (IAar, K, TA.) ― -b13- The part (IAar, K) of the sea-shore (IAar) that is near to the places where people have alighted and taken up their abode. (IAar, K.)

definition: Death: (S, Msb, K, &c.
sourceDefinition: Death: (S, Msb, K, &c.:) pl. HutuwfN . (S, K.) You say, maAta Hatofa A^anofihi , (A 'Obeyd, S, Mgh, Msb, K,) and Hatofa fiyhi , but this is rare, and Hatofa A^anofayohi , (K,) which may mean manoxirayohi , or it may mean A^anofh wafamh , the Anf being made predominant, (TA,) He died upon his bed; (A 'Obeyd, Mgh, Msb, K;) [ a natural death; ] respiring until he yielded his last breath; (Msb;) not from slaughter, nor beating, (A 'Obeyd, S, Msb, K,) nor drowning, nor burning, (A 'Obeyd, Sgh, Msb, K,) nor by a wild beast, &c.: (A 'Obeyd, TA:) the nose is particularized as meaning that the spirit passes forth from it with the breath; or because they imagined that the spirit of the sick man passes forth from his nose, and that of the wounded man from his wound; (IAth, K;) or because the spirit passes forth from the mouth and the nose, and the latter of these is made predominant: (O, TA:) and Htf is put in the accus. case in the manner of an inf. n. (TA.) This phrase was used in the time of paganism, by Es-Semow-al: (Msb, TA:) or, accord. to some, in the phrase attributed to him, the right reading is not mAt Htf Anfh , but mAt fiY firaA$ihi ; and the former was first used by Mohammad. (Ham p. 52.) It is said of a human being: (S, Mgh:) and then of any animal when it dies without any accidental cause: (Mgh:) hence, of a fish that has died, and floats upon the water. (Msb, TA.) It is said in a trad. of 'Ámir Ibn-Fuheyreh, waAlmaro'u yaA^otiY Hatofuhu mino fawoqihi [ And man, his death comes from above him ]: meaning that his caution and his cowardice will not repel from him the decree of death when it befalls him: originally said by 'Amr Ibn-Mámeh. (L, TA.) -A2- Hay~apN HatofapN [ A dead serpent ] is a phrase like AimoraA^apN EadolapN : (Z, TA:) the latter word is here an epithet. (Z, K.)
