HajabaAtN : (TA:) and in a horse, the parts of the two hips, or haunches, that project above, or beyond, the [skin called ] SifaAq , of the belly. (K.)

definition: [ A thing that prevents, hinders, debars, or precludes: ] a thing that veils, conceals, hides, covers, or protects;
sourceDefinition: [ A thing that prevents, hinders, debars, or precludes: ] a thing that veils, conceals, hides, covers, or protects; (S, Msb, K TA;) because it prevents seeing, or beholding: (Msb:) a thing, (A, K,) or body. (Msb,) that intervenes (A, Msb, K) between two things, (A, K,) or between two bodies; which is [said to be] the primary signification; (Msb;) [ a partition, a bar, a barrier, or an obstacle: ] and sometimes applied to ideal things: (Msb:) pl. jujubN . (A, Msb, K.) You say, Duriba AlHijaAbu EalaY Aln~isaA='i [ The veil, or curtain, was put, or let down, over the women ]. (A, TA.) And lahu daEawaAtN taxoriqu AlHujuba [ He has prayers that rend the veils ]. (A, TA.) And maA lidaEowapi AlmaZoluwmi HijaAbN [ There is no veil, or obstacle, to the prayer of the wronged ]. (A, TA.) It is said in a trad., mani A@T~alaEa AlHijaAbi waAqaEa maA waraA='ahu [ He who gets sight and knowledge of the veil falls into that which is behind it ]: i. e., when a man dies, he falls into what is behind [one of] the two veils, that of Paradise and that of Hell: (ISh, TA:) or, accord. to some, AiTalaAEu AlHijaAbi signifies the stretching out the head [and looking over the veil ]; for he who examines into a thing stretches out his head to see what is behind the veil, or covering. (TA.) And in another trad., a saying of Mohammad, (TA,) A_in~a A@ll~`ha yagofiru liloEabodi maA lamo yaqaEi AlHijaAbu [ Verily God forgiveth the servant (his creature) as long as the precluding event shall not have happened ]: AlHjAb here meaning the dying in the belief in a plurality of gods: (K, * TA:) as though one were precluded from true belief by death. (TA.) One says also, AlEajozu HajaAbN bayona AlA_inosaAni wamuraAdihi [ Inability is a bar between man and his desire ]. (Msb.) And AlmaEoSiyapu HijaAbN bayona AlEabodi wabayona rab~ihi [ Disobedience is a bar between the servant and his Lord ]. (Msb.) ― -b2- [Hence, in the present day, (assumed tropical:) A written charm or amulet; generally worn in a case (called bayotu HijaAbK ) suspended, on the right side, by a string passing over the left shoulder, or on some other part of the person: pl. of mult. HujubN , and of pauc. A^aHojibapN and HijaAbaAtN .] ― -b3- [Hence also,] A thin piece of flesh, (K,) resembling a piece of shin, (TA,) in the interior of the body, between the two sides, intervening between the lungs and the qSb [in the K AlqaSab , but this is evidently a mistranscription for AlquSob the lower intestines; for the HjAb is the diaphragm, or midriff ]: (K, TA:) and HijaAbu Alqalobi , (A,) or HajaAbu Aljawofi , (S,) signifies [ the same; as also HajaAbu Alkabidi ; (see xilobN ;)] what intervenes between the heart and the rest of the jwf ; (S;) the piece of skin that intervenes between the heart and the belly: (A, TA:) or HijaAbu Alqalobi signifies a certain fat that clothes the heart: (AHeyth, TA in art. $gf :) [or it signifies, or signifies also, the septum cordis: see qalobN :] pl. HujubN (A, TA.) Hence the saying, hataka Alxawofu HijaAba qalobihi (tropical:) [ Fear rent open his midriff: or his septum cordis ]. (A, TA.) ― -b4- (assumed tropical:) The horizon: [because it terminates the view:] so in the phrase, tawaArato biA@loHijaAbi (assumed tropical:) It (the sun) became concealed by the horizon; occurring in the Kur [xxxviii. 31], and in a trad. (TA.) ― -b5- (tropical:) A mountain: (A:) or an elevated part of a mountain. (K.) You say, qaEada fiY Zil~i AlHijaAbi (tropical:) He sat in the shade of the mountain. (A.) ― -b6- (assumed tropical:) The place where a [stony tract such as is called ] Har~ap ends. (K.) ― -b7- (assumed tropical:) A tract of sand uniformly continuous, and long. (K.) ― -b8- (assumed tropical:) The light of the sun: or the tract, or side, of the sun: (K, TA:) or [like HaAjibN ] a side, or part, of the sun. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , an epithet in which the quality of a subst. predominates, (TA,) A door-keeper; (Msb, K;) so called because he prevents persons from entering: (Msb:) [ a chamberlain: ] pl. Huj~aAbN (S, Msb, K) and HajabapN . (Msb, K.) And Hajabapu Albayoti [ The door-keepers and guardians of the Kaabeh: see HijaAbapN ]. (TA.) ― -b2- Each of the two bones over the eyes, with the hair and flesh upon them: (IF, Msb, K:) or the eyebrow; the hair growing on either of those bones: (AZ, K:) so called because it precludes the rays of the sun from the eye: (TA:) of the masc. gender: (Lh TA:) pl. HawaAjibu . (S Msb, K.) One says, A_in~ahu lamuzaj~aju AlHaAjibi [ Verily he has the eyebrow made narrow and long, by the removal of redundant hairs; or made narrow and long and arched; or lengthened with antimony ]. (Lh, TA.) ― -b3- [Hence, as being likened thereto,] (assumed tropical:) The piece of wood that is over the lintel of a door-frame. (Az, TA.) [See EatabapN .] ― -b4- (tropical:) The edge, (A,) or side, (K,) or upper limb of the disk, that appears when it begins to rise, (T, TA,) or the first part that appears, (Mgh,) of the sun, (T, A, Mgh, K,) and of the moon: (T, TA:) likened to the HAjb (A, Mgh) of the face (Mgh) of a man: (A:) and HawaAjbu Al$~amos the sides of the sun. (S.) You say, badaA HaAjibu Al$~amos , (T, A, TA,) and Alqamari , (T, TA,) (tropical:) The upper limb of the disk, (T, TA,) or the edge, (A,) of the sun appeared, (T, A, TA,) and of the moon. (T, TA.) ― -b5- (assumed tropical:) The edge or anything. (K.) A woman said to a man who was eating of the middle of a round cake of bread, kulo mino HawaAjibihaA (tropical:) Eat of its edges, (As, TA,) or its sides. (A.) ― -b6- (assumed tropical:) [ The beginning of the dawn.] You say, laAHato HawaAjibu AlS~uboHi (tropical:) The beginnings of the dawn appeared. (A, TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, * Mgh, Msb, K, &c.,) aor. , (Mgh, Msb, K,) inf. n. Ha*ofN , (S, Mgh, Msb,) He cut it off: (Mgh, Msb:) or he cut it [ so as to lessen it ] at its extremity; (TA;) he cut off somewhat from the extremity of it; he curtailed it; as, for instance, the tail of a beast: (Lth, TA:) and he made it to fall; dropped it; rejected it. (S, Mgh, Msb, K.) One says, Ha*afotu mino $aEariY , (S,) or mn $aEarihi , (Msb, K, *) and mn *anabi Ald~aAb~api , (S, Msb,) [ $ayoy^FA being understood,] I took, or cut off, [somewhat] from my hair, [or his hair, ] and from the tail of the beast; (S, K; *) I clipped it. (Msb.) And Ha*afa Al$~aEara [ He clipped the hair ]: said of a cupper. (TA.) And ↓ AHt*f Alv~awoba He cut off a piece from the garment, or cloth. (TA.) And Ha*afotu raA^osahu biAls~ayofi I cut off a portion of his head with the sword: (IF, Msb:) I struck his head with the sword and cut off a portion of it. (S.) ― -b2- Also, inf. n. as above, (assumed tropical:) He elided it, struck it off or out, or rejected it; namely, a letter, [and a syllable,] from a word: (MA, PS:) he omitted it. (MA.) [(assumed tropical:) He suppressed it; namely, a word of a proposition or sentence.] And Ha*afa Als~alaAma , (K,) inf. n. as above, (TA,) (tropical:) He made the salutation to be light [ of utterance ], and concise; (K, TA;) i. e., the salutation in prayer. (TA.) And Ha*afa fiY qawolihi , (Msb,) and fY AlA^a*aAni , and AlqiraA='api , aor. and inf. n. as above, (Mgh,) (assumed tropical:) He was concise, (Mgh, Msb,) and quick, in his saying, (Msb,) and in the call to prayer, and the recitation, or reading. (Mgh.) ― -b3- Ha*afahu biAlEaSaA He struck him, or beat him, with the staff, or stick: (TA:) and he cast, or threw, at him the staff, or stick. (S, K, TA.) It is said in a prov. of the Arabs, mentioned by Sb, A_iy~aAkumo wa A^ano yaHo*ifa A^aHadukumu AlA^aronaba , i. e. [ Beware ye ] lest any one of you cast at, or shoot, the hare: because this animal is of evil omen. (TA. [But the reading there given is Ay~AY : an evident mistranscription.]) Or Ha*afahu , inf. n. as above, signifies He struck, or he cast at, or shot, him, or it, from one side. (Lth, TA.) ― -b4- [Hence,] Ha*afa fulaAnFA bijaAy^izapK (tropical:) He gave such a one a gift. (Z, K.) ― -b5- And Ha*afa bihaA (assumed tropical:) He broke wind. (Ibn- 'Abbád, TA.) ― -b6- Ha*afa fiY ma$oyatihi He moved about his side and his hinder parts (in the CK he moved about his hinder parts and his shoulderjoint ) in his gait: and (in the CK “ or ”) he went with short steps. (En-Nadr, K, TA.)

sourceDefinition: , [inf. n. taHo*iyfN ,] He clipped it much: he took, or cut off, from its lateral parts, whatever it was, so as to make it even: (Msb:) he (a workman, or an artificer,) made it (a thing) becomingly even; as though he cut off from it whatever required to be cut off, so that it became free from everything unseemly, and was nicely, neatly, or properly, trimmed. (L, TA.) ― -b2- Also, inf. n. as above, (tropical:) He prepared it; or put it into a right, or good, state; and made it; or made it skilfully, or well. (S, K, TA.)

HaroSN , (T, S, K, &c.,) He rent it; or clave it: (T, S, K, &c.:) and he, or it, stripped off, scraped off, rubbed off, abraded, or otherwise removed, its superficial part, peel, rind, or the like: (T, K, &c.:) the former, (Az,) or the latter, (Az, Er-Rághib, B,) is the primary signification. (TA.) And HuriSa AlmaroEaY The pasture, or herbage, became entirely consumed, nothing of it being left; (IF, K;) as though it were stripped off from the surface of the land. (TA.) -A2- HaraSa Ealayohi , (T, S, A, Msb, K, *) aor. (T, S, Msb, K) and , mentioned by IKtt and the author of the Iktitáf, (MF,) inf. n. HaroSN ; (Msb;) and HariSa , aor. , (T, Msb, K,) inf. n. HaraSN ; (Msb; [but it seems to be indicated in the K, by its being said that the pret. is like samiEa , that it is HaroSN ;]) the latter form of the verb, however, is bad; (T, TA;) though El- Kurtubee is asserted by MF to have said that the former is of weak authority; which is clearly wrong, as the readers of the Kur are generally agreed in using it; (TA;) He desired it vehemently, eagerly, greedily, very greedily, or with avidity; he hankered after it; he coveted it; he desired it excessively, or inordinately: (S, * K, * TA:) or he desired it culpably; namely, worldly good: (Msb:) said by Az to be derived from the first of the significations mentioned in this art., or, as is also said by Er-Rághib, and in the B, from the second thereof; because, says Az, he who does so [may be said by a figure of speech to be one who] scratches off the outer skin of the faces of men by his so doing: but MF regards this as improbable; and says that most of the lexicologists hold the last to be the primary signification, and others to be taken from it: (TA:) HaraSa Ealayohi , aor. , inf. n. HaroSN , also signifies he strove, or laboured; exerted himself; took pains, or extraordinary pains; to acquire, obtain, or attain, it: (Msb, TA: *) and ↓ AHtrS signifies the same as HaraSa [ he desired vehemently, &c.]: (K:) and he strove, or laboured; exerted himself; took pains, or extraordinary pains; to acquire, obtain, or attain, a thing. (TA.) ― -b2- [Also He was excessively solicitous, or careful, and fearful, respecting him; and excessively pitiful, or compassionate, to him. See HiroSN and HariySN .]

definition: Has~a , (first pers.
sourceDefinition: Has~a , (first pers. Hasisotu , or Hasasotu , and Hasiytu , and Hasayotu , and Hasotu ,) as syn. with A^aHas~a : see 4, throughout. ― -b2- Has~a lahu , first pers. Hasasotu , aor. ; (S, K;) and first pers. Hasisotu , [aor. ;] (Yaakoob, S, K;) inf. n. His~N (S, K) and Has~N , (K,) or the latter is inf. n. of both verbs, but the former is a simple subst., (TA,) He was, or became, tender, or compassionate, towards him: (S, K:) [lit., he felt for him: ] ISd says that, for raqaqotu lahu , the explanation of Hsstu lh , he found in the book of Kr the verb written with f and q ; but that the former [?] is the right: (TA:) or he lamented for him; (Aboo-Málik, TA;) as also lahu ↓ HasoHasa . (K, * TA.) The Arabs say, A_in~a AlEaAmiriY~a layaHis~u lils~aEodiY~i Verily the 'Ámiree is tender, or compassionate, towards the Saadee; because of the relationship that subsists between them. (TA.) And Abu-l-Jarráh El-'Okeylee said, maAraA^ayotu Euqayoliy~FA A_il~aA Hasasotu lahu I have not seen an 'Okeylee without my feeling tenderness, or compassion, towards him; (S, TA;) for the same reason. (TA.) [See HaAs~apN , second signification.] -A2- Has~ahu , [aor. , inf. n. Has~N ,] He made his His~ [i. e. sound, or motion, ] to cease. (Bd in iii. 145.) ― -b2- Hence, (Bd, ubi suprà,) Has~ahumo , aor. , (S, A, Bd, Msb,) inf. n. Has~N , (Msb, K,) [and app., accord. to Fr, His~N , or this may be a simple subst.,] He slew them: (Bd, Msb, K:) and extirpated them: (K:) or he slew them quickly: (A, TA:) or he extirpated them by slaughter: (Aboo-Is-hák, S:) or he slew them with a quick and extirpating slaughter: or with a vehement slaughter: (TA:) it occurs in the Kur iii. 145: (S, A:) accord. to Fr, His~N , [so in the TA,] in this instance, is the act of slaying and destroying. (TA.) [Hence, Hus~a app. signifies It was utterly destroyed, so that nothing was left in the place thereof; and so ↓ AHts~ ; for it is said that] His~N and AiHotisaAsN , with respect to anything, signify A^ano laA yutoraka fiY AlmakaAni $aYo'N . (TA.) Also Has~ahumo , aor. as above, He trod them under foot, and despised them. (TA.) And Has~a Albarodu AljaraAda The cold killed the locusts. (S.) ― -b3- [Hence,] AljaraAdu taHus~u AlA^aroDa The locusts eat the herbage of the land. (TA.) And Has~a Albarodu AlkalaA^a , (S, K,) or Alz~aroEa , (A,) aor. , (S, TA,) inf. n. Has~N , (TA,) (tropical:) The cold nipped, shrunk, shrivelled, or blasted, (lit., burned, A^aHoraqa , q. v.,) the herbage, (S, K,) or the seed-produce. (A.) -A3- Has~a Ald~aAb~apa , (S, TA,) or Has~ahaA biAlmiHas~api , (A,) aor. , (S,) inf. n. Has~N , (S, K,) (tropical:) He curried the beast; removed the dust from it with the miHas~ap . (S, A, K, TA.) [See a proverb, voce Ha$~a .] Hence the saying of Zeyd Ibn-Soohán, on the day of the battle of the Camel, when he was carried off from the field, about to die, AidofinuwniY fiY viyaAbiY walaA taHus~uwA Ean~iY turaAbFA (tropical:) [ Bury ye me in my clothes, and ] shake not off any dust from me. (S, TA.)

definition: , (S, Msb, K,) inf.
sourceDefinition: , (S, Msb, K,) inf. n. A_iHosaAsN , (Msb,) He perceived, or became sensible of, ( wajada ,) the His~ (i. e. motion or sound, TA) of the thing: (S, K, TA:) he knew the thing by means of [ any of ] the senses: (IAth, accord. to his explanation of AlA_iHosaAsu as signifying AlEilomu biAlHawaAs~i :) he ascertained the thing as one ascertains a thing that is perceived by the senses: (Bd in iii. 45:) he knew the thing; or he perceived it by means of any of the senses; syn. Ealima bihi , (Msb,) and Ealimahu , and Earafahu , and $aEara bihi ; (TA;) as also ↓ Has~ahu , aor. , inf. n. Has~N and His~N and HasiysN ; (TA, in explanation of the saying in the K that Hasasotu Al$~aYo'a [in the CK erroneously ↓ Has~asotu ] signifies the same as A^aHosasotuhu ;) and in like manner AHs~ bihi is syn. with $aEara bihi ; (L, Msb;) and so is bihi ↓ Has~a , aor. , inf. n. His~N (L, Msb) and Has~N and HasiysN ; (L;) or His~N is a simple subst.: (M, L:) accord. to Fr, A_iHosaAsN is syn. with wujuwdN ; and Zj says that the meaning of AHs~ is Ealima and wajada : (TA:) or AHs~ signifies he perceived, or became sensible of; syn. wajada : and he thought, or opined: (Akh, S, K:) and he saw; syn. A^aboSara : and he knew: (K:) and is trans. in these senses by itself, (Akh, S,) or by means of bi : (TA:) and A^aHosasotu bihi signifies I knew it certainly; was certain, or sure, of it; (S;) as also bh ↓ Hasisotu , (S, K,) with kesr; (K;) speaking of news, or tidings: (S:) and for A^aHosasotu , some say A^aHosayotu , (S, Msb, K,) changing the [second] s into Y ; (S, Msb;) and A^aHasotu , (T, S, L, K,) with a single s , which is an extr. kind of contraction, (S, K,) but made in all other similar cases, where the last radical letter is quiescent; (Sb, L, TA;) and [thus] for A^aHosasona , we find A^aHasona ; (S;) and in like manner, for ↓ Hasisotu , (S, K,) or ↓ Hasasotu , (Msb,) some say Hasiytu , (T, S, M, L,) and Has~ayotu , (M, L, Msb, K, [in the CK Hasotu , which is the modern vulgar form,]) and Hasotu . (Abu-l-Hasan, IAar, T, M, L.) You say, AHs~hu biEayonihi [ He perceived him, or it, with his eye ]; (Ibn-Zekereeyà, TA in art. js ;) and so ↓ Has~ahu . (Sgh, TA ibid.) [In the present art. in the TA, it is said that Has~ahu bAlnSl is syn. with A^aHas~ahu : but bAln~Sl is evidently a mistranscription for biAlbaSari .] And it is said in the Kur [iii. 45], falam~aA A^aHas~a EiysaY minohumu Alkufora And when Jesus ascertained their unbelief as one ascertains a thing that is perceived by the senses: (Bd:) or opined it; or perceived it, or became sensible of it: (Akh, S:) or saw it: (Lh, TA:) or knew it, or perceived it sensibly. (Msb.) And in the same [xix. last verse], halo tuHis~u minohumo mino A^aHadK Dost thou see of them any one? (TA.) You say also, halo A^aHosasota Alxabara Hast thou known the news? (TA.) And A^aHosasotu biAlxabari , and A^aHosayotu bihi , and bh ↓ Hasisotu , and Hasiytu bh , I knew the news certainly. (S.) And A^aHosasotu Alxabara , and A^aHasotuhu , and ↓ Hasiytuhu , and Hasotuhu , I knew somewhat of the news. (T, L, TA.) And maA A^aHosasotu biAxabari , and AaHasotu bih . maA , and bh ↓ mA Hasiytu , and mA Hasotu , I knew not aught of the news. (T, L, TA.)

His~N (L, Msb) and Has~N and HasiysN ; (L;) or His~N is a simple subst.: (M, L:) accord. to Fr, A_iHosaAsN is syn. with wujuwdN ; and Zj says that the meaning of AHs~ is Ealima and wajada : (TA:) or AHs~ signifies he perceived, or became sensible of; syn. wajada : and he thought, or opined: (Akh, S, K:) and he saw; syn. A^aboSara : and he knew: (K:) and is trans. in these senses by itself, (Akh, S,) or by means of bi : (TA:) and A^aHosasotu bihi signifies I knew it certainly; was certain, or sure, of it; (S;) as also bh ↓ Hasisotu , (S, K,) with kesr; (K;) speaking of news, or tidings: (S:) and for A^aHosasotu , some say A^aHosayotu , (S, Msb, K,) changing the [second] s into Y ; (S, Msb;) and A^aHasotu , (T, S, L, K,) with a single s , which is an extr. kind of contraction, (S, K,) but made in all other similar cases, where the last radical letter is quiescent; (Sb, L, TA;) and [thus] for A^aHosasona , we find A^aHasona ; (S;) and in like manner, for ↓ Hasisotu , (S, K,) or ↓ Hasasotu , (Msb,) some say Hasiytu , (T, S, M, L,) and Has~ayotu , (M, L, Msb, K, [in the CK Hasotu , which is the modern vulgar form,]) and Hasotu . (Abu-l-Hasan, IAar, T, M, L.) You say, AHs~hu biEayonihi [ He perceived him, or it, with his eye ]; (Ibn-Zekereeyà, TA in art. js ;) and so ↓ Has~ahu . (Sgh, TA ibid.) [In the present art. in the TA, it is said that Has~ahu bAlnSl is syn. with A^aHas~ahu : but bAln~Sl is evidently a mistranscription for biAlbaSari .] And it is said in the Kur [iii. 45], falam~aA A^aHas~a EiysaY minohumu Alkufora And when Jesus ascertained their unbelief as one ascertains a thing that is perceived by the senses: (Bd:) or opined it; or perceived it, or became sensible of it: (Akh, S:) or saw it: (Lh, TA:) or knew it, or perceived it sensibly. (Msb.) And in the same [xix. last verse], halo tuHis~u minohumo mino A^aHadK Dost thou see of them any one? (TA.) You say also, halo A^aHosasota Alxabara Hast thou known the news? (TA.) And A^aHosasotu biAlxabari , and A^aHosayotu bihi , and bh ↓ Hasisotu , and Hasiytu bh , I knew the news certainly. (S.) And A^aHosasotu Alxabara , and A^aHasotuhu , and ↓ Hasiytuhu , and Hasotuhu , I knew somewhat of the news. (T, L, TA.) And maA A^aHosasotu biAxabari , and AaHasotu bih . maA , and bh ↓ mA Hasiytu , and mA Hasotu , I knew not aught of the news. (T, L, TA.)

definition: He listened to the discourse of people: (El-Harbee, K:) accord.
sourceDefinition: He listened to the discourse of people: (El-Harbee, K:) accord. to Aboo-Mo'ádh, it is similar to tasam~aEa and tabaS~ara : (TA:) or he sought repeatedly, or time after time, to know a thing, by the sense ( AlHAsp ) [of hearing &c.]: (Har p. 678:) or (so accord. to the TA, but in the K “ and, ”) he sought after, (Msb, K.) or sought after repeatedly, or time after time, (Msb,) news, or tidings, of a people, in a good cause; (K;) tjs~s signifying the doing the same in an evil cause: A'Obeyd says, you say, taHas~asotu Alxabara and tajas~asotuhu ; and Sh says that tanad~asotuhu is similar to it; and IAar, that taHas~asotu Alxabara and tabaj~asotuhu [but this is app. a mistranscription for tabaH~avotuhu ] signify the same. definition: , with fet-h, Perception by means of any of the senses;
sourceDefinition: , with fet-h, Perception by means of any of the senses; syn. wujuwdN . (L, TA.) Hence the proverb, laA HasaAsa mini A@bonaYo mawoqidK [ There is no perceiving of the two sons of the place of the kindling of fire ]: (L, TA:) for they say that two men used to kindle a fire in a road, and, when people passed by them, to entertain them as guests; and a party passing by when they had gone, a man said these words. (L.) And hence the saying, *ahaba fulaAnN falaA HasaAsa bihi Such a one has gone, and there is no perceiving him: or there is no perceiving his place. (TA.)

definition: Anything firm, strong, compact, sound, and free from defect.
sourceDefinition: Anything firm, strong, compact, sound, and free from defect. (TA.) A garment, or piece of cloth, compactly, or firmly and closely, woven: (TA:) or dense; concealing [ what is within it ]: (Kf, TA:) and ↓ muHoSafN [in like manner] signifies dense and strong. (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] (tropical:) Firm, or sound, in intellect or sense; (S, K, TA;) and ↓ HaSifN signifies the same; and firm in judgment; [or possessing firmness, or soundness, of intellect and judgment; for] it is a possessive epithet: and the former is said to signify strong in intellect, and good in judgment. (TA.) HaSiyfu AlEuqodapi , occurring in a letter of 'Omar, means (assumed tropical:) [ Firm ] in judgment, and in the management, conducting, ordering, or regulating, of affairs. (TA.)

definition: The land became abundant in HamoD [q.
sourceDefinition: The land became abundant in HamoD [q. v.]. (S.) ― -b2- AHmD Alqawomu The people, or company of men, lighted on, or found, HamoD . (TA.) ― -b3- AHmDt AlA_ibilu i. q. HamaDat , q. v. (A, TS, K.) ― -b4- [And hence,] AHmD Alqawomu (tropical:) The people, or company of men, launched into, or entered upon, cheering discourse. (A, TA.) I'Ab used to say to his companions, A^aHomiDuwA (tropical:) [ Launch ye forth, or enter upon, cheering discourse ]; (A, TA;) whereupon they would begin to recite poetry, and to relate the memorable conflicts of the Arabs; (A;) because they then entered into traditions and stories of the Arabs, being weary of the interpretation of the Kur-án, [like camels betaking themselves to the pasture termed HayoD when weary of that termed xul~ap .] (TA.) [And in like manner,] A_iHomaADN also means (assumed tropical:) The changing from seriousness to jesting or joking. (Har p. 10.) ― -b5- See also 2. [And see 5.] -A2- AHmDtu AlA_ibila ; (S, K;) or ↓ Ham~aDotuhaA , inf. n. taHomiyDN ; (ISk;) I pastured the camels upon HamoD . (ISk, S K.) ― -b2- [And hence, as camels are pastured upon HamoD after they have pastured for a time upon xul~ap ,] AHmDhu Eanohu , and ↓ Hm~Dhu , (tropical:) He shifted him from it [to another thing]. (TA.)

definition: [a coll. gen. n.] A kind of plant in which is saltness, (A, Msb,) which camels eat as though it were fruit, and after which they drink: (A:) other plants are termed xul~ap : (Msb:) or what is salt...
sourceDefinition: [a coll. gen. n.] A kind of plant in which is saltness, (A, Msb,) which camels eat as though it were fruit, and after which they drink: (A:) other plants are termed xul~ap : (Msb:) or what is salt and bitter, of plants; (S, K;) such as the rimov and the A^avol and the TarofaA=' and the like: (S:) what is sweet is called xul~ap : (S, K:) or any kind of plant that is salt, or sour, rising upon [ several ] stems, and having no [ single ] A^aSol [or stock ]: (M [as cited in the L, but I doubt whether the passage be correctly transcribed]:) or any salt, or sour, kind of trees; having a juicy and quivering leaf, which, when squeezed, bursts forth with water; and having a pungent, or strong, odour; that cleanses the garment and the hand when they are washed with it; such as the najiyl and the x*oraAf and the A_ixoriyT and the rimov and the qiDap and the qul~aAm and the harom and the HuroD and the rugl and the TarofaA=' and the like: (Lh:) or any plant that does not dry up in the rabiyE [or spring ], but endures the hot season, having in it saltness; when camels eat it, they drink upon it; and when they do not find it, they become thin and weak: (Lth, T:) the Arabs say that the xul~ap is the bread of camels, and the HamoD is their fruit, (S, A, Msb, K, *) or, as some say, their flesh-meat; (S;) or their xabiyS : (TA in art. xl :) and they say that flesh-meat is the HamoD of men: (TA:) the n. un. is with p : (Mgh:) and the pl. is HumuwDN . (S, K.) [In Isaiah xxx. 24, the word rendered “ clean ” in our authorized version is thought by some to mean “ salt ” or “ sour. ”] ― -b2- Hence the saying, jaAw^uwA muxil~iyna falaAqawoA HamoDaA (tropical:) They came eagerly desiring evil, or mischief, and found him who cured them of that which affected them: which is like the saying of Ru-beh, wanuwridu Almusotaworidiyna HamoDaA (tropical:) And him who cometh to us seeking to do evil, or mischief, we cure of his disease: for camels, when they are satiated with xul~ap , eagerly desire HamoD [to cure them of the effect of the former]. (TA. [See also xul~iY~N , in art. xl .]) ― -b3- Hence, also, by way of comparison, HamoD is applied to (tropical:) Evil, and war: and xul~ap , to ease, or repose; freedom from trouble or inconvenience, and toil or fatigue; or tranquillity; and ampleness of circumstances: (T and TA in art. xl :) and the former, to death: and the latter, to life. (Ham p. 315.) ― -b4- fuw^aAdN HamoDN and nafosN HamoDpN mean (assumed tropical:) A mind that takes fright at a thing, and shrinks from it, at first hearing it. (TA.)

definition: (assumed tropical:) Eager desire for a thing.
sourceDefinition: (assumed tropical:) Eager desire for a thing. (S, K.) It is said in a trad., AlA^u*unu maj~aAjapN waliln~afosi HamoDpN ; (S, TA;) and in another, liloA^u*uni maj~apN wllnfs HmDp ; (TA;) [both meaning the same;] (assumed tropical:) The ear is wont to reject what it hears, not retaining it, when one is exhorted to do a thing, or forbidden to do it, while the mind has eager desire to hear: (IAth:) or the ear retains not all that that it hears, while having eager desire for what it deems elegant, of extraordinary matters of discourse and speech. (Az.) This usage of the word is taken from the eager desire of camels for HamoD when they have become weary of xul~ap . (S.)

sourceDefinition: [ Sorrel; or particularly the rose-flowered sorrel; more commonly called in the present day Hum~ayoD ;] a certain plant having a red flower; (S;) a herb, or leguminous plant, of the kind termed *ukuwr , having a produce, or fruit, red like blood; (Ham p. 823;) a certain herb (K, TA) growing in the mountains, of herbs of the [ season called ] rabiyE , (TA,) the leaves of which are like those of the hinodibaA=' , (K, TA,) large and broad; (TA;) it is acid, (K, TA,) intensely so; its flower is red, and its leaves are green: (TA: [in which is here added wytnAws fY vmrh mvl Hb~ Alrm~An , app. for wayatanaw~asu Alx ; meaning that it waves much to and fro when blown by the wind, and describing its fruit as containing what resemble the grains of the pomegranate:]) it is pleasant to the taste; (K, TA;) and is eaten by men, but in small quantity: AHn and Aboo-Ziyád say, it grows very tall, and has a wide leaf, and a red flower, which, when it is near to drying up, becomes white: and Aboo-Ziyád says, in our mountain-country it is abundant; and is of two species; one of these two is acid, [ but ] pleasant to the taste; (TA;) and one species thereof is bitter; (K, TA;) in the lower parts of each, when they are full grown, is a redness; and the seeds and leaves of the acid species are used medicinally: Az says, it is a wild herb, or leguminous plant, that grows in the days of the [ season called ] rabiyE , in the channels of water, and has a red flower, and is of the herbs, or leguminous plants, which are termed *ukuwr : IB says, the places of its growth are the small channels of water, and the places to which valleys take their courses; and in it is acidity: sometimes, also, the people of settled habitations make it to grow in their gardens, and water it and sustain it so that it does not dry up in the time when the wild herbs, or leguminous plants, dry up: it is also said in the Minháj that it is both wild and growing in gardens; that the wild is called slq , [but this name is commonly applied to bete,] and in all of this there is not acidity: the garden-kind resembles the hndbA' , and in this is acidity, and an excessive viscous moisture: the best is the acid, gardenkind: here ends the quotation from the Minháj: (TA:) each species, (K, TA,) the bitter and the pleasant, or the garden-kind and the wild, (TA,) is good for thirst, and for inflammation arising from yellow bile; and strengthens the bowels; and allays heaving of the stomach, and hot palpitation, and tooth-ache; and is good for the black [or livid ] jaundice; (K, * TA;) and, when cooked, and applied externally, for the leprosy; and for the ringworm ( quwabaA=' ); and for glandular swellings in the neck, so much so that it is said to do good to him who has these even when hung upon the neck: with vinegar, also, it is good for the mange, or scab; and it is astringent; and puts a stop to malacia [so I render $ahowapAlT~iyn , lit. “ the longing for clay ”]: its seeds are cold in the first degree, and have an astringent property, particularly when fried: (TA:) they say that if these be hung, in a purse, upon a woman's left upper arm, she will not become pregnant as long as they remain upon her: (K, * TA:) they are also good for the sting of scorpions; and if some of the seeds be swallowed before the scorpion's stinging, its stinging will not hurt. (TA.) -A2- Also What is in the interior of the [ kind of citron called ] A^utoruj~ : (A, K:) n. un. with p : (A:) it is cold and dry in the third degree; used as a liniment, it removes freckles and the like, and clears the complexion; and it suppresses ( yaqomaEu ) the yellow bile; and gives appetite for food; and is good for hot palpitation; and made into a beverage, it sweetens the odour of the mouth; and is good for looseness arising from yellow bile; and is suitable for those who are fevered. (TA.) [In the present day, in Egypt, this name is applied to A species of citron, itself, with a conical apex, and very acid pulp. ]

sourceDefinition: (S, Mgh, K) and ↓ HanowN (K) Anything in which is a bending, curving, or crookedness, (K,) and the like; (TA;) of the body, (K,) such as the bone beneath the eyebrow, (K, * TA,) and the jaw-bone, and a rib; and of other things, such as the [ high ground termed ] quf~ , and the [ tract of sand termed ] Hiqof , (K,) and the bend of a valley [like maHoniyapN &c.]: (TA:) see maHoniyapN : and any curved piece of wood, (K,) such as any of the curved pieces of wood of the horse's saddle, and of the [ camel's saddle called ] qatab , (S, * CK, TA,) and of the [ camel's saddle called ] raHol : (CK, TA:) each of [ the curved pieces of wood called ] the qarobuwsaAni , the anterior and the posterior, of the horse's saddle: (Mgh:) and a bending, curving, or crookedness, of anything: whence, HinowN Aljabali [ the bend of the mountain ]: (S:) pl. [of pauc.] A^aHonaA='N (S, Mgh, K) and [of mult.] HiniY~N , [in the CK, erroneously, HaniY~N ,] and HuniY~N [originally Hunuw~N , first altered to HuniY~N , and then, because of the kesreh, to HiniY~N ]. (K, TA.) ― -b2- [The dual] HinowaAni signifies The two curved pieces of wood, with a net upon them, by means of which wheat is conveyed to the heap that is collected together in the place where it is trodden out. (K.) ― -b3- And the pl. A^aHonaA='N , i. q. jawaAnibu [as meaning (assumed tropical:) Sides, regions, quarters, or the like; and limits, bounds, or boundaries ]; like A^aEonaA='N . (S.) The saying, A^uzojuro A^aHonaA='a Tayorika means nawaAHiyahu , [i. e. (assumed tropical:) Straiten thou the limits, or bounds, of thy levity, (alluding to the restraining of birds from flight,)] on the right and left, and before and behind; by Tyrk being meant xif~atika and Tayo$ika . (S, TA.) ― -b4- A^aHonaA='u AlA^umuwri (assumed tropical:) Dubious affairs: (K, * TA:) or, as some say, it means A^aToraAfuhaA wanawaAHiyhaA [(assumed tropical:) the ends, and limits, or bounds, of affairs ]. (TA.)

HawaAniytu . (Msb, TA.) ― -b2- Also The vintner himself: (K in art. Hnt :) [like HaAniY~N &c.]

definition: A bend, or place of bending, of a valley;
sourceDefinition: A bend, or place of bending, of a valley; (S, K;) below the acclivity; (TA;) as also ↓ maHonuwapN and ↓ maHonaApN : (K:) pl. maHaAnK ; (S;) with which A^aHonaA='N [pl. of ↓ HinowN ] is syn: (TA:) and AlwaAdiY ↓ munoHanaY [in like manner] signifies the [ bending ] part of the valley that is below the acclivity. (TA.) ― -b2- Also, [in one copy of the K written maHoniy~apN ,] A bending, or curving, tract of ground, (Sb, ISd, K,) whether of sand or of any other kind: (Sb, ISd:) Sb says that the Y is substituted for w , because it is from Hanawotu ; which shows that he did not know Hanayotu . (ISd.) And maHoniyapu ramolK The part of a tract of sand over which winds [ a portion such as is termed ] a Hiqof . (TA.) ― -b3- Also A milking-vessel ( Eulobap , q. v.,) made of the skins of camels [or rather of a piece of the skin of a camel ]: sand is put into a piece of the skin, which is then suspended, and dries, becoming like a bowl: (K:) it is more convenient ( A^arofaqu ) to the pastor than other kinds. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, K,) aor. , (K,) inf. n. xabozN , (S, K,) He made [or kneaded and baked ] xuboz [or bread ]; (K, TA;) as also ↓ Axtbzhu : (Sb, S, TA:) or the ↓ the latter signifies he made [or kneaded and baked ] it for himself: (K:) or ↓ Axtbz signifies he kneaded flour, and made dough of it, and then baked it in a mal~ap [see xubozapN below] or in an oven: (T, TA:) [and ↓ yuxotabazu signifies it is made into bread: see S and K voce fav~N .] ― -b2- xabaza Alqawoma , (S, A,) aor. , (TA,) inf. n. xabozN , (A, K,) He fed the people, or company of men, with xuboz [or bread ]: (S, A, K: *) like as tamarahumo signifies “ he fed them with tamor : ” (A:) but Lh quotes the saying of certain of the Arabs, A^atayotu baniY fulaAnK faxabazuwA waHaAsuwA waA^aqaTuwA , meaning [ I came to the sons of such a one, and ] they fed me with xuboz and Hayos and A^aqiT : he does not say xabazuwniY waHaAsuwniY waA^aqaTuwniY . (TA.) -A2- xabazahu , aor. , (TK,) inf. n. xabozN , (K,) (assumed tropical:) He beat him, or it: (K, * TK:) accord. to some, with the hand: or with the two hands: (TA:) and some say that xuboz [or bread] is thus called because they beat it with their hands: but this assertion is not valid: (TA:) and you say also, xabaTaniY birijolihi , and xabazaniY , (tropical:) [ He beat me with his foot, ] and taxab~aTaniY and ↓ taxab~azaniY . (A, TA.) And xabaza AlbaEiyru , (TK,) inf. n. xabozN , (S, K,) (tropical:) The camel beat the ground with his fore foot, (S, * K, * TA,) or, as in some lexicons, with his fore feet. (TA.) And ↓ txb~zt AlA_ibilu Als~aEodaAna (assumed tropical:) The camels beat the [ herbage called ] sEadAn with their legs. (TA.)

definition: a word of well-known meaning;
sourceDefinition: a word of well-known meaning; (K;) [ Bread; ] that which is eaten. (S.) It is said in a prov., kul~u A^adaApi Alxubozi EinodiY gayoruhu [ All the apparatus of bread is in my possession except it, namely, the bread itself]: the origin of which was this: a company of men demanded hospitality of a certain man; and when they sat down, he threw down a [piece of leather such as is called] niToE , and put upon it a mill-stone, and adjusted its pivot, and covered it [with the upper stone]: and the presence of his apparatus made the company to wonder: then he took the handle of the mill, ( haAdiY Alr~aHaY ,) and began to turn it: whereupon they said to him, What dost thou? and he answered in the words of this proverb. (K.) ― -b2- [Hence,] Alxul~apu xubozu AlA_ibili (tropical:) [ Sweet herbage is the bread of camels: and AlHamoDu faAkihatuhaA , or AaHomuhaA , sour herbage is their fruit, or flesh-meat ]. (A, TA.)

(S.) ― -b2- xaraTa Al$~ajara , aor. as above, (K,) and so the inf. n., (TA,) He pulled off the leaves, (K, TA,) and the bark, or peel, (TA,) from the trees (K, TA) with his hand [ in the manner above described ]. (TA.) It is said in a prov., duwnahu xaroTu AlqataAdi [ Before one can attain it he has to strip the tragacanth of its leaves by grasping each branch and drawing his hand down it: i. e. he has to perform what will be extremely difficult, if not impossible]. (S, TA. [In the S and L in art. qtd , we find mino duwnihi .]) You say also, xaraTa AlEunoquwda He pulled off the grapes, or the like, from the bunch with all his fingers: (AHeyth:) or he put the bunch in his mouth and drew forth its stalk bare; as also ↓ AxtrThu . (K.) It is said of Mo- hammad, kaAna yaA^okulu AlEinaba xaroTFA [ He used to eat grapes by putting the bunch in his mouth and drawing forth its stalk bare: or by stripping them off with all his fingers ]. (TA.) ― -b3- xaraTa AlEuwda , aor. as above, (S, K, *) and so the inf. n., (S,) He removed the bark, or peel, from the wood, or stick, (S, K,) and planed it, or made it even, (K,) with the mixoraT , which is also called baloT and buloT , (TA in art. blaT ,) or with his hand. (TA in the present art.) ― -b4- [Hence, in modern Arabic, He turned the wood, or stick; i. e., shaped it, or made it round, with a lathe. ] ― -b5- xaraTa AlHadiyda , inf. n. as above, He made the iron long, like a column, or pole, or rod. (S.) -A2- xaraTa AljawaAhira He collected the jewels in a xariyTap [q. v.]. (MF.)

sourceDefinition: A receptacle, (S, K,) [ a pouch, ] or thing like a kiys [or purse ], (Lth, Msb,) of leather, (Lth, S, Msb, K,) or of rag, (Lth,) or other material, (S, K,) which is bound, or made fast, or closed by the insertion of its loops one into another, ( yu$oraju , Lth, S, Msb, K,) upon its contents: (Lth, S, K:) pl. xaraAy^iTu . (Msb.) ― -b2- Also A thing likened thereto, which is made for the letters of the sultán, and of prefects, or agents, to be sent therein. (Lth, L.) ― -b3- Also A similar thing [ which was formerly, in the time of paganism, ] put upon the head of the she-camel [ that was ] confined [ to perish ] at the tomb of a dead person. (Lth.) ― -b4- [Also The pod, or oblong capsule or pericarp, of sesamum and the like: pl. as above. Used in this sense by writers on botany, and in the spoken language of the present day.] ― -b5- See also bidaAdN .

sourceDefinition: , aor. , (JK, S, Msb, K,) inf. n. xasofN , (JK,) or xusuwfN , (S, K,) or both; (Msb;) [and ↓ Anxsf ;] It (a place) sank, (JK, Msb,) or went away, into the ground, or earth, (S, Msb, K,) with what was upon it. (JK.) You say, AlA^aroDu ↓ Anxsf , [and xasafat ,] The ground sank [ into the earth ] with what was upon it. (TA.) And bihi AlA^aroDu ↓ Anxsft , (JK,) or bh AlArD ↓ Anxsf , and xusifa bh AlArD , (TA,) and xasafato , (Msb in art. swx ,) The ground sank with him, or it: (JK:) or the ground, or earth, [ swallowed up him, or it; or] took and enclosed him, or it. (TA.) And Albiy^oru ↓ Anxsft The well [ sank and collapsed; or] went away into the earth with its casing of stones and wood. (Mgh.) And xasafa fiY AlA^aroDi and xusifa bihi [ He, or it, sank into the ground, or earth, and became swallowed up, or enclosed, or concealed, therein ]. (S.) It is said in the Kur [xxviii. 82], accord. to one reading, laxusifa binaA [ We had been swallowed up by the earth ]: (S:) accord. to another reading, (that of 'Abd-Allah, S, i. e. Ibn-Mes'ood, TA,) bnA ↓ laA@noxusifa , (S, K,) in the pass. form; (K;) [meaning the same;] like as one says, AunoTuliqa bnA . (S.) You say also, xasafato Eayonu AlmaA='i The spring of water sank, or went away, into the earth. (Msb, K. *) And AlEayonu ↓ Anxsft The eye sank, or became depressed, in the head; syn. gaArato ; (Msb in art. gwr ;) [and so xasafat , inf. n. xusuwfN ; for] xusuwfu AlEayoni signifies The eye's going away into the head: (S:) or ↓ Anxsft signifies its black, or part surrounded by the white, disappeared in the head: (Mgh:) or this last, (K,) as quasi-pass. of the trans. v. xasafa , (TA,) (tropical:) it (the eye) became blind; as also ↓ A^axosafat ; (K, TA;) and [in like manner] xasafat (assumed tropical:) it (the eye) lost its light [or sight ]. (Msb.) ― -b2- [Hence, app.,] xasafa Alqamaru , inf. n. xusuwfN ; (S, Msb, K;) and xusifa ; (TA;) (assumed tropical:) The moon [ suffered eclipse, or became eclipsed, or] lost its light, or part of its light; (Msb;) i. q. kasafa : (S, * Msb, * K:) and xasafati Al$~amosu and kasafat both signify the same [i. e. the sun suffered eclipse, &c.]: (Mgh:) or one says kasafat of the sun, and xasafa of the moon, (Th, S, Msb, K,) accord. to the more approved usage: (Th, S, Msb:) or, in the common conventional language, Alkusuwfu is the partial loss of the light of the sun, and Alxusuwfu is the total loss of the light thereof: (AHát, Msb:) or Alxswf is the partial loss of the light of the sun, and Alkswf is the total loss thereof, (K, TA,) accord. to AHát: (TA:) Alxswf often occurs in the trads., as said of the sun; though the term commonly known in the classical language is Alkswf [in this case]: and it is said in a trad., A_in~a Al$~amosa wa Alqamara laAyaxosifaAni limawoti A^aHadK A^awo liHayaAtihi [ Verily the sun and the moon suffer not eclipse for the death of any one or for his life ]; predominance being in this instance attributed to the moon, as being masc., over the sun, which is fem. (IAth.) ― -b3- Also, inf. n. xasofN , (assumed tropical:) It (a thing) became defective or deficient; suffered loss or diminution. (K.) ― -b4- (tropical:) It (the body) became lean, or emaciated. (TA.) And xasafato , said of camels and of sheep or goats, (tropical:) They became lean, or emaciated. (TA. [This meaning is there indicated, but not clearly expressed. See xasofapN . Accord. to the KL, the inf. n. xasofN signifies The being vile, abject, or contemptible: and also the being lean, or emaciated: and hence Golius, on that authority, has rendered the verb as meaning vilis et macer fuit. ]) ― -b5- Also (assumed tropical:) It (the colour, or complexion, of a person) became altered, or altered for the worse. (TA.) ― -b6- And (tropical:) It (a thing, K, as, for instance, a roof, TA) became pierced with a hole, or rent; (K, TA;) as also ↓ Anxsf . (TA.) ― -b7- And, xasafat , said of a she-camel, (tropical:) She, after yielding abundant milk, soon stopped [ its flow ] in winter. (K, TA.) ― -b8- And, said of a well, It was, or became, such as is termed xasiyfN [q. v.]. (TA.) ― -b9- And xasafa , said of a man, (tropical:) He recovered from a disease. (IDrd, K, TA.) -A2- xasafa , (JK, Msb, TA,) aor. , (Kur xvi. 47, &c,) inf. n. xasofN , He (God) made a place, (JK, Msb,) or the ground, (TA,) to sink, (JK, Msb, TA,) or go away, into the earth, (Msb,) with what was upon it. (JK, TA.) And xasafa bihi AlA^aroDa , (S, K,) inf. n. xasofN , (S,) He (God) made him, or it, to disappear in the earth, or ground: (S, K:) [or made the earth, or ground, to sink with, and swallow up, him, or it: ] whence, in the Kur [xxviii. 81], faxasafonaA bihi wabidaArihi AlA^aroDa [ And we made the ground to sink with, and swallow up, him and his mansion ]. (S.) And xasafotu Eayona AlmaA='i I made the spring of water to sink, or go away, into the earth. (Msb.) ― -b2- xasafa Eayona fulaAnK , (K, TA,) aor. , inf. n. xasofN , (TA,) (tropical:) He put out, or blinded, the eye of such a one, (K, * TA,) so that the black, or part surrounded by the white, disappeared in the head. (TA.) ― -b3- xasafa Al$~aYo'a , (K,) aor. and inf. n. as above, (TA,) (tropical:) He made a hole in, or rent, the thing. (K, TA.) ― -b4- And (assumed tropical:) He cut, or cut off, the thing. (K.) ― -b5- xasafa Albiy^ora , (K,) inf. n. as above, (TA,) (assumed tropical:) He dug the well in stones, so that it yielded an abundant and unceasing flow of water: (K, TA:) or he dug the well by piercing through its mountain [or rock ] to the water beneath so that it would never become exhausted: or he dug the well so as to reach an unceasing, or a copious, source of water. (TA.) Hence the saying of 'Omar, in reply to a question of El-'Abbás respecting the poets, AimoraA^u Alqayosi saAbiquhumo xasafa lahumo Eayona Al$~iEori , i. e. (assumed tropical:) [ Imra-el-Keys is he who has the precedence of them: ] he has made the source of poetry to well forth abundantly to them. (TA.) ― -b6- xasafa Aln~aAqapa , inf. n. as above, (tropical:) He (God) made the she-camel, after yielding abundant milk, soon to stop [ its flow ] in winter. (K, TA.) ― -b7- xasofN also signifies The confining a beast without fodder: (K, TA:) or making a beast to pass the night without fodder: (Ham p. 290:) and (hence, TA) (tropical:) the constraining a man to do that which he dislikes, or hates; (JK, Ham ibid., K, TA;) as also xusofN : (JK:) and (hence, Ham) (tropical:) the lowering, humbling, or abasing, another: (Ham, * K, TA:) whence, sumotuhu Alxasofa , (Ham,) or saAmahu xasofFA , &c.: [explained below: see xasofN :] (TA:) and the verb of xasofN in these three senses is xasafa . (T, K.)

sourceDefinition: [an inf. n. of 1: and hence several of the significations here following.] Deep places in the ground ( Eumuwqu ZaAhiri AlA^aroDi ; in the CK Eumuwqu mA'i AlArDi ); as also ↓ xusofN . (K, TA.) ― -b2- The place whence the water of a well issues. (AZ, S, K.) In the following saying of Sá'ideh El-Hudhalee, A^alaA yaA fataY maA Eabodu $amosK bimivolihi yubal~u EalaY AlEaAdiY wa tuw^obiY AlmaxaAsifu the last word is pl. of xasofN [app. as signifying A source of water ], after the manner of ma$aAbihu and malaAmiHu : (TA:) the meaning is, [ Truly, O young man, what is 'Abd-Shems? i. e.] how great a person is 'Abd-Shems! by the like of him the enemy is overcome [ and the sources of water become difficult of access ]. (M in art. bl .) ― -b3- A cloud, or collection of clouds, that has risen and appeared from the direction of the extreme west, [as North-western Africa is called by the Arabs,] from [ the quarter of ] the right of the Kibleh [ to one who is on the north-east of Mekkeh, towards El-'Irák ]: (Lth, K:) or it signifies, (JK, TA,) [and] so ↓ xisofN and ↓ xasiyfN , (K,) a cloud, or collection of clouds, that has risen and appeared mino qibali AlEayoni , bearing much water; (JK, K, TA;) i. e., from [ the quarter of ] the right of the Kibleh [ as explained above ]. (TA.) -A2- (tropical:) Deficiency, or imperfection; a fault; or a low, or base, quality; (S, K, TA;) as also ↓ xasiyfapN . (TA.) One says, raDiYa fulaAnN biAlxasofi (tropical:) Such a one was content with deficiency, or imperfection; &c. (S, TA.) ― -b2- (assumed tropical:) Leanness, or emaciation; (TA;) as also ↓ xasiyfapN . (JK.) ― -b3- [See also 1, last sentence. ― -b4- Hence,] baAta Alqawomu EalaY Alxasofi (tropical:) The party passed the night in a state of hunger, not having anything wherewith to feed themselves: (TA:) and baAta fulaAnN Alxasofa (tropical:) Such a one passed the night hungry: (S, K, TA:) and $aribonaA EalaY` Alxasofi (tropical:) We drank without eating. (IAar, IDrd, K, TA.) A poet says, batonaA EalaY Alxasofi laA risolN nuqaAtu bihi Hat~aY jaEalonaA HibaAla Alr~aHoli fuSolaAnaA [ We passed the night in a state of hunger: there was no milk wherewith we might be fed, until we made the ropes of the camel's saddle to serve as young camels ]: i. e. we had no food until we bound the she-camels with ropes in order that they might yield us milk [as though they had young ones to suckle], and we might feed ourselves with their milk. (O, TA.) [See also another ex., in a verse of Dhu-r-Rummeh, cited voce A_il~aA , p. 78.] ― -b5- [Hence, also,] saAmahu xasofFA and ↓ xusofFA , (S, K,) and saAmahu Alxasofa , (S, Msb,) (tropical:) He brought upon him abasement, or ignominy: (S, Msb, K:) or he required, or constrained, him to do an affair of difficulty; and to become in a state of abasement, or ignominy. (S, TA.) [See also two similar phrases voce xuT~apN .] ― -b6- [And hence,] xasofN signifies also (assumed tropical:) Wrong, wrongdoing, injustice, injuriousness, or tyranny. (TA.) [And saAmahu xasofFA , or Alxasofa , sometimes means (assumed tropical:) He brought upon him wrong, &c.] -A3- See also the next paragraph.

definition: A man dyeing, or who dyes, his hair with hinnà.
sourceDefinition: A man dyeing, or who dyes, his hair with hinnà. (Msb.) ― -b2- See also xaDiybN . ― -b3- Also (tropical:) A male ostrich (S, A, K, &c.) whose shanks (A, K) and legs (A) have become red, (A, K,) or green, [app. meaning of a dark, or an ashy, dustcolour, ] or yellow, (A,) in consequence of his lusting after the female, (A, K,) or in consequence of his having eaten the [ herbage termed ] rabiyE : (A:) or the front edges of whose shanks have become red, (S, K,) or green, (K,) or yellow, in consequence of his having eaten the [ herbage termed ] rbyE : (S, K:) or whose beak and shanks have become red from his having eaten the [ herbage termed ] rbyE : in the summer ( AlS~ayof ) he becomes bald ( yqrE ), and his shanks become white: (L:) or whose shanks have become green by reason of lust in the [ season termed ] rbyE : (ADk:) accord. to some, (TA,) it is applied only to the male ostrich: (S, K:) but some explain it without this restriction; and Lth mentions [the fem.] xaADibapN as applied to an ostrich: [it is said that] the skin of the neck, and that of the breast, and that of the thighs, of the male ostrich, but not his feathers, become intensely red when he lusts after the female: or, as some say, xADb signifies an ostrich that has eaten green food: (TA:) or the extremities of whose feathers are dyed by [ the eating of ] blossoms, and the slender parts of whose legs have become red by the same cause: accord. to an Arab of the desert, supposed to be Aboo-Kheyreh, in the [season termed] rbyE , when it eats A^asaAriyE [app. meaning certain worms so called], its legs and beak assume the red hue of the EuSofur [or safflower]: (AHn, L:) or xADb is applied to a male ostrich the slender parts of whose legs become red when the dates begin to become red, and cease to be so when the redness of the dates ceases: (AHn, K:) so that it is not from eating AsAryE , which, it is said, no ostrich is known to eat: accord. to As, the cause [of the redness above mentioned] is only the dye of blossoms; definition: (S, A, L, Msb, K) and xilaASatuhu (Fr, Sgh, K) What has become clear, of cooked butter;
sourceDefinition: (S, A, L, Msb, K) and xilaASatuhu (Fr, Sgh, K) What has become clear, of cooked butter; (S, A, L, K;) or cooked butter into which some dates have been thrown, or into which some sawiyq [i. e. meal of parched barley or wheat ] has been thrown, in order that thereby it may become clear from the remains of the milk: (Msb:) for when they cook fresh butter, to make it samon , they throw into it somewhat of swyq , or dates, or globules of gazelles' dung; and when it becomes good, and clear from the dregs, or sediment, that smn is called AlxulaASapu , and ↓ AlxilaASu also, (S, L,) mentioned by A'Obeyd, (S,) and this, namely the xilaAS , is the A_ivor : (S, L, K:) and the terms ↓ xuluwSN (S, L, K) and qilodapN (S, L) and qi$odapN (S, L, K) and kudaAdapN (S, L) are applied to the dregs, or sediment, remaining at the bottom; (S, L, K;) as also xulaASapN : (AHeyth, L in art. q$d :) the inf. n. is A_ixolaASN ; and you say, A^axolaSotu Als~amona : (S, L:) or xulaASapN and ↓ xilaASN signify dates and swyq that are thrown into smn ; and AxlS Als~amona signifies “he threw dates and swyq into the smn [and so clarified it]:” and ↓ xulaASN [thus I find it written] signifies what has become clear, of smn , when it is cooked: and xilaASN also signifies, and so ↓ A_ixolaASN , and ↓ A^ixolaASapN , butter when clear from the dregs, or sediment: and ↓ xuluwSN , the dregs, or sediment, at the bottom of the milk: (L:) ↓ A_ixolaASN and ↓ A_ixolaASapN are syn. with A_i*owaAbN and A_i*owaAbapN : (TA:) or, accord. to AZ, the latter two terms are applied to butter when it is put into the cooking-pot to be cooked into smn ; and when it has become good, and the milk has become clear from the dregs, or sediment, that milk is called A_ivorN and ↓ A_ixolaADN : Az says, I have heard the Arabs apply the term ↓ xilaASN to that with which smn is cleared, in the cookingpot, from the water and milk and dregs; for when it is not clear, and the milk is mixed with the butter, they take dates, or flour, or swyq , which they throw therein, that the smn may become clear from the remains of the milk mixed with it: this is the xilaAS : but the xlASp [i. e. xulaASap ] is what remains, of the xilaAS and dregs or milk &c., in the bottom of the cooking-pot: (L, TA:) [or] ↓ xilaASN (K) [accord. to some, ↓ xalaASN , but this is app. wrong, (see Har p. 311,)] and xulaASapN (Hr, TA) also signify what fire has clarified, or purified, ( maA A^axolaSatohu Aln~aAru ,) of butter, and of gold, and of silver: (Hr, K, TA:) or All~abani ↓ xilaASu , means what is extracted from milk; i. e. butter; (ADk, L, TA;) and so does xulaASapu All~abani : (A: [but there mentioned among tropical expressions:]) xulaASapN being applied in the manner first mentioned in this paragraph, by a secondary application is made to signify what is clear, or pure, of other things; (Msb;) [as also ↓ xaAliSN : and hence both of them often signify (assumed tropical:) the choice, best, or most excellent, part of anything; and so, probably, does ↓ xilaASN :] and xulaASapN and ↓ xulaASN also signify Inspissated juice ( rub~ ) made from dates; (JK;) or this is called ↓ xuluwSN . (TA.)

for when it is not clear, and the milk is mixed with the butter, they take dates, or flour, or swyq , which they throw therein, that the smn may become clear from the remains of the milk mixed with it: this is the xilaAS : but the xlASp [i. e. xulaASap ] is what remains, of the xilaAS and dregs or milk &c., in the bottom of the cooking-pot: (L, TA:) [or] ↓ xilaASN (K) [accord. to some, ↓ xalaASN , but this is app. wrong, (see Har p. 311,)] and xulaASapN (Hr, TA) also signify what fire has clarified, or purified, ( maA A^axolaSatohu Aln~aAru ,) of butter, and of gold, and of silver: (Hr, K, TA:) or All~abani ↓ xilaASu , means what is extracted from milk; i. e. butter; (ADk, L, TA;) and so does xulaASapu All~abani : (A: [but there mentioned among tropical expressions:]) xulaASapN being applied in the manner first mentioned in this paragraph, by a secondary application is made to signify what is clear, or pure, of other things; (Msb;) [as also ↓ xaAliSN : and hence both of them often signify (assumed tropical:) the choice, best, or most excellent, part of anything; and so, probably, does ↓ xilaASN :] and xulaASapN and ↓ xulaASN also signify Inspissated juice ( rub~ ) made from dates; (JK;) or this is called ↓ xuluwSN . (TA.)

(K.) It is also trans.: (Msb:) you say, xaAfahu and ↓ txw~fhu [ He feared, or was afraid of, him, or it ]; (Msb, TA;) both signifying the same: (TA:) [and so xaAfa minohu ; or this may mean he feared what might happen to him from him, or it: ] and Ealayohi $ayoy^FA ↓ txw~f , meaning xaAfahu [i. e. xaAfa Ealayohi $ayoy^FA He feared for him a thing ]: (S, K:) and xaAafahu EalaY maAlihi and Ealayohi ↓ txw~fhu [ He feared him, or it, for his property ]. (S in art. drd .) And He knew. (Lh, Kr, K.) Hence, waA_ini A@moraA^apN xaAfato mino baEolihaA nu$uwzFA [ And if a woman know that there is, on the part of her husband, injurious treatment, or unkindness, or estrangement ], (K,) in the Kur [iv. 127]. (TA.) And hence also, famano xaAfa mino muwSK janafFA [ And he who knoweth that there is, on the part of the testator, an inclining to a wrong course, or a declining from the right course, &c.], (K,) in the Kur [ii. 178]; thus explained by Lh. (TA.) -A2- xaAfahu , (S,) first pers. xufotuhu , (K,) aor. yaxuwfuhu , (S,) He exceeded him in fear. (S, K. *) You say, faxaAfahu ↓ xaAwafahu , (S,) inf. n. of the former muxaAwafahu , (TA,) i. e. [ He vied with him to see which of them would exceed the other in fear, and ] he exceeded him in fear. (S.)

A_ixaAfapN (S) and A_ixaAfN , like kitaAbN , (Lh, TA,) [but the latter is irreg. and rare,] He, or it, (an affair, a case, or an event, Msb,) caused him, or made him, to fear, or be afraid; put him in fear; frightened, or terrified, him; (TA;) and ↓ xw~fhu , (Msb, K,) inf. n. taxowiyfN , (S, TA,) signifies the same. (S, Msb, K.) So in the phrase AxAf Alv~agoru [ The enemies' frontier caused to fear, &c.; was insecure: ] or fear entered from it. (TA.) You say also, maAla AlHaAy^iTu faA^axaAfa Aln~aAsa [ The wall leaned, and caused the people to fear ]. (Msb.) And A^axaAfa All~uSuwSu AlT~ariyqa [for A^axaAfa All~uSuwSu A^ahola AlT~ariyqi The robbers caused the people of the road, or the passengers thereof, to fear, &c.; or it may be rendered the robbers caused the road to be insecure ]. (Msb.) And A^axafotuhu AlA^amora faxaAfahu [ I caused him to fear the thing, or affair, &c., and he feared it; making the verb doubly trans.]; as also A_iy~aAhu fataxaw~afahu ↓ xaw~afotuhu . (Msb.) It is said in a trad., A^axiyfuwA AlhawaAm~a qabola A^ano tuxiyfakumo Make ye the venomous reptiles and the like to fear before they make you to fear; (TA;) i. e. kill ye them before they kill you. (JM, TA.) ― -b2- maA A^axowafaniY Ealayoka [ How greatly do I fear for thee! ]. (TA.)

Hwf and Hyf :) or he took from its extremities; so in the A; in which it is said to be tropical: accord. to IF, it is originally [ txw~n ,] with n [in the place of the f ]. (TA.) Dhu-rRummeh says, (S,) or not he, but some other poet, for it is ascribed to several different authors, (L,) taxaw~afa Alr~aHolu minohaA taAmikFA qaridFA kamaA taxaw~afa Zahora Aln~aboEapi Als~afanu [ Her saddle abraded from a long and high, compact hump, like as when the piece of skin used for smoothing arrows has abraded from the back of a rod of the tree called nbEp ]. In the TA, in the present art., in the places of AlrHl and Zhr , I find Als~ayoru and Euwd .]) Hence, (S, K,) accord. to Fr, (TA,) A^awoyaA^axa*ihimo EalaY taxaw~ufK , (S, K,) in the Kur [xvi. 49], (S,) which Az explains as meaning [ Or are they secure from his destroying them ] by causing them to suffer loss [ by little and little ] in their bodies and their possessions, or cattle, and their fruits: or, accord. to Zj, it may mean, after causing them to fear, by destroying a town, so that the one next to it shall fear. (TA.) You say also, txw~f mino maAliY He took by little and little from my property. (JK.) And taxaw~afanaA Als~anapu [ The year of drought, or sterility, took from us by little and little ]. (JK.) And taxaw~faniY Haq~iY [ He diminished to me by little and little my right, or due ]. (JK.) And taxaw~afahu Hmoquhu (tropical:) i. q. AhoDamahu [an evident mistranscription for AihotaDamahu or haDamahu , meaning His stupidity deprived him of his right, or due ]. (TA.)

definition: A man very fearful or timorous;
sourceDefinition: A man very fearful or timorous; (S, K;) [and so, in the present day, ↓ xaw~aAfN ; the former originally] of the measure faEilN , like fariqN and faziEN ; and similar to SaAtN , meaning a man “ having a strong, or loud, voice: ” (S:) or i. q. ↓ xaAy^ifN : (TA:) accord. to Kh, it may be [originally xaAwifN ,] of the measure faAEilN , having the medial radical rejected; or [ xawofN ,] of the measure faEolN ; and in either case, the dim. is [↓ xuwayofN ,] with w : so says Sb. (TA.)

definition: A [ coat of the kind called ] jub~ap , of hide, or leather, which the collector of honey wears;
sourceDefinition: A [ coat of the kind called ] jub~ap , of hide, or leather, which the collector of honey wears; (Akh, JK, K;) and also worn by the water-carrier: (JK:) or a fur-garment, or hide with the fur or wool on it, worn by him who enters into the places occupied by bees, in order that they may not sting him: (TA:) or a [ pouch of the kind termed ] xariyTap , (S, K,) of hide, or leather, (S,) narrow in the upper part and wide in the lower part, (TA,) in which honey is collected: (S, K:) or a [ round piece of leather with a running string by means of which it may be converted into a bag, such as is termed ] suforap , like the xariyTap , made, or sewed, small, [for muSoEadapN or muSaE~adapN , which I find in different copies of the K, and to which no appropriate meaning is assignable, I read muSogarapN or muSag~arapN , (see 2 in art. Sgr , and particularly A^aSogara Alqirobapa ,)] having its head [or border ] raised, for honey; (K;) so says Skr, in explaining the following verse: or, as IB says, accord. to Aboo-'Alee, it is from the phrase Aln~aAsu A^axoyaAfN , meaning “ men, ” or “ the people, ” “ are different, one from another; ” for it is a xariyTap of hide, or leather, embellished with different kinds of embellishment; and if so it should be mentioned in art. xyf : (TA:) [but] the dim. is ↓ xuwayofapN . (JK.) Aboo-Dhu-eyb says, [describing a collector of wild honey,] taA^ab~aTa xaAfapF fiyhaA misaAbN faA^aSobaHa yaqotariY ma$adFA bi$iyqi (S,) [ He put beneath his armpit a xAfp in which was a receptacle for honey, and betook himself to making successive endeavours to reach the most difficult part of a mountain by means of a rope, or rope of palm-fibres; for] he means $iyqFA bimasadK ; the phrase being inverted: (S and TA in art. $yq :) or he means, [ betook himself to ] taking successive holds of a rope ( yatatab~aEu HabolFA ) tied to a $yq [here best rendered mountain-top ] in his descent to the place of the honey; so that there is no inversion. (TA in that art.) ― -b2- Also i. q. EayobapN [ A kind of basket, or receptacle, of hide, or leather ]; (TA;) the thing in which fruits are gathered; also called mixorafN . (Har p. 374.) ― -b3- And xaAfapu Alz~aroEi is said to mean The envelope of the grain of seed-produce; so called because it protects it: to this the believer is likened in a trad. [as some relate it]; but the reading [commonly known] is [ xaAmap ,] with m . (TA.) [See xAmp , in art. xym .]

definition: A road in which people fear: (S, * Msb, K:) or a road that is feared;
sourceDefinition: A road in which people fear: (S, * Msb, K:) or a road that is feared; (JK, TA;) as also ↓ maxiyfN , and ↓ xaAy^ifN ; which last is tropical, of the measure faAEilN in the sense of the measure mafoEuwlN ; (TA;) or, thus applied, this last [is a possessive epithet, and thus] means having fear: (JK: [see also muxaAfN :]) you should not say ↓ TariyqN muxiyfN , because the road does not cause fear, but only he who robs and slays therein. (S, * K, * TA.) One says also vagorN ↓ maxiyfN and ↓ mutaxaw~afN An enemies' frontier [ that is feared, or] from which one fears, or from the direction of which fear comes. (TA.) maxuwfN signifies A thing [of any kind] that is feared; as a lion, and a serpent, and fire, and the like. (Har p. 369.) [Hence,] HaAy^iTN maxuwfN A wall of which the falling is feared. (Lh, Msb, TA. [See also muxiyfN .]) And wajaEN maxuwfN [ A pain that is feared ]. (TA. [See, again, muxiyfN .]) And A^amorN maxuwfN [ An affair, or event, that is feared ]. (Mgh, Msb. [See, again, muxiyfN .]) And faAsiqN maxuwfN EalaY maAlihi A transgressor who is feared for his property, that he will consume it, and expend it in that which is not right. (Mgh.)

sourceDefinition: is not a word of Arabic origin: (Msb:) Ald~arobN is [the Arabic name of the ancient Derbe, near the Cilician Gates, which were the chief mountain-pass, from the direction of the countries occupied by the Arabs, into the territory of the Greek Empire: these “ Gates ” are mentioned by El-Idreesee as fortified, and guarded by troops who watched the persons going and coming:] a well-known place in Alr~uwm [or the territory of the Greek Empire ], mentioned by Imra-el-Keys, [as El-Idreesee also says,] in the words, bakaY SaAHibiY lam~aA raA^aY Ald~aroba Hawolahu [ My companion wept when he saw the drb around him; knowing himself to be in the power of the Greeks]. (MF, TA.) [Hence,] Any place of entrance, (Kh, T, M, A, Mgh [in my copy of which it is written darab in all its senses], K,) or a narrow pass, (Mgh,) to [ the territory of ] Alr~uwm : (Kh, T, M, A, Mgh, K:) or such as is not open at both ends: such as is open at both ends being called ↓ darabN : (K:) or a place of entrance between two mountains: (Msb:) or a narrow pass in mountains: and hence it has another meaning well known: (S:) [i. e.] the gate of a sik~ap [here meaning street: misunderstood by Golius, who has consequently explained darobN as having, for one of its meaning, “ porta ingressusve palmeti ”]; used in this sense by the Arabs because it [i. e. the drb properly so called] is like a gate, or entrance, to that whereto it leads: (Msb:) or the gate of a wide sik~ap : (T:) or a wide gate of a sik~ap ; and the largest gate; (M, K;) both of which explanations mean the same: (M:) and also a wide sik~ap itself: so in the phrase, zuqaAqN A^awo darobN gayoru naAfi*K [ a narrow street or a wide street not being a thoroughfare ]: (Mgh: [in my copy of which, darabN is put for darobN :]) [but in the present day, and as used by El-Makreezee and others, a by-street, whether wide or narrow, branching off from a great street, or passing through a HaArap (or quarter ), open, or having a gate, at each end: ] pl. duruwbN (Kh, T, M, Mgh, TA) and diraAbN . (Sb, K. [The former pl., the only one commonly known, is not mentioned in the K.]) ― -b2- Also A place in which dates are put to dry. (M, K.)

[Hence,] Any place of entrance, (Kh, T, M, A, Mgh [in my copy of which it is written darab in all its senses], K,) or a narrow pass, (Mgh,) to [ the territory of ] Alr~uwm : (Kh, T, M, A, Mgh, K:) or such as is not open at both ends: such as is open at both ends being called ↓ darabN : (K:) or a place of entrance between two mountains: (Msb:) or a narrow pass in mountains: and hence it has another meaning well known: (S:) [i. e.] the gate of a sik~ap [here meaning street: misunderstood by Golius, who has consequently explained darobN as having, for one of its meaning, “ porta ingressusve palmeti ”]; used in this sense by the Arabs because it [i. e. the drb properly so called] is like a gate, or entrance, to that whereto it leads: (Msb:) or the gate of a wide sik~ap : (T:) or a wide gate of a sik~ap ; and the largest gate; (M, K;) both of which explanations mean the same: (M:) and also a wide sik~ap itself: so in the phrase, zuqaAqN A^awo darobN gayoru naAfi*K [ a narrow street or a wide street not being a thoroughfare ]: (Mgh: [in my copy of which, darabN is put for darobN :]) [but in the present day, and as used by El-Makreezee and others, a by-street, whether wide or narrow, branching off from a great street, or passing through a HaArap (or quarter ), open, or having a gate, at each end: ] pl. duruwbN (Kh, T, M, Mgh, TA) and diraAbN . (Sb, K. [The former pl., the only one commonly known, is not mentioned in the K.]) ― -b2- Also A place in which dates are put to dry. (M, K.)

definition: A certain animalcule ( duwayob~apN ), (S, K,) that dives in water: (S:) or a certain black animalcule that swims upon water: (Mgh:) or a certain worm ( duwdapN ), that is in pools left by torrents...
sourceDefinition: A certain animalcule ( duwayob~apN ), (S, K,) that dives in water: (S:) or a certain black animalcule that swims upon water: (Mgh:) or a certain worm ( duwdapN ), that is in pools left by torrents when their water sinks into the earth: (IDrd, K:) or a certain worm ( dwdp ) having two heads, seen in water when it becomes little in quantity: (IB:) pl. daEaAmiySu and daEaAmiSu . (S.) ― -b2- [Hence, app.,] (assumed tropical:) One who enters much into affairs; who is a frequent visitor of kings. (K.) And hence, AlA^aTofaAlu daEaAmiySu Aljan~api , meaning (assumed tropical:) [ Infants will be ] roamers in Paradise: they will not be debarred from any dwelling: (K:) a trad.: but the words occurring in a trad. of Aboo-Hureyreh are SigaArukumo daEaAmiySu Aljan~api [ Your little children &c.]. (TA.) ― -b3- Also The embryo in the belly of a mare until the fortieth day: then its make becomes apparent, and it is called duwdapN , until three months old: when it is called saliylN . (Kr, TA.)

(K.) ― -b3- dagarato Haloqa AlS~abiY~ , (TK,) aor. , (K,) inf. n. dagorN , (S, K,) She pressed the throat, or fauces, of the child, (K, * TA,) on account of the pain termed AlEu*orapu , (S, * TA,) and (or that is to say, TA) raised his uvula with her finger, (S, K, TA,) compressing that part on the occasion of the pain's being excited by the blood. So in the trad., EalaAma tuEa*~ibona A^awolaAdakun~a biAld~agori Wherefore do ye torment your children by raising the uvula &c.: (S:) and laA tuEa*~ibona A^awolaAdakun~a biAld~agori Torment ye not your children by pressing the throat, or fauces, &c. (TA.) ― -b5- dagara Al$~aYo'a biAl$~aYo'i , (TK,) aor . and inf. n. as above, (K,) He mixed the thing with the thing. definition: (TA) and ↓ dagorapN (S, A, K) The act of snatching a thing unawares;
sourceDefinition: (TA) and ↓ dagorapN (S, A, K) The act of snatching a thing unawares; seizing it hastily when its owner is unawares: (S, A, K:) or the springing, or rushing, upon a commodity, to snatch it unawares: or the filling one's hand with a thing and carrying it off. (TA.) Hence the trad. (S, A) of 'Alee, (TA,) ↓ laAqaToEa fiY Ald~agorapi [ There shall be no amputation of the hand for snatching a thing unawares: &c. ]. (S, A, TA.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. yadiq~u , inf. n. dif~apN , (S, Msb, K,) It (a thing, S) was, or became, daqiyq , which means the contr. of galiyZ ; as also ↓ Astdq~ : (S, K:) [i. e. it was, or became, thin as meaning slender, or small in diameter or circumference as compared with length: also small in all dimensions; small in size; minute, or fine, either as a whole, or in its component particles: and sometimes, as said of a garment or the like, thin, or fine, as opposed to thick or coarse; like raq~a :] contr. of galuZa : (Msb:) ↓ Astdq~ is said of the hilaAl [or moon a little after or before the change], and of other things. (TA.) [See also riq~apN .] ― -b2- And [hence], aor. and inf. n. as above, (tropical:) He, or it, was, or became, little in estimation, paltry, inconsiderable, mean, vile, or contemptible. (TA.) One says to him who refuses to confer a benefit, daq~a bika xuluquka (assumed tropical:) [ Thy nature, or natural disposition, hath rendered thee mean, &c.; the verb being made trans. by bi , agreeably with a common usage mentioned in p. 141]. (TA.) ― -b3- Also, [aor. and] inf. n. as above, said of a thing, an affair, or a case, [and of speech, or language,] (assumed tropical:) It was, or became, subtile, nice, abstruse, recondite, or obscure. (Msb.) And you say, daq~a fiY kalaAmihi (tropical:) [ He was, or became, subtile, nice, abstruse, &c., in his speech, or language ]. (TA.) -A2- daq~ahu , (S, M, Msb, K,) aor. , inf. n. daq~N , (M, Msb,) He broke it, (M, K, TA,) or crushed it, (M,) in any manner: (M, TA:) or he bruised, brayed, or pounded, it; i. e., he beat it with a thing so that he broke it, or crushed it: (M, K: *) namely, a thing, (S, M, TA,) such as medicine, &c. (TA.) ― -b2- [And hence, He beat it; namely, a garment or the like; in washing and whitening it. And daq~a AlbaAba He knocked at the door for admission.] ― -b3- And [hence also, (in the CK, erroneously, “ or, ”) as appears from what follows,] (assumed tropical:) He made it apparent; showed, exhibited, manifested, or revealed, it: (K:) so says IAar, citing the following verse of Zuheyr: tadaArakotumaA EabosFA wa*uboyaAna baEodamaA tafaAnawoA wadaq~uwA bayonahumo EiTora mano$imi (TA:) i. e. Ye two repaired the condition of the tribes of 'Abs and Dhubyán by peace, ( talaAfayotumaA A^amorahumaA biAlS~uloHi ,) after they had shared, one with another, in destruction, and had brayed [ among themselves ] the perfume of Menshim as a sign of their having leagued together against their enemy; i. e., after slaughter had come upon the last of their men, as upon the last of those who perfumed themselves with the perfume of Menshim: for [it is said that] mn$m is the name of a woman who sold perfume in Mekkeh, and a party bought of her some perfume, and leagued together to fight their enemy, making the dipping of their hands in that perfume to be a sign of their league; and they fought until they were slain to the last of them: whence the prov., A^a$oA^amu mino EiTori mano$ima : (EM p. 117:) [so that, accord. to this explanation, which is one of many, mn$m is made perfectly decl. for the sake of the rhyme:] or the meaning is, (assumed tropical:) after they had manifested enmities and faults. (TA.) One says also, in cases of enmity, laA^aduq~an~a $uEuwraka , meaning (assumed tropical:) I will assuredly manifest thy circumstances. (TA.) -A3- duq~a , inf. n. daq~N and diq~N , He was seized with the malady termed diq~ [i. e. hectic fever ]. (MA.)

definition: Soft dust swept by the wind (S, K) from the ground: pl.
sourceDefinition: Soft dust swept by the wind (S, K) from the ground: pl. duqaqN : (S:) or dust swept from the ground; as also ↓ duqaAqapN : (TA:) or duqaqu Alt~uraAbi signifies fine dust; and duq~apN is its sing.: (M:) or, accord. to IB, the sing. of duqaqN is ↓ duq~aY , like as the sing. of julalN is jul~aY . (TA.) ― -b2- Also Seeds that are used in cooking, for seasoning food, (IDrd, M, K,) bruised, or brayed, (M,) and what are mixed therewith; (IDrd;) such as are termed qazoH , and the like: all such seeds of the cooking-pot are called duq~ap by the people of Mekkeh: (IDrd, Sgh:) and salt with such seeds mixed therewith: (M, K:) this is the application now commonly obtaining: (TA:) or salt alone: (M:) or salt bruised, or brayed: (Lth, K:) whence the saying, maA lahu duq~apN He has not salt. (Lth, M, K. *) ― -b3- And [hence,] (tropical:) Beauty, or prettiness: (M, K, TA:) whence the phrase AimoraA^apN laA duq~apa lahaA , (M,) or qaliylapu Ald~uq~api , (K,) or maA lahaA duq~apN , (TA,) (tropical:) A woman who is not beautiful, or pretty; (M, K; *) who has not beauty, or prettiness. (TA.) ― -b4- Also A certain ornament ( HaloYN ) of the people of Mekkeh. (K.) ― -b5- And The small, or young, ( Ha$ow ,) of camels. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: contr. of galiyZN (JK, * S, M, * Msb, K) and jaliylN ; (Msb;) as also ↓ duqaAqN and ↓ diq~N ; (S, K;) the last contr. of jil~N : (JK, S, M:) [i. e. Slender, or small in diameter or circumference as compared with length: also small in all dimensions; small in size; minute, or fine, either as a whole, or in its component particles: and sometimes, as applied to a garment or the like, thin, or fine, as opposed to thick or coarse; like raqiyqN : but properly,] daqiyqN differs from raqiyqN ; the former signifying the contr. of galiyZN [as stated above], and the latter, the contr. of vaxiynN : therefore one says HasFA raqiyqN and HasFA vaxiynN [“ thin soup ” and “ thick soup ”], but not HasFA daqiyqN ; and one says sayofN daqiyqu AlmaDoribi [ a sword thin in the edge, or in the part next the point ]; and rumoHN daqiyqN [ a slender spear ]; and guSonN daqiyqN [ a slender branch ]; and HabolN daqiyqN [ a slender rope ]: (IB, TA:) pl. [of mult. diqaAqN and of pauc.] A^adiq~apN . (Msb.) One says, walaA jil~N ↓ maA lahu diq~N [ He has neither slender, or small, or fine, nor thick, or great, or coarse ]; i. e. daqiyqN walaA jaliylN . (S in art. jl .) And A^axa*otu wajil~ahu ↓ diq~ahu [ I took the slender, &c., thereof, and the thick, &c., thereof ]; like as one says, Ax*t qaliylahu wa kaviyrahu . (S in the present art.) And it is said in a trad., wajil~ahu ↓ Aall~`hum~a A@gofiroliY *anobiY kul~ahu diq~ahu [ O God, forgive me all my sin, the small thereof and the great thereof ]. (TA.) ↓ $ajarN diq~N means Shrubs, bushes, or small trees: (M:) opposed to $ajarN jil~N . (Lth in art. jl , and Mgh in art. bql .) Accord. to AHn, ↓ diq~N signifies Plants that are slender and soft to the camels, so that the weak of the camels, and the young, and such as has its teeth worn down to the sockets, and the sick, eat them: or, as some say, their small leaves: (M:) or slender and long leaves of the A^araAk : and grain trodden out but not winnowed: pl. A^adoqaAqN . (JK.) And ↓ Hulalu diq~K means Thin, or fine, [ garments, or dresses, of the kind called ] Hulal ; opposed to Hulalu jil~K : (Mgh:) or ↓ diq~N signifies the contr. of jil~N as applied to carpets, and to the garments called A^akosiyap [pl. of kisaA=' ] and the like, and to the [ cloth called ] Hilos , and to the mat and the like. (TA in art. jal .) ― -b2- [Hence,] daqiyqN is also applied to a thing, an affair, or a case, as meaning (assumed tropical:) Little in estimation, paltry, inconsiderable, mean, vile, or contemptible; in this case, contr. of jaliylN : (IB, TA:) and means also (tropical:) niggardly, stingy, or avaricious; (M, TA;) in whom is little, or no, good; (M, K, TA;) applied to a man: (M:) pl. [of pauc.] A^adiq~apN and [of mult.] diqaAqN and A^adiq~aA='u . (TA.) ― -b3- Also, applied to a thing, an affair, or a case, (assumed tropical:) Subtile, nice, abstruse, recondite, or obscure: (M, K, TA:) [applied likewise to speech; and so ↓ diq~N :] you say, jaA='a bikalaAmK diq~K and daqiyqK (tropical:) [ He uttered subtile, nice, abstruse, recondite, or obscure, speech ]. (TA.) ― -b4- [The fem.] ↓ dqyqp [used as a subst.] signifies (tropical:) Small cattle; i. e. sheep or goats; opposed to jaliylapN (JK, K, TA) which signifies camels: (JK, TA:) pl. daqaAy^iqu . (TA.) You say, maA lahu daqiyqapN walaA jaliylapN (tropical:) He has neither sheep, or goats, nor camels: (TA:) or neither a sheep, or goat, nor a she-camel. (M.) And kamo daqiyqatuka (tropical:) How many are thy sheep, or goats? (TA.) And huwa raAEiY Ald~aqaAy^iqi (tropical:) He is the pastor of sheep, or goats. (TA.) And A^aEoTaAhu mino daqaAy^iqi AlmaAli (tropical:) [ He gave him of the small cattle ]. (TA.) ― -b5- Also, [i. e. ↓ daqiyqapN ,] as a conventional term of the astronomer, (assumed tropical:) [ A minute of a circle; ] the sixtieth [in the O, and in some copies, app. most, of the K, erroneously, “ thirtieth, ” as remarked by MF and SM and others,] part of a darajap [or degree of a circle: pl. daqaAy^iqu , as above]. (K, TA.) ― -b6- ↓ [And (assumed tropical:) A minute of time; the fourth part of a darajap (or degree ) of time: pl. as above. ― -b7- ↓ daqiyqapN is also sing. of daqaAy^iqu as syn. with madaAq~N , q. v.] -A2- daqiyqN signifies also Flour, or meal, (S, M, Msb, K, &c.,) of wheat &c.; (Msb;) [thus used as a subst.; as though] in the sense of madoquwqN . (Msb, TA.) ― -b2- [Hence, Farina, ] You say, jaraY Ald~aqiyqu fiY Als~unobuli [ The farina pervaded the ears of wheat ]. (L in art. qmH .) And Hamala Ald~aqiyqa [ It bore farina ] is said of seed-produce [or corn]. (TA in art. Hnq . [See 4 in that art.])
