definition: (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K) and ↓ DaboEN , (Msb, K,) the former of the dial.
sourceDefinition: (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K) and ↓ DaboEN , (Msb, K,) the former of the dial. of Keys and the latter of the dial. of Temeem, (Msb,) [The female hyena; or the hyena, male and female; ] a certain animal of prey, ( sabuEN , [but see what follows,]) (K,) well known, (S, O,) the worst, or most abominable, of sibaAE , (Mgh,) resembling the wolf, except that, when it runs, it is as though it were lame, wherefore it is called AlEarojaA='u : it flees from him who holds in his hand a colocynth: [and they assert that] the dogs bark not at him who retains with him its teeth: if its skin is bound upon the belly of her that is pregnant, she casts not her young: if seed is measured in a measure covered with its skin, the seed-produce is secure from the banes thereof: and the application of its gall-bladder as a collyrium sharpens the sight: (K:) it is not reckoned among the hostile animals to which the appellation of sabuEN is applied, wherefore the Sunneh allows that its flesh may be eaten, and requires that a compensation be made for it [by the sacrifice of a ram] if it be smitten [and killed] in the sacred territory by a person in the state of ihrám: (TA voce sabuEN :) the word is of the fem. gender, (S, * Mgh, * O, * Msb, K, *) and is [said to be] applied peculiarly to the female; (Msb;) the male being called ↓ DiboEaAnN , (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K,) of which the pl. is DabaAEiynu ; (S, O, Msb, K;) but AHát disapproved this pl.; (O;) and the female is called [also] ↓ DiboEaAnapN , of which the pl. is DiboEaAnaAtN ; (S, O, K;) or DiboEaAnapN has not been heard applied to the female, but DabuEN only, and it seems that J has mentioned DiboEaAnapN as applied to the female from his having supposed DiboEaAnaAtN to be pl. of DiboEaAnapN , whereas it is pl. of DiboEaAnN , being like rijaAlaAtN and jimaAlaAtN : (IB in a marginal note in one of my copies of the S:) but some say that DabuEN or DaboEN is applied to the male; and the female is termed DaboEapN , thus with a quiescent letter: (Msb:) or, accord. to Ibn-'Abbád, the female is termed DabuEapN , and its pl. [or rather the coll. gen. n.] is DabuEN ; (O, K;) or DabaEapN is not allowable: (S, K:) the pl. of DabuEN or DaboEN is A^aDobuEN , (K,) a pl. of pauc., (TA,) and DibaAEN , (K,) or the former is pl. of DaboEN , (Msb,) and the latter is pl. of DabuEN , (Mgh, Msb,) and is of the male and of the female, (S, K,) and DubuEN , (K,) as though this were pl. of DibaAEN , (AAF, TA,) and DubEN [a contraction of DubuEN ] (K) and DubuEaAtN and DubuwEapN (TA [in which it is indicated that this last is pl. of DaboEN ]) and [quasi-pl. n.] ↓ maDobaEapN . (O, K.) One says A^amodaru ↓ DiboEaAnN , [in the CK, erroneously, DaboEaAnu ,] meaning, [ A male hyena ] inflated in the sides, big in the belly: or, accord. to some, whose sides are defiled with earth, or dust. (S.) And sayolN jaAr~u AlD~abuEi A torrent that draws forth the DabuE from its den; (O, K; in the CK, jAr~N AlS~abuEa ;) hence meaning (assumed tropical:) a torrent produced by vehement rain. (TA.) And dalojapu AlD~abuEi [ The night-journeying of the hyena ]; because the DabuE goes round about until midnight. (O, K.) And maA yaxofaY *`lika EalaY AlD~abuEi [ That is not unapparent to the hyena ]: because the DabuE is deemed stupid. (TA.) A^aHomaqu mina AlD~abuEi [ More stupid than the hyena ] is a prov. (Meyd.) And A^akalatohumu AlD~abuEu (tropical:) [ The hyena devoured them ] is said of such as are held in mean estimation. (TA.) [But this may be otherwise rendered, as will be seen from what follows.] The saying of a poet, tafar~aqato ganamiY yawomFA faqulotu lahaA yaA rab~i sal~iTo EalayohaA Al*iy^oba waAlD~abuEaA [ My sheep, or goats, dispersed themselves, one day, and I said in relation to them, O my Lord, set upon them the wolf and the hyena ], is said to mean an imprecation, that the wolf might kill the living of them, and the hyena devour the dead of them: or, as some say, it means that the speaker prayed for their safety; because, when both fall upon the sheep, or goats, each of them is diverted from the sheep, or goats, by the other; and thus means the saying, Aall~`hum~a DabuEFA wa*iy^obFA [ O God, send a hyena and a wolf ]: but the more probable meaning of the poet is an imprecation, the consequence of his anger and fatigue; and the word sal~iTo imports a notification of this meaning. (IB, TA.) ― -b2- [The pl.] AlD~ibaAEu is applied to (assumed tropical:) Numerous stars below banaAt naEo$ : (O, K:) or [ the stars beta, gamma, delta and mu, of Bootes; i. e.] the star upon the head, and that upon [ each of ] the shoulders, and that upon the club, of AlEaw~aA=' : and the name of A^awolaAdu AlD~ibaAEi is given to [ The stars θ, ι, κ and λ, app. with some other faint stars around these, of Bootes; i. e.] the stars upon the left hand and fore arm, and what surround the hand, of the faint stars, of AlEaw~aA=' . (Kzw.) ― -b3- AlD~abuEu also signifies (tropical:) The year of drought or sterility or dearth; (S, IAth, O, Msb, K, TA;) that is destructive; severe: of the fem. gender. (TA.) So in a verse cited in art. AmA [voce A^am~aA , and again, with a variation, voce A_im~aA ]. (S, O. [But it is here said in the TA that AlD~abuEu in this instance means the animal of prey thus called.]) [Hence also,] it is related in a trad. of Aboo-Dharr, that a man said, yaA rasuwla A@ll~`hi A^akalatonaA AlD~abuEu (tropical:) [ O Apostle of God, the year of drought has consumed us ]: and he prayed for them. (TA.) [See also two other exs. voce *iy^obN .] ― -b4- Also (tropical:) Hunger. (Ibn-'Abbád, O, TA.) ― -b5- And (assumed tropical:) Evil, or mischief. (TA.) El-'Okeyleeyeh said, “ When a man whose evil, or mischief, we feared removed from us, we used to light a fire behind him: ” and being asked “ Why? ” she said, liyataHaw~ala DabuEuhu maEahu , i. e. (assumed tropical:) In order that his evil, or mischief, might go away with him. (IAar, TA.)

A_iDaAEapN ; (S;) both signify the same; (S, O, Msb, K;) He made, or caused, the thing to perish, or become lost; he destroyed it, wasted it, or lost it. (Msb, K, TA.) Hence, Day~aEuwA fulaAnFA is used by the vulgar as meaning They beheaded such a one with the sword. (TA.) It is said in a prov., AlS~ayofa Day~aEoti All~abana [ In the spring, or in the summer, thou losedst the milk ], in which the t is with kesr when the words are addressed to a male, or to a female, or to a pl. number, because originally addressed to a woman, the wife of a wealthy man, whom she disliked because of his being aged, wherefore he divorced her, and a poor man married her, and she sent to her first husband requesting a gift, and he answered her thus; (S, O, K; *) AlSyf being in the accus. case as an adv. n.: so says Yaakoob: (S, O:) or El-Aswad Ibn-Hurmuz divorced his wife El- ' Anood Esh-Shenneeyeh, (O, K,) of the BenooShenn, (TA,) preferring to her a beautiful and wealthy woman of his people; (O, K; *) then there occurred between them what led to their separation, and he sought to obtain [again] El- ' Anood, and sent a message to her; but in replying to him she said, A^ano$aA^ota taTolubu waSolanaA fiY AlS~ayofi Day~aEota All~abano [ Thou hast begun to seek our union: in the spring, or in the summer, thou losedst the milk ]: (O, * K:) the t in this case being with fet-h. (K. [See more in Freytag's Arab. Prov. ii. 197-8, or in Har p. 577; in both of which, however, and in the O, Dy~Et is with kesr in the latter case, as in the former.]) [One says also, Dy~E Eahodahu , meaning He broke his compact, contract, or covenant ]. The phrase, in a trad., nahaY Eano AlmaAli ↓ A_iDaAEapi means He forbade the expending of wealth otherwise than in obedience to God, and the squandering thereof, and extravagance. (TA.) ― -b2- See also the next paragraph.

sourceDefinition: an inf. n. of 1. (S, &c.) ― -b2- See DayaAEN , below, last sentence but one. ― -b3- Also A single case, or occasion, of perishing, coming to nought, passing away, or becoming lost; or of being left, left or let alone, or neglected. (TA.) ― -b4- tarakotuhu biDayoEapK means I left him unsought-after, or unminded, or unmissed. (TA. [See also a similar phrase voce DayaAEN .]) -A2- Also i. q. EaqaArN [meaning An estate consisting of land, or of land and a house, or of a house or land yielding a revenue, or of a house and palm-trees, or the like ]; (S, O, Msb, K;) and [particularly] land yielding a revenue; (K;) or with the people of the towns and villages and cultivated lands it signifies the property, of a man, consisting of palm-trees and grape-vines and land: but the Arabs [of the desert] know not the word in this sense: (Az, TA:) IF says, I do not reckon the application of this word as a name for the EaqaAr to be of the original language, but think it to be an innovation in speech; and I have heard it said that this is termed a DyEp because, when frequent attention to it is neglected, it perishes; and if it be so, this is an evidence of what we have said, that it is of the innovated speech: (O, TA:) the dim. is ↓ DuyayoEapN , for which one should not say DuwayoEapN : (S, O, K:) the pl. is DiyaAEN and DiyaEN , (S, O, Msb, K,) as though the latter were a contraction of the former, (Msb,) and DayoEaAtN : (K:) accord. to Lth, the first of these pls. signifies places of alighting or abode or settlement; which are thus called because, when the paying frequent attention to them, or taking good care of them, and the keeping them, or putting them, in a good state, or state of repair, is neglected, they come to nought: and DayoEaAtN occurs in a trad. as meaning the means of subsistence. (TA.) And, (T, O, Msb, K,) as used by the Arabs [of the desert], who know not the word in any other sense than this, (T, O,) A craft, or handicraft, by which one gains his subsistence; a mode, or manner, of gain; or any habitual work or occupation of a man; (T, O, Msb, K) as the sewing of skins or boots and the like; and the twisting of ropes; and the weaving, or plaiting, of palm-leaves; and the culture of palm-trees ( Eamalu Aln~axoli ); and the pasturing of camels; and the like thereof; (T, O;) including the sowing, or tilling, of land: (TA:) or the DayoEap of the Arabs was the management, or tending, of camels and of sheep and goats: and the term includes a man's craft, or handicraft, or means of gain: (Sh, O:) and his traffic: (Sh, O, K:) one says to a man, qumo A_ilaY DayoEatika [ Arise to thy craft, &c.]: (Sh, O:) and kul~u rajulK waDayoEatahu , [ Every man should occupy himself with his proper craft, &c.] (Msb.) A^afo$aY A@ll~`hu , DayoEatahu , occurring in a trad., means God made or may God make, his means of subsistence to be abundant. (TA.) And one says, fa$ato DayoEatuhu , [or, more commonly, fa$ato Ealayohi DayoEatuhu , as in the TA in art. f$w , &c.,] which is said to mean His property was, or became, large, or abundant, [or wide-spread, ] so that he was unable to collect it together: and [hence] his means of attaining his object [or his affairs (as in the TA in art. f$w )] became disordered so that he knew not with which of them to begin: (TA:) or he took to doing an affair that did not concern him: (TA, and Ham p. 33:) it is nearly like the saying Ait~asaEa Alxaroqu EalaY Alr~aAqiEi [expl. in art. xrq ]. (Ham ibid.) And A_in~iY laA^araY DayoEapF laA yuSoliHuhaA A_il~aA DajoEapN [ Verily I see property that nothing but a sleep will restore to a right state ] a prov.; said by a pastor whose camels had dispersed themselves, and who, desiring to collect them together, and being unable to do so, sought aid of sleep. (O.)

EaqaArN [meaning An estate consisting of land, or of land and a house, or of a house or land yielding a revenue, or of a house and palm-trees, or the like ]; (S, O, Msb, K;) and [particularly] land yielding a revenue; (K;) or with the people of the towns and villages and cultivated lands it signifies the property, of a man, consisting of palm-trees and grape-vines and land: but the Arabs [of the desert] know not the word in this sense: (Az, TA:) IF says, I do not reckon the application of this word as a name for the EaqaAr to be of the original language, but think it to be an innovation in speech; and I have heard it said that this is termed a DyEp because, when frequent attention to it is neglected, it perishes; and if it be so, this is an evidence of what we have said, that it is of the innovated speech: (O, TA:) the dim. is ↓ DuyayoEapN , for which one should not say DuwayoEapN : (S, O, K:) the pl. is DiyaAEN and DiyaEN , (S, O, Msb, K,) as though the latter were a contraction of the former, (Msb,) and DayoEaAtN : (K:) accord. to Lth, the first of these pls. signifies places of alighting or abode or settlement; which are thus called because, when the paying frequent attention to them, or taking good care of them, and the keeping them, or putting them, in a good state, or state of repair, is neglected, they come to nought: and DayoEaAtN occurs in a trad. as meaning the means of subsistence. (TA.) And, (T, O, Msb, K,) as used by the Arabs [of the desert], who know not the word in any other sense than this, (T, O,) A craft, or handicraft, by which one gains his subsistence; a mode, or manner, of gain; or any habitual work or occupation of a man; (T, O, Msb, K) as the sewing of skins or boots and the like; and the twisting of ropes; and the weaving, or plaiting, of palm-leaves; and the culture of palm-trees ( Eamalu Aln~axoli ); and the pasturing of camels; and the like thereof; (T, O;) including the sowing, or tilling, of land: (TA:) or the DayoEap of the Arabs was the management, or tending, of camels and of sheep and goats: and the term includes a man's craft, or handicraft, or means of gain: (Sh, O:) and his traffic: (Sh, O, K:) one says to a man, qumo A_ilaY DayoEatika [ Arise to thy craft, &c.]: (Sh, O:) and kul~u rajulK waDayoEatahu , [ Every man should occupy himself with his proper craft, &c.] (Msb.) A^afo$aY A@ll~`hu , DayoEatahu , occurring in a trad., means God made or may God make, his means of subsistence to be abundant. (TA.) And one says, fa$ato DayoEatuhu , [or, more commonly, fa$ato Ealayohi DayoEatuhu , as in the TA in art. f$w , &c.,] which is said to mean His property was, or became, large, or abundant, [or wide-spread, ] so that he was unable to collect it together: and [hence] his means of attaining his object [or his affairs (as in the TA in art. f$w )] became disordered so that he knew not with which of them to begin: (TA:) or he took to doing an affair that did not concern him: (TA, and Ham p. 33:) it is nearly like the saying Ait~asaEa Alxaroqu EalaY Alr~aAqiEi [expl. in art. xrq ]. (Ham ibid.) And A_in~iY laA^araY DayoEapF laA yuSoliHuhaA A_il~aA DajoEapN [ Verily I see property that nothing but a sleep will restore to a right state ] a prov.; said by a pastor whose camels had dispersed themselves, and who, desiring to collect them together, and being unable to do so, sought aid of sleep. (O.)

(Msb.)

definition: The [ article of apparel called ] TayolasaAn [q.
sourceDefinition: The [ article of apparel called ] TayolasaAn [q. v.]: (O, K:) it was not known to the Arabs. (O.) [See De Sacy's Chrest. Arabe, sec. ed., ii. 267-269: and Dozy's Dict. des Noms des Vêtements chez les Arabes, pp. 254-262. It is now applied in Egypt to a kind of head-veil worn by women, the two ends of which generally hang down behind, nearly reaching to the ground: but it is often worn in another manner; about a quarter of it hanging down behind, and the remainder being turned over the head, and under the chin, and over the head again, so that the middle part covers the bosom, and both ends hang down behind: it is a piece of muslin, or the like, often embroidered at each end; about three quarters of a yard in width, and in length nearly equal to twice the height of the wearer.]

sourceDefinition: , aor. and , (S, M, Msb, K) inf. n. TumuwsN (S, M, A, Msb, K) and TamosN , (Zj;) It (a thing, as, for instance, a road, or path, T, S, M, Msb, and a writing, T, or a relic, trace, or vestige, A) became effaced, or obliterated; (T, S, M, A, Msb, K;) the trace, or mark, thereof (i. e. of a road &c.) became effaced, or obliterated: (M:) or it (a thing) quitted, or went from, its form, or shape: (Zj:) and ↓ AnTms (said of a relic, or remain, or of a mark, or trace, and of a writing, TA, or other thing, S) has the first of the significations above; (S, A, K;) and so ↓ tTm~s . (S, K.) ― -b2- It ((assumed tropical:) a star, T, M, and (assumed tropical:) the moon, and the sight, or eye, M) lost, or became deprived of, its light. (T, M.) [See also the pass. form in what follows.] ― -b3- Tumuwsu Alqalobi means The heart's becoming in a bad, or corrupt, state. (O. [See also the last sentence of this paragraph.]) ― -b4- Tamasa Alr~ajulu The man was, or became, distant, or remote; or went to a distance, or far away. (T, M, O, K.) ― -b5- And Tamasa biEayonihi , (M, O, K,) inf. n. TamosN , (IDrd, O,) He looked far: (M, O, K:) or he looked at a thing from afar. (IDrd, O.) -A2- Tamasahu , (S, IKtt, Msb, K,) and Tamasa Ealayohi , (M, TA,) aor. , (M, Msb,) inf. n. TamosN , (S, Msb, K,) He effaced it, or obliterated it; (S, M, Msb, K;) he effaced, or obliterated, (M,) or removed, (TA,) or extirpated, (K,) the trace, or mark, thereof; (M, K, TA;) as also ↓ Tm~shu , (M, TA,) inf. n. taTomiysN : (TA:) or he destroyed it: (IKtt:) and Tamasa Almakotuwba is also expl. as signifying he covered the writing by folding. (Har p. 505.) You say, Tamasatohu Alr~iyHu The wind effaced, or obliterated, it; namely, the trace, or mark, of a thing. (A.) And it is said in the Kur [lxxvii. 8], faA_i*aA Aln~ujuwmu Tumisato And when the stars shall have their traces extirpated: (O, K:) or shall lose their light. (T, TA.) ― -b2- Tamasa A^aEoyunahumo , [as in the Kur liv. 37,] (A,) and EalaY A^aEoyunihimo , (T, A,) as in the Kur xxxvi. 66, (T,) He (God) blinded them. (T, TA.) ― -b3- [Hence, app.,] Tamasa Algayomu Aln~ujuwma (tropical:) [ The clouds, or mist, covered, or concealed, the stars; as though it put out their light]. (A.) ― -b4- And [hence also,] Tamasa , aor. , (O, K,) inf. n. TamaAsapN , (O, * K, * TK,) (assumed tropical:) He conjectured, or computed by conjecture, (O, K, TA, TK,) a thing: (TK:) because the doing so is generally accompanied by the putting of the eyelids together, as though one were blinded. (TA.) ― -b5- Tamasahu , inf. n. TamosN , also signifies He (God) transformed, or metamorphosed, him or it. (TA.) definition: The seventeenth letter of the alphabet: called ZaA='N [and ZaA ].
sourceDefinition: The seventeenth letter of the alphabet: called ZaA='N [and ZaA ]. (TA.) It is a letter peculiar to the Arabic language; and is one of the letters termed majohuwrap [or vocal, i. e. pronounced with the voice, not with the breath only]; and of the letters termed livawiy~ap [or gingival], like v and * . (TA.) As it does not exist in the language of the Nabathæans, they change it into T . (IF, TA.) [It is substituted for the t in the measure AifotaEala and the forms inflected therefrom when immediately following Z ; as in AiZ~alama , for AiZoZalama , for AiZotalama :] and it is substituted for * ; as in tarakotuhu waqiy*FA and waqiyZFA ; as is related on the authorities of ISk and Kr; and as in A^aroDN jilo*aA='N and jiloZaA='N , as is mentioned in the Nawádir el-Aaráb. (TA.) -A2- [As a numeral, it denotes Nine hundred. ]

definition: A certain animal, (TA,) well known;
sourceDefinition: A certain animal, (TA,) well known; (S, Msb, K, TA;) the gazaAl [or gazelle; to which the former word is applied when used unrestrictedly, and which is app. here meant by the latter word, though this seems properly to signify “ a young gazelle ”]; (M;) [it is the gazella dorcas, also called antilope dorcas, of which the ariel, or antilope Arabica, is said to be a variety; or, accord. to some, each is a distinct species of gazelle: the name seems to be properly, but not always (as is shown by an explanation of riy^omN ), applied only to the true antelope of Arabia and adjacent countries, as distinguished from the cervine and bovine antelopes: ] it is a name for the male; which is also called tayosN , when he has become what is termed a vaniY~ [q. v.], which he continues to be termed until he dies: (AHát, Msb, TA:) the female is called ZaboyapN , (AHát, T, M, Msb, K, TA,) and EanozN and maAEizapN : (AHát, Msb, TA:) the dual is ZaboyaAni : (Msb, TA:) and the pl. is A^aZobK , (S, M, Msb, K,) originally A^aZobuYN , (S, Msb,) a pl. of pauc., (S,) and ZubiY~N and ZibaA='u , (S, M, Msb, K,) which last is of the masc. and fem., (M, Msb,) and ZabayaAtN , (S, M, Msb, K,) which is of the fem. (M, Msb.) One says, bihi daA='u ZaboYK [lit. In him is the disease of a gazelle ]; meaning in him is no disease; as there is [said to be] no disease in the ZbY . (AA, T.) And laka EinodiY miAy^apN sin~a AlZ~aboYi [ To thee I owe a hundred camels of the age of the gazelle ], i. e., all of them vunoyaAn [pl. of vaniY~N , q. v.], because the ZbY does not exceed what is termed A_ivonaA='N . (M.) [See also a verse cited voce sin~N ; in which the phrase fajaA='ato kasin~i AlZ~aboYi means And they came; like the age of the gazelle was the age of every one of them.] It is said in a prov., ↓ laA^atorukan~ahu taroka ZubaY~K Zil~ahu [ I will assuredly forsake him as a little gazelle forsakes the place of its shade ]; because the ZbY , when it leaves its covert, does not return to it: it is said in confirming the relinquishing of anything. (T. [See Zil~N , where other relations of this prov. are mentioned.]) And in another prov., AlZ~ibaA='a EalaY Albaqari , said when the tie of relationship and friendship between two men is severed, and it was used in the Time of Ignorance as a form of divorce: AlZbA' is in the accus. case by reason of Aixotarotu , or AixotaAra , understood, [so that the meaning is I have preferred, or he has preferred, the gazelles to the wild cows, ] by the bqr being meant the women: whence the saying, jaA='a yajur~u baqarahu [expl. in art. bqr ]. (Meyd. [See also Freytag's Arab. Prov. ii. 61.]) And one says, A^atayotuhu Hiyna $ad~a AlZ~aboYa Zil~uhu i. e. [ I came to him when its shade ] confined the ZbY [or gazelle ] by reason of the vehemence of the heat: or, as some relate it, Hiyno na$ada AlZ~aboYu Zil~ahu , meaning Talabahu [i. e., when the gazelle sought its shade ]. (TA.) And it is said in a trad., A_i*aA A^atayotahumo faA@robiDo fiY daArihimo ZaboyFA [expl. voce rabaDa ]. (T, TA.) bihi laA biZaboYK , (S, TA,) or bihi laA biZaboYK A^aEofara , a prov., meaning May this accident befall him, ( liyanozilo bihi h`*ihi AlHaAdivapu ,) not a white antelope, (Meyd,) is said on an occasion of rejoicing at another's affliction, (S, Meyd, TA,) by way of imprecation, i. e. may God make that which has befallen him to cleave to him. (S, TA. [See also Freytag's Arab. Prov. i. 148.]) ― -b2- [ AlZ~ibaA='u and A^awolaAdu AlZ~ibaA='i are mentioned by Freytag as names of Certain stars: in relation to the former of which he refers to Ideler's “ Unters. ” pp. 20-21; and in relation to the latter, to the same work p. 21.] ― -b3- And AlZ~aboYu is the name of A brand, or mark made with a hot iron, peculiar to some of the Arabs. (T, K.)

sourceDefinition: a subst. from Zamiy^a (S, M, K) in both of its senses; (M, K;) [i. e.] it signifies Thirst: (MA:) [or most vehement thirst: or the slightest degree of thirst: ] pl. A^aZomaA='N . (MA.) ― -b2- [And (tropical:) Desire, or a longing, (or, as we often say, a thirsting, ) to meet with a person. See 1.] ― -b3- And (S, M, K) The time, or interval, or period, between two drinkings, or waterings, (T, S, M, K,) in the coming of camels to water: (T:) and the keeping of camels from the water [ during that interval, i. e.] until the extreme limit of the coming thereto: (S:) pl. A^aZomaA='N . (T, S, M.) The shortest Zimo'N of camels is that termed gib~N , i. e., when they come to the water one day and return, and are in the place of pasture a day, and come to the water [again] on the third day; the interval between their two drinkings being termed a Zimo' : this is during the greatest heat: but when Suheyl [i. e. Canopus] rises [aurorally, which it did in Central Arabia, about the commencement of the era of the Flight, on the 4th of August, O. S.], they increase the Zimo' , so that the camels remain in the place of pasture two days, and come to the water on the fourth; and one says, waradato riboEFA : then follow the ximos and the sidos to the Ei$or : and the interval between their two drinkings is termed Zimo'N , whether long or short. (T.) One says, maA baqiYa mino Eumurihi A_il~aA Zimo'u AlHimaAri , (T, S, * K, * TA,) meaning There remained not of his life save a little; [lit., save the period between the two drinkings of the ass; ] (S, K, * TA;) because there is no beast that bears thirst for a shorter time than the ass; (T, S, * K, * TA;) for he comes to the water in summer every day twice. (T, TA.) ― -b4- AlZ~imo'u also signifies (assumed tropical:) The period from birth to death; (K;) or so Zimo'u AlHayaApi . (S, M, TA.) ― -b5- ZimowN is a dial. var. of Zimo'N . (T and M in art. Zmw .)

sourceDefinition: The mountain-rose ( warod jabaliY~ [one of the appellations now applied to the eglantine, or sweet brier, more commonly called the nisoriyn ]): (S, Msb, K:) AHn says, and Arab of the desert informed me that the EabaAl is the rose of the mountain ( warodu Aljabali ), of which is the white, and the red, and the yellow; (O, TA;) having a goodly hip ( daliyk [thus correctly written in the O, but afterwards altered to dil~iyk ,]) in size and redness like the full-grown, unripe date, which, when it becomes ripe, is sweet, and delicious, like the fresh ripe date, and is sent from one to another as a present: (O:) [n. un. with p :] the EabaAlap , he says, has short, curved thorns, its rose is sweet-scented, and it grows so as to compose thickets, (O, TA,) and is depastured, (O,) and it becomes thick, (K,) and staves (O, K) thick and good, (O,) or thick and strong, (TA,) are cut from it: (O, K, TA:) the staff of Moses is said to have been from it: (K, TA:) or, as AHn says, the people assert that the staff of Moses was an EabaAlap . (O.)

sourceDefinition: , inf. n. taEojiylN : see 4, in two places. ― -b2- [It generally relates to some inanimate object.] It is said in the Kur [xxxviii. 15], rab~anaA Eaj~ilo lanaA qiT~anaA qabola yawomi AlHisaAbi [ O our Lord hasten to us our portion before the day of reckoning ]: (TA:) accord. to some, our portion of punishment: but accord. to Sa'eed Ibn-Jubeyr, it means, of Paradise. (TA in art. qT .) And you say, Eaj~alotu A_ilayohi AlmaAla I brought, or conveyed, hastily, or speedily, to him the property; or hastened its coming to him. (Msb.) And Eaj~alotu lahu mina Alv~amani ka*aA I paid him in advance, of the price, such a sum. (S, O.) And Eaj~alahu mina AlkiraA='i ka*aA He gave him in ready money, [or promptly, or quickly, or in advance, ] of the hire, such a sum. (Mgh.) And Eaj~ala lahu Alv~amana He gave to him [ in ready money, or promptly, or quickly, or in advance, the price ]. (Mgh.) And Ej~l naqodahu [ He paid it in ready money, promptly, or quickly ]. (ISk, S and K in art. zkA^ .) And biEotuhu taEojiylFA bitaEojiylK [ I sold it, or I sold to him, present, or ready, merchandise, for present, or ready, money]. (S voce naAjizN , q. v.) And Eaj~alotu All~aHoma , (S, O,) inf. n. as above, (TA,) I cooked the flesh-meat in haste. (S, O.) And ↓ lawo Eaj~alota biA^ay~imika AlEajuwla , a prov., [which, app., is properly rendered Would that thou didst hasten, with thy husbandless woman, the early portion of food called Eajuwl , or the right reading may be AlEij~awola ,] meaning Eaj~ilo bihaA Alz~awaAja [(assumed tropical:) hasten thou, with her, i. e. with thy husbandless woman, marriage ]. (TA.) One says also Eaj~alotumo like as one says lah~anotumo [i. e. Ye supplied, or fed, with the early portion of food called luhonap ; which is also called Eajuwl , or Eij~awol , &c.]. (S, TA. [For lah~anotumo , Golius appears to have read lah~ayotumo , which is evidently wrong.]) ― -b3- Ej~l A^aqiTahu , inf. n. as above; and ↓ tEj~lhu ; He made his [ preparation of dried curd called ] AqT into what are termed EajaAjiyl , (K, TA,) pl. of Euj~aAlN : (TA:) or you say, Eaj~alotu A^aqiTiY EajaAjiyla [ I made my AqT into EjAjyl ]. (O.) -A2- See also 1, first sentence.

sourceDefinition: [inf. n. muEaAjalapN ] i. q. baAdarahu [ He hastened, or made haste, or strove to be first or beforehand, in doing, or attaining, or obtaining, it ]; (M and K in art. bdr ;) namely, a thing. (M ibid.) And EAjl gayorahu A_ilayohi i. q. badarahu Alyh , (M and K in art. bdr ,) like baAdarahu Alyh [ He hastened with another, or vied or strove with him in hastening, to it, or to do, or attain, or obtain, it ]. (M ibid.) ― -b2- [Also He dealt hastily with him. ] And EAjlhu bi*anobihi He punished him for his sin, or crime, or offence, ( A^axa*ahu bihi ,) not granting him any delay, (S, TA. [For bi*anobihi , Golius appears to have read bi*anabihi .])

definition: , (S, Mgh, Msb, TA,) inf.
sourceDefinition: , (S, Mgh, Msb, TA,) inf. n. A_iEojaAlN ; (TA;) and ↓ Ej~lhu , inf. n. taEojiylN ; (S, O, TA;) and ↓ tEj~lhu ; (S;) and ↓ AstEjlhu ; (K, TA;) He incited, excited, urged, instigated, induced, or made, him to haste, hasten, make haste, speed, or be quick; (S, Mgh, Msb, K, TA;) and commanded, or bade, him, to haste, &c. (K.) One says, A^aEojalaniYfaEajilotu lahu [ He incited me, &c., to haste, &c., and I hasted, &c., to him ]. (O, TA.) And it is said in the Kur [xiii. 7], ↓ wayasotaEojiluwnaka biA@ls~ay~iy^api qabola A@loHasanapi [ And they incite thee to haste with that which is evil before that which is good ]: and [in xxii. 46 and xxix. 53,] ↓ wayasotaEojiluwnaka biA@loEa*aAbi [ And they incite thee to haste with the punishment ]: (TA:) and binafosihi ↓ AstEjl signifies He hastened himself. (MA.) ― -b2- AEjlhu signifies also [ He incited him to haste, &c., by going before him: and hence it is expl. as meaning also] sabaqahu [i. e. he preceded him, or it; he had, got, or took, precedence of him, or it; he was, or became, beforehand with him, or it; or he anticipated him, or it ]; as also ↓ Ej~lhu ; and ↓ AstEjlhu : (K:) or ↓ AisotaEojalotuhu signifies I went before him, or preceded him, (S, O, TA,) and so incited him to haste: (TA:) and A^amora rab~ikumo ↓ A^aEajilotumo , in the Kur [vii. 149], means A^asabaqotumo [i. e. Have ye anticipated the command of your Lord? ]: (S, O:) or have ye left [ the fulfilment of ] the command of your Lord incomplete? (Ksh, Bd;) Eajila being made to imply, (Ksh,) or as though it were made to imply, (Bd,) the meaning of sabaqa , wherefore it is made trans. like this latter verb; (Ksh, Bd;) the phrase meaning A^aEajilotumo Eano A^amori rab~ikumo . (Ksh.) wamaA A^aEojalaka Eano qawomika , in the Kur [xx. 85, lit. And what caused thee to hasten from thy party? ], means [virtually] kayofa sabaqotahumo [i. e. how is it that thou camest before thy party? ]. (O.) ― -b3- One says also, AEjl Al$~aYo'a Eano waqotihi [ He did the thing hastily, or hurriedly, before its time ]. (O and K in art. grD .) And AEjlhu Eano A_idoraAkihi [ He made it, or did it, hastily, or hurriedly, or he hurried it, before, or so as to prevent, its becoming mature ]. (S and K * in art. fTr .) And A^aEojalotuhu Eani A@sotilaAli sayofihi i. e. ↓ Eajilotu bihi [ I was quick, or beforehand, with him, and ] I flurried him, so that he could not draw his sword: whence the saying, raA^aY SayodFA farakiba farasahu waA^uEojila Eano Harobatihi A^awo sawoTihi [ He saw an animal of the chase, and he mounted his horse, or mare, and was incited by haste so as to be prevented from taking his dart or his whip ]: and the saying, halaAku AlmaAli A^aEojalahu Eano A^adaAy^ihaA , meaning manaEahu [i. e. The perishing of the cattle, or property, prevented, or precluded, him from paying it ], namely, the zakaAp [or poor-rate ]; which is an instance of the extension of the signification. (Mgh.) ― -b4- A^aEojalato said of the pregnant, (O,) or of a she-camel, (K,) [as though for AEjlt waladahaA ,] She brought forth, (O,) or cast, (K,) her offspring before its maturity. (O, K.) ― -b5- And AEjl said of palmtrees, ( naxol ,) They had ripe fruit before its full time. (Mgh.) ― -b6- And, said of a camel, He leaped [ up ] when the rider had mounted him and had not yet become firmly seated upon him. (TA.) [See muEojilN .]

definition: and ↓ EajalapN , both inf.
sourceDefinition: and ↓ EajalapN , both inf. ns. of Eajila [q. v.], (Mgh, Msb,) are Syn. with suroEapN ; (K;) contr. of buTo'N : (S, O:) the latter is expl. by Th as signifying the seeking, and pursuing, or endeavouring after, a thing before its proper time, or season; and as proceeding from the desire of the soul; wherefore it is generally discommended in the Kur-án, so that it is said to be from the Devil. (TA.) It is said in the Kur [xxi. 38], xuliqa A@loA_inosaAnu mino EajalK , meaning, it is said, Man is composed of haste; (O;) so says Fr, and in like manner says Aboo-Is-hák; (T, TA;) to denote the excess of this attribute in him: (T, O, TA:) or, accord. to Th, (TA,) the phrase is inverted, the meaning being, haste is created from man; (Msb, TA;) but IJ disapproves this explanation, and also another which will be mentioned in what follows. (TA.) -A2- EajalN signifies also Food that is hastily prepared, and brought, before the [ meal called ] gadaA=' has become matured. (TA.) [See also Euj~aAlN .] -A3- Also Clay, or earth; syn. TiynN : (IAar, O, K:) or black mud, or black fetid mud; syn. HamoA^apN : and ↓ EajalapN has both of these meanings, i. e. TiynN and HamoA^apN : (O, * K:) the former of these two significations of EajalN is said by AO to be of the dial. of Himyer; and IAar says that it is what is meant in the phrase in the Kur [xxi. 38] cited above; but Ibn-'Arafeh disapproves this; (O, TA;) and so does Az; and Er-Rághib says that some expl. it as meaning in this instance stinking black mud, but that their saying is nought. (TA.) -A4- See also EajalapN , in four places.

(IAth, O, TA.)

EazomN (S, Msb, K) and EuzomN (S, K) and EazomapN (TA) and EuzomaAnN (K) and EaziymapN and EaziymN (S, K) and maEozamN and maEozimN ; (K;) and Eazamahu ; (Msb, K;) both signify the same; (IB, TA;) and ↓ AEtzm Ealayohi , (S, K,) and ↓ AEtzmhu ; and ↓ tEz~m [app. tEz~m Elyh , but accord. to the TK tEz~mhu ]; (K;) [ He determined, resolved, or decided, upon it, or upon doing it, namely, an affair;] he desired to do it, and decided, or determined, upon it; (S, K;) he settled, or determined, his heart, or mind, firmly ( Eaqada Damiyrahu ) upon doing it: (Msb:) or he strove, laboured, or toiled, in it, namely, an affair; or exerted himself or his power or efforts or endeavours or ability therein: (K:) or so Eazama : (TA:) or Eazama , inf. n. EaziymapN and EazomapN , signifies also he strove, &c., in his affair: (Msb:) and Eazama AlA^amora signifies he made the affair to have, or take, effect; and settled it firmly: (Har p. 3:) or, accord. to Ktr, he so settled it, and confirmed it. (Id. p. 105.) [See also EazomN and EaziymapN , below.] walamo najido lahu EazomFA , in the Kur [xx. 114], means [ And we found him not to have ] a quality of deciding an affair. (S.) Hzm .] ― -b2- One says also, Eazama AlA^amoru , meaning Euzima Ealayohi : (K, TA:) and hence, in the Kur [xlvii. 23], faA_i*aA Eazama AlA^amoru [ And when the affair is determined upon ]: or the meaning may be, faA_i*aA Eazama A^arobaAbu AlA^amori [ and when the disposers of the affair determine upon it]: but accord. to Zj, the meaning is, and when the affair is serious, or earnest, and the command to engage in fight becomes obligatory. (TA.) ― -b3- Eazama EalaY Alr~ajuli means He conjured the man: (S, * K, TA:) or he commanded him, or enjoined him, earnestly: layafoEalan~a ka*aA [ that he should surely do such a thing ]: (TA:) or Eazamotu Ealayoka means I make thy informing me to be a decided thing in which there shall be no exception: and one says also, Eazamotu Ealayoka A_il~aA faEalota and lam~aA faEalota [virtually meaning I conjure thee to do such a thing]; as though one said, By Allah, I demand not of thee [ aught ] save [ thy doing ] this: so says Mtr, referring to “ the Book ” of Sb. (Har pp. 21 and 22. [But Eazama is there, inadvertently, put for A_il~aA .]) ― -b4- And one says, Eazama Alr~aAqiY The charmer recited EazaAy^im , meaning charms, or spells, [for the cure of a disease, &c.;] (K, TA;) as though he conjured the disease [&c.]: and in like manner, Eazama AlHaw~aA='u [ The serpent-charmer recited charms, or spells, ] is said when he draws forth the serpent; as though he conjured it. (TA.) [See an ex. voce daAda , in art. dwd . ― -b5- Hence, Eazama is used in the present day as meaning He invited to an entertainment. ― -b6- And Freytag mentions its occurring often in the book entitled bgyp Almstfyd fY mdynp zbyd as signifying He went, or tended, to, or towards, ( A_ilaY ,) some place: but this signification is probably post-classical: it is correctly expressed by 8, q. v.]

sourceDefinition: , aor. , (K,) inf. n. EaSobN , (S, A, Mgh, O, K,) He twisted [a thing], or wound [it] round: (A, K, TA:) this is the primary signification: (TA:) and he folded [it]; (A, K;) or he folded [it] tightly: (S, O, TA:) and he bound [it], or tied [it]: (A, Mgh, K, TA:) EaSobN denotes the binding, or tying, a thing with another thing, lengthwise, or [more commonly] around. (O.) See also 2, first sentence. [And see maEoSuwbN .] ― -b2- He twisted, or spun, thread. (K, * TA.) And He put together thread, and bound it, previously to dyeing it. (TA.) ― -b3- EaSaba Alkabo$a , (S, O, Msb, K, *] aor. as above, (K,) and so the inf. n., (S, Msb, K,) He bound, or tied, ( tightly, TA) the testicles of the ram, in order that they might fall, without his extracting them: (S, O, Msb, K:) and in like manner one says of a goat, (K,) and of other beasts. (TA.) ― -b4- EaSaba Aln~aAqapa , (O, Msb, K, *) aor. as above, (K,) and so the inf. n., (Msb, K, TA,) and EiSaAbN also; (TA;) and ↓ AEtSbhA ; (O, K;) He bound the thighs of the she-camel, (Msb, K, TA,) or the lower parts of her nostrils, (TA,) with a cord, (Msb, TA,) in order that she might yield her milk copiously: (Msb, K, TA:) and (O) EaSaba faxi*a Aln~aAqapi [ He bound the thigh of the she-camel ] for that purpose. (S, O.) [See EaSuwbN .] Hence one says, A^aEoTaY EalaY AlEaSobi (tropical:) He gave by means of force. (TA.) And mivoliY laA yadir~u biAlEiSaAbi (assumed tropical:) Such a one as I am will not give by means of force. (A, TA.) ― -b5- EaSabato farojahaA She (a woman) bound her vulva with a bandage. (Msb.) ― -b6- EaSaba Al$~ajarapa , (S, O, K,) aor. , inf. n. EaSobN , (K,) He drew together the branches of the tree (S, O, K, TA) that were straggling, (K, TA,) by means of a rope, (TA,) and then beat it, (S, O, K, TA,) in order that its leaves might fall. (S, O, TA.) [Golius assigns this signification also to EaS~aba , as on the authority of the S, in which I do not find it.] El-Hajjáj said, (S, TA,) when preaching to the people at El-Koofeh, (TA,) laA^aEoSiban~akumo EaSoba Als~alami (S) or Als~alamapi (TA) [ I will assuredly draw you together and beat you as one does the selem or the selemeh ]. The salamap is a tree of the kind called EiDaAh , having thorns, and its leaves are the qaraZ with which hides are tanned: [but see qaraZN :] the removal of the leaves with the hand being difficult on account of the many thorns, its branches are drawn together and bound tightly with a rope; then the beater pulls them towards him, and beats them with his staff; whereupon the leaves become scattered for the cattle and for him who desires to gather them. (TA.) Or this is done, (S, O, TA,) accord. to A 'Obeyd, (S, O,) only (TA) when they desire to cut down the selemeh, that they may get at the stock. (S, O, TA.) [Hence,] one says, fulaAnN laA tuEoSabu salamaAtuhu [ Such a one will not have his selemehs bound round with a rope, and beaten ]: a prov., applied to a strong, mighty man, not to be subdued nor abased. (A, * TA.) And one says also of winds, taEoSibu Al$~ajara Einoda duruwjihaA fiyhi (assumed tropical:) [ They compress the branches of the trees, as though they bound them round, in their passage among them ]: and such winds are termed ↓ EaSaAy^ibu . (O.) And EaSaba Alqawoma , aor. , inf. n. EaSobN , (assumed tropical:) It (an affair, or event,) drew the people together, and became severe to them. (Az, TA.) ― -b7- EaSaba SadoEa AlzujaAjapi biDab~apK mino fiD~apK He (a smith) repaired the crack of the glass vessel by putting round it a band of silver. (O, TA.) ― -b8- EaSaba biraA^osi qawomihi AlEaAra (assumed tropical:) He made disgrace to befall his people [ as though he bound it upon the head of their chief or upon the head of each of them ]. (O.) It is related in a trad. respecting the battle of Bedr, that 'Otbeh the son of Rabee'ah said, AirojiEuwA walaA tuqaAtiluwA waA@EoSibuwhaA biraA^osiY (assumed tropical:) [ Return ye, and fight not; and bind it upon my head ]; meaning attach and attribute to me the disgrace that will befall you for relinquishing the battle and inclining to peace. (IAth, TA.) And it is said in another trad., quwmuwA bimaA EaSabakumo bihi (assumed tropical:) Fulfil ye the obligations with which He (meaning God) has bound you; or which He has imposed upon you and attached to you; by his commands and prohibitions. (TA.) ― -b9- EaSaba Al$~aYo'a and EalaY Al$~aYo'i , aor. , inf. n. EaSobN and EiSaAbN , He grasped the thing with his hand. (K, * TA.) A poet, cited by IAar, says, wakun~aA yaA qurayo$u A_i*aA EaSabonaA yajiYo'u EiSaAbunaA bidamK EabiyTi [ And we were, O Kureysh, when we grasped our opponents, such that our grasping brought fresh blood ]; EiSaAbunaA meaning our grasping those whom we opposed with the swords. (TA.) ― -b10- And EaSaba , aor. , inf. n. EaSobN , He clung, or kept, to a thing. (K.) One says, EaSaba AlmaA='a He kept to, or by, the water. (IAar, TA.) And EaSaba Alr~ajulu bayotahu The man remained, or stayed, in his house, or tent, not quitting it. (O, TA.) ― -b11- And He went round, encompassed, or surrounded, a thing. (K.) It is said in a trad., of the angel Gabriel, on the day of Bedr, qado EaSaba raA^osahu AlgubaAru The dust had overspread, [or surrounded, ] and clung to, his head: or, as some relate it, qado EaSama vaniy~atayohi AlgubaAru ; and if this be not a mistake, the latter verb is syn. with the former: b and m being often interchangeable: (L, TA:) the latter phrase means, as also with EaSaba , the dust had stuck to his two central incisors. (TA in art. ESm .) And Ibn Ahmar says, A_i*o EaSaba Aln~aAsa $amaAlN waqurN [ waquro being for waqur~N ] i. e. When north wind and cold environ me. (L, TA.) And one says also, EaSaba AlgubaAru biAljabali The dust encompassed, or surrounded, the mountain. (L, TA.) And EaSabuwA bihi They encompassed, or surrounded, him: (S, A, Mgh, O, TA:) and they encompassed, or surrounded, him, looking at him: (S, O:) and, (Msb, K,) as also EaSibuwA , (K,) aor. of the former , (Msb, K,) and inf. n. EaSobN , (Msb,) and aor. of the latter , (K,) they assembled around him (Msb, K) for fight or defence. (Msb. For another explanation of EaSaba and EaSiba , see 12.) And EaSaba Alqawomu biAln~asabi i. q. A^aHaATuwA bihi [app. meaning The people, or party, included, or comprehended, the relations, or kinsmen; for Aln~asabu is often used for *awuw Aln~asabi ]. (Msb.) And EaSabati AlA_ibilu biAlmaA='i The camels surrounded, or encircled, the water. (S, O.) ― -b12- EaSaba Alr~iyqu bifiyhi , (S, O, K, * TA,) aor. , inf. n. EaSobN ; (K, TA;) and EaSiba , aor. ; (TA;) The saliva became dry in his mouth. (S, O, K, * TA.) And EaSaba Alr~iyqu faAhu (S, O, TA) The saliva by its drying made his mouth dry: and the saliva adhered to his mouth. (TA.) Aboo-Mohammad El-Fak'asee says, yaEoSibu faAhu Alr~iyqu A^aY~a EaSobi EaSoba AljubaAbi bi$afaAhi AlwaTobi [ The saliva makes his mouth dry, with what a drying ! as the drying of the spume of camels' milk on the lips of the skin ]. (S, O.) And EaSaba fuwhu , aor. , inf. n. EaSobN , His mouth, with his saliva, became dry. (O.) And EaSaba Alfamu , (K, * TA,) aor. , inf. n. EaSobN and EuSuwbN , meaning [ The mouth, or teeth, (the latter accord. to the explanation in the K,)] became foul, or dirty, from dust and the like, (K, TA,) as from vehement thirst, or fear. (TA.) ― -b13- EaSaba , aor. , inf. n. EuSuwbN , He was, or became, [ hungry; or] very hungry; or his bowels were almost dried up with hunger: because it is said of the practice of a hungry man's binding round his belly, as expl. voce maEoSuwbN [q. v.]. (TA.) ― -b14- EaSaba AlA^ufuqu The horizon became red. (S, O. [In Freytag's Lex. EaSiba , as from the K, in which I do not find it. See EaSobN .]) -A2- EaSiba , (S, O, K,) with kesr, (S, O,) like fariHa , (K,) said of flesh, or flesh-meat, It had many EaSaba [i. e. sinews, or tendons ]. (S, O, K.) ― -b2- And EaSiba , aor. , inf. n. EaSobN , [so in the TA, and so in a verse there cited, not EaSabN ,] He was, or became, firm and compact in flesh. (TA.) ― -b3- [Other meanings of this verb have been mentioned above.]

(Msb.) ― -b6- EaSaba Al$~ajarapa , (S, O, K,) aor. , inf. n. EaSobN , (K,) He drew together the branches of the tree (S, O, K, TA) that were straggling, (K, TA,) by means of a rope, (TA,) and then beat it, (S, O, K, TA,) in order that its leaves might fall. (S, O, TA.) [Golius assigns this signification also to EaS~aba , as on the authority of the S, in which I do not find it.] El-Hajjáj said, (S, TA,) when preaching to the people at El-Koofeh, (TA,) laA^aEoSiban~akumo EaSoba Als~alami (S) or Als~alamapi (TA) [ I will assuredly draw you together and beat you as one does the selem or the selemeh ]. The salamap is a tree of the kind called EiDaAh , having thorns, and its leaves are the qaraZ with which hides are tanned: [but see qaraZN :] the removal of the leaves with the hand being difficult on account of the many thorns, its branches are drawn together and bound tightly with a rope; then the beater pulls them towards him, and beats them with his staff; whereupon the leaves become scattered for the cattle and for him who desires to gather them. (TA.) Or this is done, (S, O, TA,) accord. to A 'Obeyd, (S, O,) only (TA) when they desire to cut down the selemeh, that they may get at the stock. (S, O, TA.) [Hence,] one says, fulaAnN laA tuEoSabu salamaAtuhu [ Such a one will not have his selemehs bound round with a rope, and beaten ]: a prov., applied to a strong, mighty man, not to be subdued nor abased. (A, * TA.) And one says also of winds, taEoSibu Al$~ajara Einoda duruwjihaA fiyhi (assumed tropical:) [ They compress the branches of the trees, as though they bound them round, in their passage among them ]: and such winds are termed ↓ EaSaAy^ibu . (O.) And EaSaba Alqawoma , aor. , inf. n. EaSobN , (assumed tropical:) It (an affair, or event,) drew the people together, and became severe to them. (Az, TA.) ― -b7- EaSaba SadoEa AlzujaAjapi biDab~apK mino fiD~apK He (a smith) repaired the crack of the glass vessel by putting round it a band of silver. (O, TA.) ― -b8- EaSaba biraA^osi qawomihi AlEaAra (assumed tropical:) He made disgrace to befall his people [ as though he bound it upon the head of their chief or upon the head of each of them ]. (O.) It is related in a trad. respecting the battle of Bedr, that 'Otbeh the son of Rabee'ah said, AirojiEuwA walaA tuqaAtiluwA waA@EoSibuwhaA biraA^osiY (assumed tropical:) [ Return ye, and fight not; and bind it upon my head ]; meaning attach and attribute to me the disgrace that will befall you for relinquishing the battle and inclining to peace. (IAth, TA.) And it is said in another trad., quwmuwA bimaA EaSabakumo bihi (assumed tropical:) Fulfil ye the obligations with which He (meaning God) has bound you; or which He has imposed upon you and attached to you; by his commands and prohibitions. (TA.) ― -b9- EaSaba Al$~aYo'a and EalaY Al$~aYo'i , aor. , inf. n. EaSobN and EiSaAbN , He grasped the thing with his hand. (K, * TA.) A poet, cited by IAar, says, wakun~aA yaA qurayo$u A_i*aA EaSabonaA yajiYo'u EiSaAbunaA bidamK EabiyTi [ And we were, O Kureysh, when we grasped our opponents, such that our grasping brought fresh blood ]; EiSaAbunaA meaning our grasping those whom we opposed with the swords. (TA.) ― -b10- And EaSaba , aor. , inf. n. EaSobN , He clung, or kept, to a thing. (K.) One says, EaSaba AlmaA='a He kept to, or by, the water. (IAar, TA.) And EaSaba Alr~ajulu bayotahu The man remained, or stayed, in his house, or tent, not quitting it. (O, TA.) ― -b11- And He went round, encompassed, or surrounded, a thing. (K.) It is said in a trad., of the angel Gabriel, on the day of Bedr, qado EaSaba raA^osahu AlgubaAru The dust had overspread, [or surrounded, ] and clung to, his head: or, as some relate it, qado EaSama vaniy~atayohi AlgubaAru ; and if this be not a mistake, the latter verb is syn. with the former: b and m being often interchangeable: (L, TA:) the latter phrase means, as also with EaSaba , the dust had stuck to his two central incisors. (TA in art. ESm .) And Ibn Ahmar says, A_i*o EaSaba Aln~aAsa $amaAlN waqurN [ waquro being for waqur~N ] i. e. When north wind and cold environ me. (L, TA.) And one says also, EaSaba AlgubaAru biAljabali The dust encompassed, or surrounded, the mountain. (L, TA.) And EaSabuwA bihi They encompassed, or surrounded, him: (S, A, Mgh, O, TA:) and they encompassed, or surrounded, him, looking at him: (S, O:) and, (Msb, K,) as also EaSibuwA , (K,) aor. of the former , (Msb, K,) and inf. n. EaSobN , (Msb,) and aor. of the latter , (K,) they assembled around him (Msb, K) for fight or defence. (Msb. For another explanation of EaSaba and EaSiba , see 12.) And EaSaba Alqawomu biAln~asabi i. q. A^aHaATuwA bihi [app. meaning The people, or party, included, or comprehended, the relations, or kinsmen; for Aln~asabu is often used for *awuw Aln~asabi ]. (Msb.) And EaSabati AlA_ibilu biAlmaA='i The camels surrounded, or encircled, the water. (S, O.) ― -b12- EaSaba Alr~iyqu bifiyhi , (S, O, K, * TA,) aor. , inf. n. EaSobN ; (K, TA;) and EaSiba , aor. ; (TA;) The saliva became dry in his mouth. (S, O, K, * TA.) And EaSaba Alr~iyqu faAhu (S, O, TA) The saliva by its drying made his mouth dry: and the saliva adhered to his mouth. (TA.) Aboo-Mohammad El-Fak'asee says, yaEoSibu faAhu Alr~iyqu A^aY~a EaSobi EaSoba AljubaAbi bi$afaAhi AlwaTobi [ The saliva makes his mouth dry, with what a drying ! as the drying of the spume of camels' milk on the lips of the skin ]. (S, O.) And EaSaba fuwhu , aor. , inf. n. EaSobN , His mouth, with his saliva, became dry. (O.) And EaSaba Alfamu , (K, * TA,) aor. , inf. n. EaSobN and EuSuwbN , meaning [ The mouth, or teeth, (the latter accord. to the explanation in the K,)] became foul, or dirty, from dust and the like, (K, TA,) as from vehement thirst, or fear. (TA.) ― -b13- EaSaba , aor. , inf. n. EuSuwbN , He was, or became, [ hungry; or] very hungry; or his bowels were almost dried up with hunger: because it is said of the practice of a hungry man's binding round his belly, as expl. voce maEoSuwbN [q. v.]. (TA.) ― -b14- EaSaba AlA^ufuqu The horizon became red. (S, O. [In Freytag's Lex. EaSiba , as from the K, in which I do not find it. See EaSobN .]) -A2- EaSiba , (S, O, K,) with kesr, (S, O,) like fariHa , (K,) said of flesh, or flesh-meat, It had many EaSaba [i. e. sinews, or tendons ]. (S, O, K.) ― -b2- And EaSiba , aor. , inf. n. EaSobN , [so in the TA, and so in a verse there cited, not EaSabN ,] He was, or became, firm and compact in flesh. (TA.) ― -b3- [Other meanings of this verb have been mentioned above.]

definition: , (S, A, O, &c.,) inf. n. taEoSiybN , (S, A, O,) [ He bound, or wound round, a thing with several circumvolutions: ] he bound [or wound round ] a man's head with a turban, fillet, bandage, or the...
sourceDefinition: , (S, A, O, &c.,) inf. n. taEoSiybN , (S, A, O,) [ He bound, or wound round, a thing with several circumvolutions: ] he bound [or wound round ] a man's head with a turban, fillet, bandage, or the like; (S, * O, * Msb, K, * TA;) as also ↓ EaSaba , inf. n. EaSobN : (MA:) and he bound a broken limb, or a wound, with a piece of rag or a bandage. (L, TA.) He turbaned a man; attired him with a turban. (A, TA.) ― -b2- Hence, (A, O,) taEoSiybN signifies (tropical:) [The crowning a man: (see the pass. part. n.:)] the making a man a chief: (A, O, K, TA:) for turbans are the crowns of the Arabs: (O:) when a man's people made him a chief, they bound his head with a turban: (A, TA:) as kings wore crowns, so the chiefs of the Arabs wore red turbans: (L, TA:) there were brought to the desert, from Haráh ( haraAp ), red turbans, which the nobles among the Arabs wore. (Az, TA.) ― -b3- [Hence also,] ES~bhu biAls~ayofi i. q. Eam~amahu bihi (assumed tropical:) [ He cut, or wounded, him in the place of the turban, with the sword ]. (A, TA.) ― -b4- And ES~bhu , inf. n. as above, He, or it, [ caused him to bind his waist by reason of hunger: (see the pass. part. n.:) and hence,] made him to hunger: (K:) and EaS~abatohumu Als~inuwna The years of drought, or sterility, made them to hunger: (TA:) or ES~bthu Als~inuwna The years of drought, or sterility, ate up his property, or cattle. (A 'Obeyd, S, O.) And It [i. e. drought or the like] destroyed him: (K:) and ES~b Ald~ahoru maAlahu Adverse fortune destroyed his cattle, or camels &c. (TA.) ― -b5- And He called him muEaS~ab [meaning poor ]: so says IAar; and he cites as an ex., yudoEaY AlmuEaS~aba mano qal~ato Haluwbatuhu wahalo yuEaS~abu maADiY Alham~i miqodaAmu [ He is called the poor, whose milch-cattle have become few: but should one whose purpose is effectual, one of great boldness, be called poor? ]. (TA.) ― -b6- Al*~akaru yuEaS~ibu AlA^unovaY means The male makes the female to be such as is termed EaSabapN [by his being consociated with her as such]. (Mgh.)

sourceDefinition: i. q. $ad~a AlEiSaAbapa [i. e. He bound the turban, or fillet, round his (own) head; a meaning well known, whence that explained in the next sentence: (see also 8:) and he bound a bandage of some kind round his (own) body, by reason of hunger: see muEaS~abN ]. (S, O, Msb, * K.) ― -b2- And (assumed tropical:) He was made a chief; quasi-pass. of 2 [q. v.]. (L, TA.) ― -b3- And it has also another signification, from AlEaSabiy~ap ; (S, O;) [i. e.] it signifies also A^ataY biAlEaSabiy~api ; (K, TA;) which means [ He aided his people, or party, against hostile conduct: or he was angry, or zealous, for the sake of his party, and defended them: (see EaSabiY~N and EaSabiy~apN :) or] he invited, or summoned, others to the aid of his party, and to combine, or league, with them against those who acted towards them with hostility, whether they were wrongdoers or wronged. (TA.) And you say, taEaS~abuwA Ealayohimo They leagued, or collected themselves, together against them: and taEaS~abonaA lahu , and maEahu , We [ leagued together for him, and with him, and ] defended him. (TA.) [See also De Sacy's Chrest. Ar., see. ed., i. 445-6; where it is shown that Alt~aEaS~ubu in religion means The being zealous, or a zealot: and see Har pp. 423 and 573.] ― -b4- And tES~b biAl$~aYo'i He was, or became, content with the thing; as also ↓ AEtSb . bihi . (K.)

definition: and ↓ EaSobN and ↓ EaSabN (K, TA) Certain trees that twine round other trees, having weak leaves;
sourceDefinition: and ↓ EaSobN and ↓ EaSabN (K, TA) Certain trees that twine round other trees, having weak leaves; (TA;) the kind of tree called labolaAb [ dolichos lablab of Linn.]; (K;) said by Sh to be a kind of plant that twines round trees, i. q. labolaAbN : [coll. gen. ns.:] the ns. un. are EuSobapN and EaSobapN and EaSabapN : (TA:) accord. to Abu-lJarráh, (O, TA,) EaSobapN signifies a certain thing [app. meaning plant ] that twines about a qanaAdap [or tragacanth ], (O, K, TA,) thus, correctly, in many copies of the K, but in some fataAp , and in some qanaAp , both of which are wrong, though some assert the latter to be correct, (TA,) not to be pulled off from it but with an effort: (O, K, TA:) [see EiTofapN :] one says of a man strong in struggling for the mastery, qataAdapN luwiyato biEuSobapK (assumed tropical:) [ A tragacanth twined about by a lebláb; the strong man being app. likened to a tragacanth, and his antagonist to a lebláb]: (TA:) and in a trad. of Ez-Zubeyr Ibn-El-'Owwám, he is related to have said, Ealiqotuhumo A_in~iY xuliqotu EuSobaho qataAdapF taEal~aqato binu$obaho (O, TA:) he puts ESbh for Elqh , [evidently, I think, a mistranscription for EaliqFA , (see nu$obapN , in its proper art., for a confirmation,)] the meaning being xlqt Elqp lxSwmY [in which for Elqp I read EaliqFA ]; then he likens himself to a tragacanth in respect of his excessive tenaciousness; for bn$bh means “ by the help of a thing of great tenaciousness: ” [or n$bh may be here an inf. n., i. e. of na$iba : the meaning of the verse may therefore be, I clung to them: verily I have been created a grasper, and a tragacanth that has clung by means of a strong holdfast, or that has clung with great tenaciousness: ] (TA:) Sh explains EuSobap (O, TA) with damm on the authority of Ed-Deenawaree [i. e. AHn], and EaSobap with fet-h on the authority of AA, (O,) as meaning a certain plant that twines about a tree, and is called labolaAb ; and nu$obap as meaning a man who, when he sports with a thing ( Eabiva bi$aYo'K [but probably the right reading is $abiva b$Y' or ta$ab~ava i. e. clings to a thing]), hardly, or never, quits it. (O, TA.)

(TA.) ― -b3- And The heirs of a man who has left neither parent nor offspring: and [particularly], with respect to the [portions of inheritances termed] faraAy^iD [pl. of fariyDapN q. v.], all such as have not a fariyDap named, and who receive if there remain anything after [ the distribution of ] the faraAy^iD : (K, TA:) thus accord. to those who treat of the frAy^D , and accord. to the [other] lawyers: (TA:) or the relations by the side of the males: this is the meaning of what is said by the leading lexicologists: (Msb:) or, as is said by Az, a man's heirs consisting of male relations: (Msb, TA:) or his sons, and relations on the father's side: (S:) so called because they encompass him; the father being a Taraf [i. e. an extremity in the right line], and so the son, and the paternal uncle being a jaAnib [i. e. a collateral relation], and so the brother: (Az, S, TA:) or a man's relations on the father's side; (Mgh, TA;) because they encompass him and he is strengthened by them: (TA:) afterwards it became applied to a single person as well as to a pl. number, and both a male and a female: (Mgh:) or the lawyers apply it to a single person when there is no other than he, because he stands in the place of the collective number in receiving the whole of the property; and in the language of the law it is applied to a female in certain cases relating to emancipation and inheritances, but not otherwise either in the proper language or in the language of the law: (Msb:) and ↓ EuSuwbapN is used as its inf. n. [meaning the state of being persons, or a person, to whom the term EaSabapN is applied ]: (Mgh:) it is said [by Az] in the T, “ I have not heard any sing. of EaSabapN : accord. to analogy it should be EaASibN , like as TaAlibN is sing. of TalabapN : ” (TA: [and the like is also said in the Mgh: in the Msb it is said that EaSabapN is pl. of EaASibN , like as kafarapN is pl. of kaAfirN :]) the pl. is EaSabaAtN . (Az, S, TA.)

[meaning the state of being persons, or a person, to whom the term EaSabapN is applied ]: (Mgh:) it is said [by Az] in the T, “ I have not heard any sing. of EaSabapN : accord. to analogy it should be EaASibN , like as TaAlibN is sing. of TalabapN : ” (TA: [and the like is also said in the Mgh: in the Msb it is said that EaSabapN is pl. of EaASibN , like as kafarapN is pl. of kaAfirN :]) the pl. is EaSabaAtN . definition: A thing with which another thing is bound, or wound round;
sourceDefinition: A thing with which another thing is bound, or wound round; as also ↓ EiSaAbN (K, TA) and ↓ EaSobN : (L, TA:) or a thing with which the head is bound, or wound round: (S, A, Mgh, O, TA;) and ↓ EiSaAbN signifies a thing with which a thing other than the head is bound, or wound round; (A, TA;) anything, such as a piece of rag, or a fillet, or bandage, with which a broken limb, or a wound, is bound, is termed thus, i. e. EiSaAbN : (L, TA:) and EiSaAbapN signifies also a turban; syn. EimaAmapN : (A, Mgh, Msb, K, TA:) or this [in the TA by mistake written EmAmp ] signifies a small thing that serves as a covering for the head, [ such as a kerchief or a fillet, ] being wound round it; and what is larger is termed EimaAmapN : ('Ináyeh of Esh-Shiháb, MF, TA:) or whatever is bound, or wound, round the head, whether it be a turban or a kerchief or a piece of rag: (TA, from an explanation of a trad.:) and ↓ EaSobN [likewise] signifies a turban, and anything with which the head is bound, or wound round: (S, O:) the pl. of EiSaAbapN is EaSaAy^ibu . (Mgh, TA.) El-Farezdak says, warakobN kaA^an~a Alr~iyHa taTolubu minohumu lahaA salabFA mino ja*obihaA biAlEaSaAy^ibi [ And a company of riders in such a state that it seemed as though the wind desired to take for itself spoil from them, by its dragging away the turbans ]: he means that the wind untwisted their turbans by its violence, as though it despoiled them thereof. (TA.) ― -b2- And [hence] (assumed tropical:) A crown. (A, TA.) ― -b3- See also EaSobN , latter half. ― -b4- And see EuSobapN , in four places. ― -b5- And for the pl. applied to winds, see 1, former half.

sourceDefinition: He contended with him for superior glory (K, TA) and generosity and excellence (TA) in the hocking, or slaughtering, ( Eaqor [see 1],) of camels. (K, TA.) It was customary for two men thus to contend for superior munificence, [giving away the flesh of the victims,] but they did so for the sake of display and vain glory; wherefore the eating of the flesh of camels slaughtered on an occasion of this kind is forbidden in a trad., and they are likened to animals sacrificed to that which is not God. (TA.) ― -b2- And EAqrhu , (TK,) inf. n. muEaAqarapN , (S, K,) He held a dialogue or colloquy, or a disputation or debate, with him, (S, K,) and encountered him with mutual reviling and satire (S, TA) and cursing. (TA.) -A2- Also EAqrhu , (K,) inf. n. muEaAqarapN , (S, O, K,) He, or it, kept, confined himself or itself, clave, clung, or held fast, to him, or it: (S, O, K: *) he kept, or applied himself, constantly, or perseveringly, to him, or it. (TA.) You say EAqr Alxamora , (S, * TA,) and simply EAqr , (TA,) He kept, or applied himself, constantly, or perseveringly, to the drinking of wine: (S, TA:) or muEaAqarapu Al$~araAbi signifies the contending with wine for superiority; as when a man says, I have more, or most, strength for drinking, and so contending with it for superiority, and being overcome thereby. (Aboo-Sa'eed, TA.) You say also, EaAqarati Alxamoru Ald~an~a The wine remained long confined to the [ jar called ] dan~ ; syn. laAzamatohu . (S, K.) And EAqrt Alxamoru AlEaqola [app., The wine took hold upon the intellect: or contended with it for superiority ]. (S.)

definition: The act of wounding;
sourceDefinition: The act of wounding; &c.: [see 1:] a mark, or wound, ( A^avarN ,) like a notch, ( kAlHaz~i , K, TA, [in the CK, kAlxar~i ,]) in the legs of a horse, and of a camel. (K.) [Hence, EaqorFA HaloqFA , and EaqoraY HaloqaY : see 1.] -A2- See also EuqorN , first sentence: -A3- and again in the last quarter. -A4- Also What is, or constitutes, the most essential part, of anything; or the prime, or the principal part, thereof; syn. A^aSolN : [such appears to me to be the meaning of ASl as here used, from what follows.] (S, IF, Msb.) ― -b2- The principal part ( A^aSol ) of a daAr [i. e., a country]; (As, S, Msb, K;) which is the place where the people dwell, or abide; (As, S;) as also ↓ EuqorN : (As, S, Msb, K:) the former of the dial. of Nejd; (As, TA;) and the latter of the dial. of the people of El-Medeeneh, (As, S,) or of the dial. of El-Hijáz; (TA;) or both of the dial. of the people of El-Hijáz; and the latter, in the dial. of others, signifies the chief, or main, part of a dAr ; (Msb;) and the latter also signifies the middle [or heart ] of a dAr : (K:) or Eaqoru Ald~aAri and ↓ EuqoruhaA both signify the principal part ( ASl ) of the place of abode of a people, upon which they rest their confidence. (L.) (TA.) Lth has confounded in explaining what is the Euqor of a dAr and what is the Euqor of a tank or trough for watering beasts &c. (Az.)

sourceDefinition: (S, M, &c.) and ↓ EaqorN , (M,) or ↓ EaqorapN and ↓ EuqorapN , (A, K,) Barrenness, in a woman, (S, K, &c.,) and in a man. (S, TA.) You say also laqiHati Aln~aAqapu Eano EuqorK [ The she-camel conceived after having been barren ]. (S, O.) And laqiHa liqaAw^uka Eano EuqorK [app., (assumed tropical:) The meeting thee hath been productive of good after barrenness thereof ]. (A, TA.) And laqiHona A_ilaY EuqorK , a phrase used by Dhu-r-Rummeh, referring to wars; i. e. (assumed tropical:) They returned to stillness. (TA.) And rajaEati AlHarobu A_ilaY EuqorK (assumed tropical:) The war became languid. (A, TA.) ― -b2- EuqorN in a palm-tree means [ Barrenness, or a drying up, and perishing, occasioned by ] having the [ fibrous substance called ] liyf stripped off (O, K, TA) from the heart, (O, TA,) and the heart itself taken away; (O, K, TA;) which being done, it dries up and perishes. (Az, O, TA.) -A2- Also, or ↓ EuqurN , or the latter is used only by poetic license, Anything which a man drinks, and in consequence thereof has no offspring born to him. (O, TA.) -A3- Also, EuqorN , A kind of dowry, (S,) or compensation, (IAth,) which is given to a woman when connection has been had with her in consequence of dubiousness, or a likeness [ on her part to the man's wife ]: ( A_i*aA wuTiy^ato Eano $ubohapK , S; or bi$ubohapK , Mgh; or EalaY waTo'i Al$~ubohapi , IAth:) or a recompense which is given to a woman for connection with her: (AO:) or a mulct, or fine, which is paid to a woman for ravishing her: (Lth, Msb, K:) or what is given to a female slave who has been ravished, like a dowry in the like case to a free woman: (Ahmad Ibn-Hambal:) so called because devirgination wounds the object of it: pl. A^aEoqaArN . (IAth, TA.) ― -b2- Hence, in consequence of frequency of usage, (Msb,) A woman's dowry; (Msb, K;) i. q. buDoEuhaA . (O.) ― -b3- Also The exploration of a woman to see if she be a virgin or not: (Kh, O, K, TA:) but Az says that this is unknown. (TA.) [Perhaps it is a meaning inferred from what here follows.] ― -b4- bayoDapu AlEuqori is That [ egg ] with which a woman is tested on the occasion of devirgination: (K: [but what is meant by this, I have not been able to learn:]) or the first egg of the hen; (K, TA;) because it wounds her: (TA:) or the last egg of the hen; (O, K, TA;) when she is old and weak: (TA:) or the egg of the cock, which [ they say ] he lays once in the year, (O, K,) [or once in his life, for] they assert that it is the egg of the cock, because he lays, in his life, one egg, somewhat inclining to length; so called because the virginity of the girl, or young woman, is tested with it: hence, they say of a thing given one time [only], kaAnato bayoDapa AlEuqori : or, as some say, it is like the phrases bayoDu AlA^anuwqi and AlA^abolaqu AlEaquwqu ; so that it is a phrase proverbially used as applied to a thing that never is: (S, O:) accord. to A'Obeyd, when a niggard gives once, and not again, one says [of the gift], kaAnato bayoDapa Ald~iyki ; and when he gives a thing, and then stops doing so, one says of the last time [of his giving], kaAnato bayoDapa AlEuqori . (TA.) One says also, kaAna *`lika bayoDapa AlEuqori meaning * That happened once, not a second time. (TA.) And bayoDapu AlEuqori means also (tropical:) He who has no offspring. (K, TA. [See also EaAqirN .]) And (assumed tropical:) He who stands another in no stead. (TA.) -A4- Also A grant of land; syn. TuEomapN ; (O, K;) and so ↓ EuqorapN . (K. [See 4.]) ― -b2- And A place where people alight ( maHal~apu qawomK , K, TA) between the house, or abode, and the trough, or tank, for watering beasts &c.; (TA;) as also ↓ EaqorN : (K, TA:) or (TA, but in the K “ and ”) the hinder part of a trough, or tank, for watering beasts &c., (S, K, TA,) where the camels stand when they come to water; as also ↓ EuqurN : (S:) or the station of the drinker; (K;) as in all the copies of the K; but accord. to the T and Nh, the station of the animals drinking: (TA:) or the place where the bucket is emptied, at the hinder part of the trough, or tank; the place at the fore part being called its A_izaA=' : (IAar:) pl. A^aEoqaArN . (S, O.) It is said in a prov., A_in~amaA yuhodamu AlHawoDu mino Euqorihi [lit., The trough, or tank, for watering beasts &c. is demolished only by commencing from its hinder part ]; meaning, an affair is performed only by setting about it in the proper way. (TA.) ― -b3- Also The part of a well where the fore feet of the animals watering stand when they drink. (TA.) ― -b4- See also EaqorN , in two places.

definition: signifies maA Euqira [ What is wounded, or hocked, or struck or cut in the legs, ] of wild animals that are snared or hunted or chased, and the like;
sourceDefinition: signifies maA Euqira [ What is wounded, or hocked, or struck or cut in the legs, ] of wild animals that are snared or hunted or chased, and the like; (K;) of the measure faEiylapN in the sense of the measure mafoEuwlapN . (TA.) See EaqiyrN . ― -b2- A man of high rank who is slain. (S, K.) So in the saying, maA raA^ayotu kaA@loyawomi EaqiyrapF wasoTa qawomK [ I have not before seen, as on this day, a man of high rank who is slain in the midst of a people ]. (S.) ― -b3- A leg, or shank, cut. (S, O, K.) ― -b4- Hence, The voice, or a cry; (S;) the voice of a singer (K, TA) singing; (TA;) the voice of a weeper (K, TA) weeping; (TA;) the voice of a reciter or reader (K, TA) reciting or reading; (TA;) the utmost extent of the voice or of a cry. (TA.) You say rafaEa fulaAnN Eaqiyratahu Such a one raised his voice: the origin of the saying was this: a man had one of his legs cut, or cut off, and he raised it, and put it upon the other, and cried out with his loudest voice: so this was afterwards said of any one who raised his voice: (S, O:) or it is expl. thus: a man had one of his limbs wounded, and he had camels which were accustomed to his singing in driving them, and which had become dispersed from him; so he raised his voice, crying, by reason of the wound; and his camels, hearing, and thinking that he was singing to drive them, came together to him: and hence this was afterwards said of any one who raised his voice, singing. (Az, TA.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. EamalN , (S, O, Msb, K,) He worked, or wrought; laboured; served, or did service: he did, acted, or performed: (K, TA:) [generally, he did, &c., with a sort of difficulty, or with intention; but sometimes said of an inanimate thing: (see EamalN , below:)] he did, or he made, wrought, manufactured, or constructed, a thing. (Msb. [See, again, EamalN , below.]) Accord. to Az, Eamila is the only trans. verb of its measure having the inf. n. of the measure faEalN , except habilat , said of a mother, inf. n. habalN ; other similar verbs having the inf. n. of the measure faEolN ; as sariTotu All~uqomapa , inf. n. saroTN ; and baliEotuhu , inf. n. baloEN . (TA. [But see arts. srT and blE ; with respect to the former of which I must here state that, since it was printed, I have found an authority for saroTN as inf. n. of sariTa in a copy of the S; though in the K it is said to be muHar~akap , and accord. to the Msb it is like taEabN .]) You say, Eamilotu EalaY AlS~adaqapi I officiated in the collecting of the poor-rate. (Msb.) [And Eamila bimaA fiY kitaAbi A@ll~`hi He did according to what is enjoined in the Book of God. ] And Eamila fiY halaAkihi [ He laboured to destroy him, or to kill him ]. (K in art. $yT .) [And Eamila fiyhi It acted upon him, or it: and, said of a sword &c., it had effect, or made an impression, upon him, or it. ] ― -b2- [Hence,] Eamila fiyhi signifies [also (assumed tropical:) It governed it syntactically; or caused it to be marofuwE or manoSuwb or majoruwr &c.; i. e.] it produced in it a certain species of syntactical desinence. (K.) ― -b3- And Eamila Albaroqu The lightning was continual. (K.) And Eamilato biA^u*unayohaA , said of a she-camel, (K,) and also, in a trad., of [the beast] AlburaAq , (O, * TA,) She went quickly, or swiftly; (O, K, TA;) because she that does thus puts her ears in motion by reason of the vehemence of the pace. (TA.) And Eamilat [alone] said of a she-camel, signifies [the same: or] She was, or became, brisk, light, active, or quick. (K.) ― -b4- And [hence, app.,] lamo A^ara Aln~afaqapa taEomalu kamaA taEomalu bimak~apa , a saying mentioned by Lh, is expl. by ISd as meaning tanofaqu [i. e. I have not seen the money that that one expends pass away as it passes away in Mekkeh ]. (TA.)

(S and TA in art. sqY .)

definition: He made him to work, labour, serve, or do service;
sourceDefinition: He made him to work, labour, serve, or do service; or to do, act, or perform; (S, * O, * K, TA;) as also ↓ AstEmlhu : (S, K:) he made him, or caused him, to do, or to make, manufacture, or construct, a thing. (Msb.) And one says also, yuEomilu nafosahu fiY AlA^amori [ He plies himself in the affair ]. (S in art. Esm .) ― -b2- And [hence,] He worked with it, [i. e. employed it, or used it, or plied it, ] namely, his judgment, or opinion, and [properly] his instrument, or implement, (K, TA,) and his tongue; (TA;) as also ↓ AstEmlhu . (K, TA.) And A^aEomala *ihonahu fiY ka*aA waka*aA [ He employed, or used, his intellect, or understanding, in such and such things; ] meaning he considered, or forecast, the issues, or results, of such and such things with his intellect, or understanding. (TA.) ― -b3- And A^aEomalotu Aln~aAqapa [ I hastened, and urged, the she-camel ]: whence the saying, in a trad., laA tuEomalu AlmaTiY~u A_il~aA A_ilaY valaAvapi masaAjida , meaning [ The camels that are used for riding ] shall not be hastened nor urged [or plied, save to three mosques; that of Mekkeh, that of El-Medeeneh, and that of ElAksà at Jerusalem: see also a variation of this saying in the first paragraph of art. Drb ; and another voce EurowapN ]: and in a trad. of Lukmán, yuEomilu Aln~aAqapa waAls~aAqa [ He hastens, and urges, the she-camel and the shank ], meaning he is strong to journey, riding and walking. (TA.) ― -b4- See also 2, last sentence. -A2- [ maA A^aEomalahumo biEamali A^aholi Aln~aAri , a phrase occurring in art. Sbr in the K, means How much do they occupy themselves in doing the deed of the the people of the fire of Hell!] -A3- A^aEomalotu Alr~umoHa means I thrust, or pierced, with the EaAmil [q. v.] of the spear. (Har p. 77.) [Or one says, A^aEomalotuhu biAlr~umoHi , meaning I thrust him, or pierced him, with the EaAmil of the spear. (See De Sacy's Chrest. Ar., sec. ed., iii. 191.)]

definition: [mentioned in the beginning of this art.
sourceDefinition: [mentioned in the beginning of this art. as an inf. n.] is syn. with miahonapN and fiEolN : (K:) [accordingly, when used as a simple subst., it may be rendered Work, labour, or service: and a deed, or an action: ] or it has a more particular meaning than fiEolN ; for it is a fiEol [or deed ] with a sort of difficulty; and therefore it is not attributed to God: or, accord. to Er-Rághib, it is any fiEol [i. e. deed or action ] that proceeds from an animate being by his intention; and thus it has a more particular meaning than fiEolN ; for the fEl is sometimes attributed to animate beings from which it proceeds without intention; and sometimes to inanimate things, to which the Eamal is seldom attributed; and this is not used in relation to [irrational] animals except [as implied] in the phrases A_ibilN EawaAmilu and baqarN EawaAmilu : or, accord. to MF, the Eamal is a motion of the whole, or of a portion, of the body; and sometimes, of the mind; so that it is the utterance of a saying, as well as the doing a deed with the member, or limb, with which things are gained or earned; though most readily understood as applied particularly to the latter; and some apply it particularly to that which is not a saying: it is also said that a saying is not termed EamalN in the common conventional language: and the truth is said to be, that it is not included in the terms EamalN and fiEolN otherwise than tropically: (TA:) [see also EamilapN :] the pl. of EamalN [used as a simple subst.] is A^aEomaAlN . (K.) In the following saying, of a woman dandling her child, (S,) or of Keys Ibn-Ásim, (O, TA,) dandling his child Hakeem, (TA,) A^a$obiho A^abaA A^um~ika A^awo A^a$obiho Eamalo the last word is a proper name of a man: (S, O, TA:) or, accord. to Aboo-Zekereeyà, [the meaning is, Share thou in the qualities of the father of thy mother, or share thou in the qualities of my course of action; for he says that] by Eamalo is here meant EamaliY . (TA.) Aibonu EamaliY means He who does my work, or the like of what I do. (TA in art. bnY .) And [hence,] fulaAnN A@bonu EamalK Such a one is strong. (TA.) And banuw EamalK Those who journey on foot. (O, K, * TA.) [And Eamalu Aln~axoli , occurring in the T, voce DayoEapN , means The culture of palm-trees: like as Eamalu AlA^roDi means agriculture ]. ― -b2- And EamalN signifies also The striving, labouring, or toiling, in work; or the holding on, or continuing, in work: so in the saying of El- Kutámee faqado yahuwnu EalaY AlmusotanojiHi AlEamalu [ For verily the striving, &c., in work is a light matter to him who seeks success ]. (TA.) ― -b3- [Also An office of administration; and particularly the office of governor of a province; and the office of collector of the poor-rates, and the like: and an agency of any kind; the management of the affairs and property of another; an employment. ― -b4- Also A province; or territory under a governor appointed by a sovereign. Pl. in this and other senses as above.]

sourceDefinition: [ Working; labouring; serving, or doing service: doing, acting, or performing: and doing, making, working, manufacturing, or constructing, a thing:] act. part. n. of Eamila : (T, Msb, TA:) pl. EaAmiluwna (Msb, K, TA) and Eum~aAlN (Msb) and EamalapN , (K, TA,) which last signifies [particularly] workers with their hands, (Mgh in art. fEl , K, TA,) in various sorts of work, (TA,) in clay (Mgh, TA) or building (Mgh) or digging (Mgh, TA) &c.; (TA;) like faEalapN [a pl. of faAEilN ]: (Mgh:) and EawaAmilu , (K, TA,) as pl. of [the fem.] EaAmilapN , (TA,) [and likewise in this case of EaAmilN ,] signifies oxen that plough, and that tread the corn, (K, TA,) and upon which water is drawn, and that are employed in other labours; and in like manner applied to camels: and it is said in a trad. that in the case of such animals no poorrate is required. (TA.) ― -b2- Also [ An administrator of public affairs; and particularly a governor of a province; and] a collector of the poor-rates [and the like ]: and an agent who manages the affairs and property of another. (TA.) -A2- EaAmilu Alr~umoHi (S, O, K) and ↓ EaAmilatuhu (K) The part, of the spear, that is next to the head, exclusive of the vaEolab [or portion that enters into the head ]: (S, O:) or the Sador [or fore part ] of the spear, (K, TA,) exclusive of the head, accord. to A'Obeyd two cubits in length: (TA:) or, as some say, the spear-head itself is called EaAmilN : (O, TA:) pl. EawaAmilu . (TA.) See also *iraAEN , last sentence.
