sourceDefinition: An excellent, or a strong, light, and swift, he-camel; (O, K;) though disallowed by Kh: (O:) and (O, K) yaEomalapN an excellent, or a strong, light, and swift, she-camel, adapted, or disposed, by nature, to work, labour, or service: (S, O, K: *) or, accord. to Kr, the former signifies a swift she-camel; [but see what follows, as well as what precedes;] and is a subst. applied thereto, derived from AlEamalu : and the pl. is yaEomalaAtN : (TA: see also EamilN :) neither of them is used as an epithet, each being only a subst., (M, K, TA,) accord. to Sb, for one does not say jamalN yaEomalN nor naAqapN yaEomalapN , but only yaEomalN and yaEomalapN as meaning a he-camel and a she-camel; and hence, he says, we know not yafoEal occurring as [the measure of] an epithet: but some make yaEomal to be an epithet. (M, TA.) yawomu AlyaEomalapi was one of the days [meaning days of conflict] of the Arabs. (O, K.)

definition: A she-camel not conceiving in the first year after having been covered: (Ks, Az, S, O:) or a she-camel, (Lth, K,) and a woman, (K,) not conceiving for several years, without being barren;
sourceDefinition: A she-camel not conceiving in the first year after having been covered: (Ks, Az, S, O:) or a she-camel, (Lth, K,) and a woman, (K,) not conceiving for several years, without being barren; (Lth, K;) as also ↓ muEotaATN : (Lth, IAth, O, * TA:) and a she-camel not conceiving when covered; (K;) as also ↓ muEotaATN , or ↓ muEotaATapN : (accord. to different copies of the K:) or not conceiving when her womb has attained to maturity: (TA:) ↓ muEotaATN is also applied to a ewe or she-goat, as meaning not conceiving, by reason of the abundance of her fat; (IAth;) and occurs in a trad., so applied, (S, IAth,) and expl. as signifying Aal~atiY lamo talido waqado HaAna wilaAduhaA ; but by this is app. meant that has not conceived, although the time for her conceiving has come: (IAth:) the pl. of EaAy^iTN is EuwTN , (Ks, S, M, O, K,) which is also applied to women, and she-goats, (M,) and EiyTN (Ks, S, O, K) and Euy~aTN (M, O, K) and EawaAy^iTu (TA) and ↓ EuwTaTN [which is irregular, like HuwlalN ,] (Ks, S, O, K) and EawoTaTN (accord. to the CK) and EuwTuTN , (K,) but this is a dial. var. of EuwTaTN accord. to those who assert it to be an inf. n., (As, O, TA,) for some assert this last to be an inf. n., not a pl., and in like manner HuwlalN , (A'Obeyd, S, O,) but Sb holds it to be a subst. in the sense of an inf. n., originally EuyoTaTN . (L, TA.) sourceDefinition: , (S,) or biAlA^amori , (MA, Msb, K,) and Ean AlA^amori , (MA,) and AlA^amora also, (MA, and Ham p. 717,) and EayiYa , (S, Msb, K,) [which is the original form,] but EaY~a is more common, (S, TA,) and A^aEoyaA bihi is not allowable, (TA,) first pers. Eayiytu , (S,) pl. EayuwA , (S, TA,) like HayuwA [from HaY~a and HayiYa ], (S,) and Eay~uwA also, which is used by a poet, (S, TA,) aor. yaEoyaA , (Msb, TA), inf. n. EiY~N ; (Msb, TA;) as also ↓ tEy~A , and ↓ tEAyA , and ↓ AstEyA ; (K;) He found not the right way, or manner, (S, Msb, K, TA,) that he desired, (K, TA,) or the way, or manner, of his acting [i. e. in which he should act ], (TA,) to perform, or accomplish, his, or the, affair: (S, Msb, K, TA:) or he lacked power, strength, or ability, for it; (MA, Mgh, * K, TA;) and was unable to perform it, or execute it, thoroughly. (K, TA.) [Hence,] one says, $ifaA='u AlEiY~iAls~uw^aAlu (tropical:) [ The remedy of inability is the asking information ]. (TA in art. $fY .) ― -b2- And in like manner one says, Eay~a Eano Huj~atihi , (Msb, TA,) and EayiYa , aor. and inf. n. as above, i. e. He found not the right way, or manner, of adducing his argument, plea, or evidence. (Msb, TA. *) ― -b3- And EaY~a fiY manoTiqihi , (S, Msb,) and EayiYa , (S, Msb, K,) aor. as above, (Msb,) and so the inf. n., (Msb, K,) He found not the right way, or manner, in his expressing of his ideas: (Msb:) or i. q. HaSira ; (K;) or [nearly so, i. e.] EayiYa [or EaY~a ] signifies he was, or became, unable to express his mind, to say what he would, to find words to express what he would say; he faltered in speech; like HaSira , except that the latter denotes what is by reason of shame and confusion of mind, or some [other] accidental cause: (TA in art. HSr , from the Expos. of the “ Mufassal ” of Z:) AlEiY~u is the contr. of AlbayaAnu [q. v.]: (S, TA:) or, accord. to Er-Rághib, it is an inability that ensues to one who has taken upon himself an affair or a speech. (TA.) One says, jaA='a biAlEiY~i waAl$~iY~i [app. meaning He exhibited much impotence of expression ]; (S and K and TA in art. $wY ;) using the latter noun as an imitative sequent to the former [for the purpose of corroboration]. (TA in that art.) ― -b4- And Eayiytuhu I was ignorant of it: (K, TA:) originally meaning I was unable to give information respecting it when asked, by reason of ignorance of it. (TA.) One says, laA yaEoyaAhu A^aHadN No one will be ignorant of it. (TA.)

You say, A^a*am~a and AEyA bihi baEiyruhu , both meaning the same [i. e. His camel became jaded, and lagged behind with him ], aor. yuEoyiY , and some incorporate [one Y into the other, transferring the kesreh of the former Y to the E ], as is done in a verse of El-Hotei-ah. (TA.) -A2- AEyAhu It made him to be without power, or strength, or ability; disabled, or incapacitated, him; (S, * MA, TA;) said of an affair; (S, MA;) and [app. in like manner] of God. (S.) It is also said of a disease, meaning It disabled him, or incapacitated him, from curing it: (K, * TA:) [or] one says of a difficult disease, for which there is no cure, kaA^an~ahu A^aEoyaA AlA^aTib~aA='a [It is as though it disabled, or incapacitated, the physicians; or frustrated their skill; or baffled them ]. It was, or became, difficult, or arduous, to him; (MA, TA;) or [ impracticable, i. e.] such that he found not the right way, or manner, to perform it, or accomplish it; (TA;) or veiled, or hidden. (MA.) -A3- maA A^aEoyaAhu [ How wanting is he in ability to find the right way, or manner, of acting! or how impotent is he! &c.]. (S and K in art. $wY : see 4 in that art.)

definition: , (S, MA, Msb, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, MA, Msb, K,) aor. , (Msb, K,) inf. n. gabonN (S, MA, Msb, K, KL) and gabanN , or the former is [the inf. n. used in this case, i. e.] in selling [and the like], and the latter is in judgment, or opinion, (K, agreeably with a positive statement in the S,) He cheated, deceived, overreached, or defrauded, him, (S, MA, K, KL, TA,) in selling; (S, MA, K, TA;) he endamaged him, or made him to suffer loss or damage or detriment, (Msb, KL, TA,) in selling, (KL, TA,) &c., (KL,) or in the price, or otherwise: (Msb:) [or] he overcame him in selling and buying. (Msb.) And gubina He was cheated, or deceived [&c. in a purchase]: (S, K, TA:) and ↓ Angbn [in like manner signifies] he became [ cheated or endamaged or] overcome in selling and buying. (Msb.) And it is said that gabana fiY AlbayoEi , inf. n. gabonN , signifies He was unmindful, or inadvertent, [or perhaps gabana is here a mistranscription for gubina , signifying thus, and therefore meaning he was made to suffer loss, ] in selling or in buying. (TA.) And one says also, gubina Alr~ajulu A^a$ad~a AlgabanaAni [ The man was cheated or deceived &c. with the utmost degree of cheating &c.]. (Ibn-Buzurj, TA.) gabonN yasiyrN [ A petty overreaching or endamaging ] is one of which the rate is such as has been estimated [ as allowable by custom ] by one estimator, not by every one: and gabonN faAHi$N [ An exorbitant overreaching or endamaging ] is one of which the rate is such as has not been estimated [ as allowable by custom ] by any one. (Dict. of Technical Terms used in the Sciences of the Musalmans.) [ Algubonu waAlgabanu mentioned by Freytag as occurring in the Fákihet el-Khulafà, and expl. by him as meaning “ Fraus omnimoda, ” should, I doubt not, be Algabonu waAlgabanu , the two inf. ns. mentioned in the first sentence above.] ― -b2- gabanahu , aor. , inf. n. gabonN , signifies also He passed by him (i. e. a man) inclining, or leaning, [or bending down, so as as to elude his observation, i. e.] so that he [the latter] did not see him, and was not cognizant of him. (TA.) ― -b3- [And it is said in the TA that gayanuwA Aln~aAsa means None but they obtained it: whence it appears that fiyhi or the like has been omitted after Aln~aAsa : with this addition, the phrase may be rendered, they overreached, or prevented, the other people in respect of it, by obtaining it themselves. ] ― -b4- h`*aA yagobinu Eaqolaka , said to a man whom another had cheated ( gabana ) in a sale, means This [man] attributes defect, or imperfection, to thy intellect. (TA.) ― -b5- qado gabanuwA xabarahaA , and gabinuwA , aor. of the former verb , and of the latter , i. e. lamo yaEolamuwA EilomahaA [meaning They have not know her case or state or condition, or her qualities ], (ISh, K, ast; TA,) is a phrase relating to a she-camel, of which it is said that she is what one would desire a she-camel to be as a beast for riding and in generousness of race, but she is ↓ magobuwnapN , [i. e.] one of which the qualities are not known to be as above mentioned. (ISh, TA.) ― -b6- gabanota raA^oyaka [if not a mistranscription for gabinota (see gabina raA^oyahu in what follows)] means Thou hast lost, and forgotten, thy judgment, or opinion. (TA.) ― -b7- gabina Al$~ay^ao and fiY Al$~ay^o , aor. , inf. n. gabonN and gabanN , signify He forgot the thing: or he was unmindful, neglectful, or heedless, of it; (K, TA;) and ignorant of it: (TA:) or he made a mistake in respect of it; (K, TA;) as in the saying, gabina ka*aA mino Haq~ihi Einoda fulaAnK [ he made a mistake in respect of such a thing, of his right, or due, to be required at the hand of such a one ]. (TA.) ― -b8- gabina raA^oyahu , inf. n. gabanN (S, Msb, K) and gabaAnapN , (S, * K,) means He was, or became, deficient in his judgment, or opinion: (S:) or he was, or became, weak [ therein ]: (K:) or his intelligence, or sagacity, and his sharpness, or acuteness, of mind, went away: (Msb:) the parsing of this phrase has been [fully] expl. voce safiha [q. v.]. (S.) -A2- gabana Alv~awoba , (S, Mgh, Msb, TA,) inf. n. gabonN , (K,) from magobinN [q. v.], (Msb,) He folded, or doubled, the garment, (T, Mgh, Msb, K, * TA,) it being [too] long. (T, TA,) and then sewed it; (Mgh, Msb;) like xabanahu [q. v.] (S, Mgh) and kabanahu . (Mgh.) And gabana Ald~alowa He folded, or doubled, [ the edge of ] the leathern bucket, to shorten it. (TA: but only the inf. n. of the verb thus used is there mentioned.) ― -b2- And gabana Al$~ay^o He hid, or concealed, the thing in the magobin [or armpit or groin or the like ]; (TA;) as also ↓ Agtbnhu . (K, TA.) gabana AlT~aEaAma is like xabanahu [i. e. He concealed, kept, or stored, wheat, or food, for a time of dearth, or adversity. ] (S.)

sourceDefinition: signifies Mutual gabon [i. e. cheating or endamaging or overcoming in selling and buying: and ↓ mugaAbanapN signifies the same; or mutual endeavoring to cheat &c: see 3 in art zbn ]. sourceDefinition: (tropical:) A spear-wound, or the like, that passes through: (S, A, Msb, K:) the epithet properly applies to the person who inflicts the wound, because he thrusts in ( yagomis ) the spearhead so that it passes through, or so that its extremity protrudes: and it is such as cleaves the flesh: (A:) or wide, and passing through; that plunges into the flesh. (ISd, TA.) ― -b2- A^amorN gamuwsN (tropical:) A difficult, or distressful, affair; (S, A, Msb, K;) that plunges people into trial, or affliction. (A, K. *) ― -b3- Hence, (A,) yamiynN gamuwsN (tropical:) An oath that plunges its swearer ( tagomisuhu ) into sin, (S, K,) and then into the fire [ of Hell ]: (K:) or a false oath, (Mgh, Msb,) known by its swearer to be so; (Msb;) so called because it plunges its swearer into sin, (A, Mgh, Msb,) and then into the fire [of Hell]: (A, Mgh:) or a false oath which one purposely swears, knowing the case to be the contrary thereof, (K, TA,) in order to cut off the rights of others: (TA:) or an oath by which one cuts off for himself the property of another: (K:) or an oath in which there is made no exception [by saying A_ino $aA='a A@ll~`hu (if God will), or the like]. (TA.) [See also Algamiysap .] ― -b4- rajulN gamuwsN (assumed tropical:) A strong, courageous man; as also ↓ mugaAmisN : which latter epithet is also applied to a lion. (TA.) And (assumed tropical:) A man who, in journeying, does not alight to rest in the night until he enters upon the time of dawn or morning. (TA.) ― -b5- And naAqapN gamuwsN A she-camel whose pregnancy is not plainly known (S, O, K) until she is near to bringing forth ( Hat~aY tuqoriba ). (S, O.) And (O, K) accord. to En-Nadr, (O,) A she-camel that has a young one in her belly and that does not raise her tail so that the case should become manifest: (O, K:) pl. gms [app. gumusN , agreeably with analogy, like SuburN pl. of SabuwrN , &c.]. (TA.) And (some say, TA) A she-camel respecting whose marrow one doubts whether it be in a corrupt and melting state or be fat, or thick and fat. (O, K.)

sourceDefinition: A [ basin such as is termed ] Tasot ; (M, L, K;) thus it means with the vulgar: (L:) or a Tasot of gold, or of silver: (O:) or the TasotaxaAn , (T, K,) or Ta$otaxaAn , (O, and so in some copies of the K,) [i. e. a large circular tray, of brass or other metal, which serves as a table for food, being generally placed upon a stool, the persons who eat sitting on the floor]; (Lth, T, Z, O, K;) thus it means with the vulgar: (Lth, T, Z, O:) or a xiwaAn [or table upon which food is eaten ], made of marble, (Lth, T, S, M, O, K,) by the people of Syria, who thus call it, (Lth, T, O,) or of silver, (T, S, M,) and the like, (S,) or of gold: (M, K:) or of any kind accord. to some: (TA:) or a jaAm [q. v.] of silver, (T, Nh, TA,) or of gold: (Nh, TA:) [but this seems to be virtually a repetition; for it is said that] ↓ faAvuwriy~apN , occurring in a verse of Lebeed, means A^axowinapN [pl. of pauc. of xiwaAnN ] (T, O) and jaAmaAtN [which is pl. of jaAmN accord. to IAar, or of jaAmapN accord. to IB, who holds jaAmN to be likewise a pl. of jaAmapN ]: (T:) faAvuwrN is a word of the people of Syria and ElJezeereh: (M:) and it signifies (S, O, L) in the dial. of the people of El-Jezeereh, (L,) a maAy^idap [sometimes meaning table in an absolute sense, but properly one with food upon it ]: (S, O, L:) [hence,] one says, humo EalaY faAvuwrK waAHidK (Lth, T, S, M, O, L, TA) i. e. EalaY maAy^idapK waAHidapK , (S, O, L, TA,) and manozilapK waAHidapK , (S, O, TA,) and basaATK waAHidK , (O, TA, [in both of which the former word is without any vowel-sign to the b so that it may be either basaATK or bisaATK ,]) or basoTK wAHdK , (TT as from the M,) or as though meaning ElY bsATK wAHdK , thus expl. by Lth, as said of the people of Syria and El-Jezeereh: (TT as from the T:) [it means, app., They are living upon one kind of fare; upon one footing; upon one level or stratum: ] in the copies of the K, [or in the generality of the copies thereof,] AlfaAvuwru is expl. as signifying Almanozilapu and Aln~a$aATu ; but Aln$AT is a mistake for AlbsAT . (TA. [My MS. copy of the K has the right reading ( AlbsAT ), without any trace of alteration.]) ― -b2- Also (tropical:) The breast, or bosom: (K:) or a wide breast or bosom; applied by a poet to that of a woman; as being likened to the xiwaAn so called. (M.) ― -b3- And (tropical:) The disk of the sun (S, * O, K) is called its fAvwr as being likened to the Tasot so called. (O.) ― -b4- And (tropical:) A [ bowl such as is termed ] jafonap ; (M, K, TA;) thus with [the tribe of] Rabee'ah; (M, TA;) for the like reason. (TA.) ― -b5- And A [ vessel such as is termed ] naAjuwd and baATiyap (AA, T, O, K) and miSoHaAp ; all which words mean the same thing. (AA, O, TA.) ― -b6- And, accord. to the R, A [ molten piece such as is termed ] sabiykap of silver: and some say, a silver A_iboriyq [or ewer ]. (TA.) -A2- Also A company of men upon the frontier of a hostile country, that go after the enemy, in pursuit. (Ibn-'Abbád, O, K.) ― -b2- And A spy; syn. jaAsuwsN . (Ibn-'Abbád, O, K.)

sourceDefinition: (S, O, K) and ↓ fujulN , (O, K,) both mentioned by AHn, (O, TA,) or ↓ fijolN , (Msb,) thus, with kesr, commonly pronounced by the vulgar, (TA,) [The radish, raphanus sativus; (Forskål's Flora Ægypt. Arab., lxix. no. 327; and Delile's Floræ Ægypt. Illustr., no. 608;)] a certain A^aruwmap [or root of the kind termed rhizoma ], (K, TA,) that occasions abominable eructation; (TA;) a herb, (Msb,) well known: (S, Msb:) said by IDrd to be not a genuine Arabic word; and thought by him to be derived from fajila signifying as expl. above: (Msb:) n. un. with p , (K,) i. e. fujolapN (S, O) and fujulapN (O) [and fijolapN ]: it is a gardenplant, found in abundance; and there is a Syrian sort, said to be produced by putting together the seeds of the colza and [ those of ] the fjl : (TA:) it (i. e. each sort, TA) is good for pain of the joints, and jaundice, (K, TA,) and sciatica, and the niqoris [i. e. gout, or specially in the foot or feet ], (TA,) and pain of the liver (K, TA) arising from cold, (TA,) and the biting and stinging of vipers and scorpions: (K, TA: [several other supposed properties thereof mentioned in the K, and many more mentioned in the TA, I omit as unimportant:]) what is most potent thereof is its seed; then, its peel; then, its leaf; then, its flesh. (K, TA.) What is called Hab~u Alfujoli is Another remedial thing: (K:) this fjl is not of the species of herb mentioned above: (O, Msb, TA:) so says AHn: the hakeem Dáwood says, it is one of the species of this fjl , a wild species, elongated, abounding in the Sa'eed of Egypt: (TA:) [it is the raphanus oleifer, mentioned by Delile (Floræ Ægypt. Illustr., no. 609,) as cultivated in Nubia and in Egypt, and called in Arabic “ symâgah: ”] from it (or from its seed, TA) is made the oil of the fjl ( duhonu Alfuijoli ); (Msb, K, TA;) and it is known by the appellation of Als~ayomaEapu [correctly Als~ayomagapu ]. (TA.) [Delile, ubi suprà, no. 571, mentions fijol Aljamal , as a name of The cakile maritima of Tournefort; the bunias cakile of Linn.: and in the same, no. 396, he mentions fijol Aljabal as the Arabic name of The rumex spinosus of Linn.; as does also Forskål, in his work cited above, p. lxv., no. 213, and again in p. 76.]

definition: He scattered the contents of the kr$ [or stomach of a ruminant animal ]: (T:) or he ripped the kr$ , and threw away what was in it: (ISk, S, O:) or Alkari$a Eani ↓ faravotu Alfarovi , aor.
sourceDefinition: He scattered the contents of the kr$ [or stomach of a ruminant animal ]: (T:) or he ripped the kr$ , and threw away what was in it: (ISk, S, O:) or Alkari$a Eani ↓ faravotu Alfarovi , aor. , inf. n. farovN ; and A^aforavotuhaA , and ↓ faravotuhaA ; I ripped the kr$ , and scattered what was in it. (M, TA.) Accord. to the K, one says, Afrv Alkabida , meaning He ripped the kbd [or liver ], and threw away the furaAvap , i. e., what was in it: but this is taken from two passages in the M and T, which the author of the K has confounded. (TA.) ― -b2- And [hence, app.,] Afrv A^aSoHaAbahu (assumed tropical:) He exposed his companions (T, S, M, O, K) to the ruling power, (T,) or to the censure of men: (T, S, M, O, K:) or he pronounced them to be liars, in the presence of a people, or party, in order to lessen them in their estimation: or he exposed to reproach their secret: (M:) or he calumniated, or slandered, them. (IF, O.) And Afrv Alr~ajula (assumed tropical:) He reviled, vilified, or vituperated, the man; charged him with a vice, fault, or the like; defamed him; or detracted from his reputation. (M, O.) ― -b3- See also 1.

definition: Skilful, or possessing skill;
sourceDefinition: Skilful, or possessing skill; (S, Msb, K;) part. n. of faruha , irregularly formed, for by rule it should be fariyhN : (S:) accord. to Z, it is applied to a man; and also, without p , to a qayonap [i. e. female slave, or slave-songstress]. (Msb.) ― -b2- And it is applied as an epithet to a hackney, (Az, S, Msb,) and a mule, (S,) and an ass, (Az, S, Msb,) or to a horse, or similar beast, (Az,) meaning Brisk, lively, sprightly, active, agile, or light; (Az, * Msb;) sharp; strong; that goes, or journeys, much; a great goer: (Az, TA:) it is not applied to a faras , (Az, S,) i. e. to an Arabian horse; (Az, Msb;) such being termed jawaAdN , (Az, S, Msb,) and raAy^iEN : (S:) 'Adee Ibn-Zeyd has applied it to the latter; but As has charged him with error in so doing; saying that he possessed not knowledge of horses: (S:) the pl. is furohN , (S, Msb,) like buzolN and HuwlN pls. of baAzilN and HaAy^ilN , (S,) or furuhN , like kutubN , (K,) and farahapN , with two fet-hahs, (Msb,) or furohapN , (S, K,) but this is held by Sb to be a quasi-pl. n., (ISd, TA,) and fur~ahN , like ruk~aEN , and fur~ahapN , like suk~arapN , (K,) as in the A, but MF says that no pl. of this measure is known. (TA.) ― -b3- Also, applied to a gulaAm [i. e. youth, young man, or male slave], Beautiful, or comely, of countenance. (IAar, TA.) And [the fem.] faArihapN signifies A beautiful, or comely, girl, or young woman: (K:) [and] so ↓ farohaA='u , [of which the masc. is A^aforahu , and] of which the pl. is furohN ; but Az says, I do not think that they use this word in relation to girls, or young women, though they may apply it peculiarly to female slaves like as they apply faArihN and faArihapN peculiarly to hackneys and mules and jades, exclusively of Arabian horses. (Msb.) ― -b4- And faArihapN is also syn. with fatiy~apN [i. e. A youthful females, or one in the prime of life ]: (thus accord. to several copies of the K and accord. to the TA:) or qayonapN [i. e. a female slave, or a slave-songstress: see the first sentence of this paragraph]. (Thus in the CK.) ― -b5- And it signifies also [A woman] who eats vehemently: (K:) and faArihN applied to man, A vehement eater. (IAar, TA.)

sourceDefinition: , of a ring, or signet, (S, M, A, Msb, K,) signifies [The stone, or gem, or] what is set therein, (Lth, M, L, Msb,) of a different substance therefrom; (Msb;) and is also written ↓ fiS~N , (M, A, K,) thus pronounced by the vulgar, (Lth, S,) but J's saying this does not necessarily mean that it is incorrect, which, as in opposition to what is said by J, it is asserted not to be in the K [and A], (TA,) or the latter form is bad, accord. to ISk and El-Fárábee; (Msb;) and ↓ fuS~N ; (A, K;) all of which three forms are mentioned by Ibn-Málik and others; but they assert that the first is the most correct and the most commonly known: (TA:) pl. [of pauc.] A^afuS~N (Lth, M) and [of mult.] fuSuwSN (S, M, A, Msb, K) and fiSaASN . (Lth, M.) ― -b2- [Also, Any gem, or similar stone, rare or common, and natural or factitious: and any hard stone cut for inlaying or for construction. ― -b3- A die, such as is used in the game of tables, or backgammon: and an ossicle that is used in like manner: see kaEobN .] ― -b4- (tropical:) A clove ( sin~N ) of garlic; (Lth, A, O, K;) [and] so ↓ faS~apN . (S and L in art. sn .) ― -b5- (assumed tropical:) The yolk of an egg. (M, voce muH~N .) ― -b6- (assumed tropical:) The bubbles of water. (M.) ― -b7- (assumed tropical:) What leaps, or leap, up, [i. e., the particles that leap up, in effervescence, ] of wine. (M.) ― -b8- (tropical:) The black ( Hadaqap ) of the eye: (M, K:) [or the pupil: for] you say, Earafotu AlbagoDaA='a fiY faS~i Hadaqatihi (tropical:) [ I knew vehement hatred in the pupil of the black of his eye ]: and ramawohu bifuSuwSi A^aEoyunihimo (tropical:) [ they cast piercing glances at him with their eyeballs ]. (A, TA.) ― -b9- (tropical:) A joint, or place of separation between two parts of an animal: (M, A:) or any joint, (AZ, M,) or any place of meeting of two bones, (ISk, S, Msb, K,) except ( of ) the fingers, (AZ, M,) for the joints thereof are not so called: (M:) pl., in this and all the other senses which we have mentioned, [of pauc.] A^afuS~N (M) and [of mult.] fuSuwSN : (S, M, A, Msb:) or, as some say, contradicting AZ, the fSwS are the baraAjim and the sulaAmayaAt : [see these two words:] (Sh, TA:) and ISh says, in the “ Book of Horses, ” that the fSwS of the horse are the joints of the knee and pasterns, in which latter are the sulaAmayaAt , these being the bones of the pasterns. (TA.) One says of a horse, A_in~a fuSuwSahu laZimaA='N (tropical:) Verily his joints are hard; not flabby nor fleshy. (S, A.) [And hence, app., from the place in which it is mentioned by Z in this art., the saying,] fulaAnN Haz~aAzu AlfuSuwSi [in a copy of the A, Haz~aAru ; and in the TA, DrAr ; but I have no doubt that the right reading is that which I have given; lit., Such a one is the great cutter of joints; ] meaning, (tropical:) Such a one is often right in his judgment, or opinion, and in his answer. (A, TA.) ― -b10- Hence, [immediately,] accord. to Abu-l-'Abbás; or [originally] from faS~N in the first of the senses expl. above, accord. to IDrd; (Mtr, cited in De Sacy's Chrest. Arabe, see. ed. iii. 232;) faS~u A^amorK (tropical:) The point upon which a thing, or an affair, turns, or hinges; or the point in which it is distinguished, or discriminated, from other things; syn. mafoSiluhu ; (Abu-l- 'Abbás ubi suprà, S, Msb, K;) or maHaz~uhN : (Mtr ubi suprá:) [or its utmost point, or particular; syn. munotahaAhu : (Msb in art. fSl , in explanation of mafoSilu A^morK :)] or its origin, or source; syn. A^aSoluh ; (M; and Mtr ubi suprà, and L;) and maxorajuhu Al~a*Y qado xaraja minohu : (L, TA:) and its essence, or very essence; its substance; its most essential, or elementary, part; its pith; the ultimate element to which it can be reduced or resolved; syn. Haqiyqatuhu , (M, L, TA,) and kunohuhu , i. e. jawoharuhu , and nihaAyatuhu : (L, TA:) or its real, as opposed to its apparent, state; syn. maxobaruhu . (A, TA.) Hence the saying, (S, Msb, TA,) of a poet, (S, TA,) or of Ez-Zubeyr Ibn-El-'Owwám, (TA,) or of 'AbdAllah Ibn-Jaafar Ibn-Abee-Tálib, (Mtr ubi suprà, and TA,) wayaA^otiyka biAlA^amori mino faS~ihi (tropical:) [ And he will tell thee the thing, or affair, tracing it from the point on which it turns, or hinges; &c.: but it appears to be originally without wa ; forming an incomplete hemistich: see Freytag's Arab. Prov. ii. 918]: (S, M, * A, * Mtr, TA:) or he will tell thee the thing, or affair, distinctly. (Msb, TA. *) You say also, qaraA^otu fiY faS~i AlkitaAbi ka*aA (tropical:) [ I read, in the most essential part of the book or writing, such a thing ]. (A, TA.) And hence, fuSuwSu AlA^axobaAri (tropical:) [ The most essential parts or particulars of narrations ]. (A.)

definition: He (a colt) became fit for riding upon his faqaAr [or vertebræ ];
sourceDefinition: He (a colt) became fit for riding upon his faqaAr [or vertebræ ]; like A^arokaba : (O:) or he (a colt, Msb), or it (the back of a colt, L), became [ strong in the vertebræ and ] fit for being ridden. (L, Msb.) -A2- Afqrhu naAqatahu , (S, O,) or baEiyrahu , (ISk, K,) or Zahora baEiyrihi , (TA,) or baEiyrFA , (Mgh,) or daAb~atahu , (A 'Obeyd, TA,) or Almuhora , (Msb,) He lent him the vertebræ [meaning the back ] of his she-camel, that he might ride thereon: (S, O:) and he lent him the back of his camel (ISk, K, TA) during a journey, (ISk, TA) for carrying a burden, and for riding, (ISk, K, TA,) to be returned afterwards: (ISk, TA:) and he lent him a camel, that he might ride thereon; from faqaAr signifying the “ vertebræ ” of the back: (Mgh:) and he lent him his beast to ride as long as he pleased during a journey and then to return it to him: (A 'Obeyd, TA:) and he lent him the colt to ride upon its vertebræ [or back ]. (Msb.) ― -b2- Hence, Afqrhu A^aroDahu (tropical:) He lent him his land for sowing. (TA, from a trad.) ― -b3- A^afoqaraka AlS~ayodu means The object of the chase has enabled thee to have its vertebræ within thy power; therefore shoot it, or shoot at it: (O, TA:) or has enabled thee to have its side [which is sometimes termed fuqor ] within thy power: (K:) or has become near to thee. (TA.) [The Khaleefeh] El-Weleed the son of Yezeed the son of 'AbdEl-Melik is related to have said, A^afoqara baEoda masolamapa AlS~ayodu limano ramaY i. e. The object of the chase has enabled the shooter at it to have its vertebræ within his power after Meslemeh; meaning that, since the death of his paternal uncle Meslemeh, the territory of the Muslims had become assailable to him who might attempt it. (TA.) -A3- Afqrhu also signifies He (i. e. God, S, O, K, or a man, Msb) rendered him faqiyr [meaning poor, or needy, &c.]. (S, O, Msb, K.) -A4- maA A^afoqarahu [i. e. How poor, or needy, &c., is he! ] and maA A^agonaAhu [which has the contr. meaning] are [said to be] anomalous; for their [respective primitive] verbs are Aifotaqara and AisotagonaY , from either of which the verb of wonder is not properly [or regularly] formed. (S, O. [But see 8.])

definition: He clave, slit, or rent;
sourceDefinition: He clave, slit, or rent; and opened: [see also 1, fourth sentence:] hence its usage in a trad. of 'Omar, in which, after his saying that Imra-el-Keys was the foremost of the poets, and had made the source of poetry to well forth abundantly to them, [see xasafa ,] he is related to have added, waA@fotaqara Eano maEAnK EuwrKA^aSaH~a baSarK : in saying this, he attributed a sound and an opened sight to the poetry, [which he thus personified,] and in like manner he described obscure and occult meanings by applying to them the epithet Euwr [generally meaning “ blind of one eye ”]: he meant that Imra-el-Keys had made the meanings of poetry clear and perspicuous, and unveiled them, and shunned substitution and obscure diction: Eano with what is [to be understood as] antecedently connected with it occupies the place of a noun in the accus. case as a denotative of state: it is as though he said, fataHa lil$~iEoriA^aSaH~a baSarK mujaAwizFA lilomaEaAniY AlEuwrimutaxaTiyFA lahaA [lit. He opened, to poetry, a most sound vision, passing over half-blind meanings ]. (O.) -A2- Also, (O,) He was, or became, faqiyr [meaning poor, or needy, &c.]; (S, O, Msb, K, &c.;) and so ↓ faqira , aor. , inf. n. faqarN ; (Msb;) and ↓ faqura , aor. ; (K;) or they said Aftqr , (Sb, Msb, TA,) like as they said Ai$otad~a , (Sb, TA,) but they did not say faqura , (Sb, Msb, TA,) like as they did not say $aduda , (Sb, TA,) Aftqr serving them instead of faqura ; (Msb;) nor did they use any unaugmented form of this verb. (Sb, TA.) ― -b2- And one says, Aftqr A_ilayohi He, or it, wanted, needed, or required, him, or it; [a phrase of frequent occurrence; like faqiyrN A_ilayohi ;] i. q. AiHotaAja Alyh . (TA in art. Hwj .)

sourceDefinition: and ↓ fuqorN signify the same, (S, O, Msb, K,) but the latter is bad, (Lth, TA,) and sometimes they said ↓ fuqurN , (MF, TA,) Poverty, want, or need; contr. of ginFY : (K:) or the state of a man when he has [ only ] what suffices for his household, or those who dwell with him and whose maintenance is incumbent on him: (ISd, K:) [other meanings are indicated by explanations of the epithet faqiyrN , q. v.:] ↓ mafAaqiru [signifying needs, or wants, ] is said by some to be a pl. of faqrN , anomalous, like ma$aAbihu [pl. of $abahN ] and malaAmiHu [pl. of lamoHapN ]: or it may be a pl. of ↓ mufoqarN , an inf. n. of A^afoqarahu ; or pl. of ↓ mufoqirN ; or it has no sing.: (TA:) you say, ↓ sad~a A@ll~`hu mafaAqirahu God rendered him, or may God render him, free from want; (S, Msb, K;) [lit.] God supplied, or may God supply, his various needs, or wants. (S, K.) ― -b2- And faqorN signifies also Anxiety; or disquietude, or trouble, of mind: pl. fuquwrN : (O, K, TA:) one says, $akaY A_ilayohi fuquwrahu He complained to him of his anxieties; &c.: and it means also, his circumstances, and wants: (TA:) [for,] accord. to IAar, the phrase fuquwru Aln~afosi is like $uquwruhaA . (O.) -A2- See also faqorapN .

definition: A hollow dug in the ground: pl.
sourceDefinition: A hollow dug in the ground: pl. fuqarN . (O, K, TA.) ― -b2- And The [ incision termed ] quromap (IAar, O, TA) that is made in the nose [or muzzle ] (IAar, O) of the camel, (IAar, O, TA,) [ in order to render him tractable, (see 1, near the beginning,)] after which [ if necessary ] another is made, [ above it, ] and then another, until he becomes gentle: (IAar, O:) pl. [of pauc. A^afoqurN , occurring in the L, evidently as a pl. of fuqorapN in this sense, and, of mult., but also used as a pl. of pauc.,] fuqarN . (O, TA.) Hence the saying of 'Aacute;ïsheh, in relation to [the murder of] 'Othmán, [app. alluding to its involving three violations, namely, the violation of the sacredness of the city in which it was perpetrated and of the month in which it occurred and of the person of the Khaleefeh,] balagotumo minohu Alfuqara Alv~alaAva , meaning (tropical:) Ye have done to him the like of your deed to the camel above mentioned [ upon which ye have inflicted the three fuqar ]: thus expl. by AZ. (TA.) Accord. to AHeyth, fuqarN means (assumed tropical:) Great, or grievous, or formidable, events. (O.) And the three fuqaraAt of the son of Adam are said to be (assumed tropical:) The day of birth and the day of death and the day of resurrection. (O.) ― -b3- Also The part, of a shirt, that is the place into which the head is inserted. (K.) -A2- Also Nearness. (K.) And one says, huwa min~iY fuqorapF , meaning He is near to me. (K, * TA.) -A3- See also mufoqirN .

definition: ― -b2- [Hence] AlfiqaraAtu is a name of (assumed tropical:) The star [or stars ] in the xarazaAt [meaning joints of the tail ] of Scorpio.
sourceDefinition: : see faqaArN . ― -b2- [Hence] AlfiqaraAtu is a name of (assumed tropical:) The star [or stars ] in the xarazaAt [meaning joints of the tail ] of Scorpio. (Kzw in his descr. of Scorpio.) And fiqarN signifies (assumed tropical:) Certain ornaments, moulded, or fashioned, in the form of the vertebra of the back: (A, KT, TA, and Har p. 34:) one of which is termed fiqorapN . (Har ibid.) ― -b3- And hence, (KT,) or as being likened to a vertebra of the back, (S, O, KT,) (tropical:) The best verse in an ode is termed fiqorapN . (S, O, K, KT.) ― -b4- And hence, as being likened to the best verse in an ode, fiqorahN means (tropical:) (tropical:) Any choice phrase or sentence: (KT:) one says, maA A^aHosana fiqara kalaAmihi i. e. [ How beautiful are ] the points, or points of wit, ( sukat [pl. of nukotapN ]) of his speech, or language! (A, TA.) ― -b5- And in like manner it is applied to signify (assumed tropical:) The end [or final word ] of every verse of an ode and [ of every clause ] of a xuTobap [which is in rhyming prose]. (Msb.) ― -b6- And (assumed tropical:) [ A pair of clauses of rhyming prose, both ending with the same rhyme; i. e.] the fiqorap is that which in [ rhyming ] prose is like the verse in poetry. (Kull p. 208.) -A2- Also A piece of land, such as is termed qaraAH [q. v.], for sowing. (O, K.) -A3- And A thing that serves as a mark, or sign, (Lth, K, TA,) to men contending, or competing, in shooting, or casting, (Lth,) such as a mountain, (K,) or such as a hill, or a hollow dug in the ground, (Lth.) or a hadaf [or butt, &c. ], (Lth, K, TA,) and the like: (K, TA:) they say, in such contending or competing, A^uraAmiyka mino A^adonaY fiqorapK [ I will contend, or compete, with thee in shooting, or casting, from the nearest fqrp ] and mino A^aboEadi fiqorapK [ from the furthest fqrp ]. (Lth, TA.)

definition: The vertebra of the back;
sourceDefinition: The vertebra of the back; (S, * Msb, K;) the bones of the spine, which are set in regular order, one upon another, from the part where is the kaAhil to the Eajob : (K, * TA:) [it is sometimes used as a sing., as in the S and O and K voce TabaqN : but properly] the sing., (Msb, K,) or n. un., (S, TA,) is ↓ faqaArapN , (S, Msb, K,) for which one should not say fiqaArapN , with kesr: (ISk, Msb:) and ↓ fiqorapN , of which the pl. is fiqarN and fiqoraAtN and fiqaraAtN and fiqiraAtN , signifies the same as faqaArapN ; (S, Msb, K:) as does also ↓ faqorapN . (K.) ― -b2- [Hence,] faqaAru AljawozaA='i (assumed tropical:) The three very bright stars [d and e and z] disposed obliquely in the midst of the constellation AljwzA=' [i. e. Orion ]. (Har p. 456. [See art. jwz .) ― -b3- And [hence also,] *uw AlfaqaAri (assumed tropical:) the name of A [ celebrated ] sword of the Prophet, (S, O, K,) and afterwards, of 'Alee: it had previously belonged to El-'As Ibn-Munebbih, who was slain at Bedr, (O, K,) by 'Alee, by whom his sword was given to the Apostle: (O:) accord. to Abu-l-'Abbás [i. e. Th]. it was thus named because there were in it small beautiful hollows [app. meaning small scallops in the edge, such as some modern swords have, for the more easy cleaving of coats of mail]: it is also, accord. to some, called *w AlfiqaAr ; but this is said by El-Khattábee to be vulgar. (TA.) ― -b4- It (i. e. *uwAlfaqaAri ) is also used, metaphorically, as meaning (tropical:) The spear. (TA.)

definition: A hollow that is dug around the shoot, or offset, of a palm-tree, when it is planted: (S, O:) or a well [or the like thereof ] in which the shoot, or offset, of a palm-tree is planted, (K, TA,) then...
sourceDefinition: A hollow that is dug around the shoot, or offset, of a palm-tree, when it is planted: (S, O:) or a well [or the like thereof ] in which the shoot, or offset, of a palm-tree is planted, (K, TA,) then alluvial soil with dung of camels or the like is pressed down around it: (TA:) pl. fuqurN , with two dammehs: (K, TA:) or this [app. the pl., but accord. to the TA the sing.,] signifies wells, (K, TA,) three, and more, together, (TA,) or communicating, one with another. (K, TA.) The sing. signifies also A well: (Mgh, O:) or an old well: (O:) or a well having little water: (TA:) pl. as above. (Mgh.) ― -b2- And A plain, or soft, place, in which wells are dug forming a regular series. (O, K,) And rakiy~apN faqiyrapN signifies A dug well. (TA.) And faqiyru baniY fulaAnK fiY Alr~akaAyaA is expl. by A 'Obeyd as meaning The share of the sons of such a one of the wells. (TA.) ― -b3- Also The mouth, (K, TA,) or the place whence the water issues, (S, O, TA,) of a subterranean channel, or conduit: (S, * O, * K, * TA:) pl. as above. (TA.) ― -b4- And it is said to signify A [ hollowed ] trunk of a palm-tree, by means of which one ascends to an upper chamber: but the word commonly known in this sense is naqiyrN [q. v.], with n . (IAth, TA.) -A2- As an epithet applied to a camel, it means Having an incision [or two incisions or three ] made in his nose [or muzzle ] in the manner explained in the first paragraph of this art.; and so ↓ mafoquwrN . (K, TA.) -A3- Also, applied to a man, (TA,) Having the vertebræ of the back broken; (S, O, K, * TA;) and so ↓ faqirN and ↓ mafoquwrN : (K:) or having a complaint of the vertebræ of his back, arising from fracture or from disease: (Msb:) or having his vertebræ pulled out from his back, so that his spine is interrupted: (T, L:) and ↓ faqirN , a man having a complaint of his vertebræ: (S, O, TA:) and fqyr and ↓ mafoquwrN , a man afflicted [lit. having the vertebræ of his back broken ] by a calamity. (Msb.) -A4- Hence, as though having the vertebræ of his back broken, (IDrst, TA in art. jbr ,) [but said to be irregularly formed from Aifotaqara , like maA A^afoqarahu , q. v.,] Poor: or needy; contr. of ganiY~N ; (as implied in the K;) having [ only ] what suffices for his household, or those who dwell with him and whose maintenance is incumbent an him: (ISd, K:) or one who finds food sufficient to sustain life: (K:) or one who possesses only what is sufficient for life: (ISk, S, K: *) or one whose property is, or has become, little: further expl. in art. skn : (Msb:) or one who has what to eat; (Aboo-'Amr Ibn-El-'Alà;) differing from misokiynN , which signifies one who possesses nothing; altogether destitute: (Aboo-'Amr Ibn-El-'Alà, ISk, S, O, K:) or both mean destitute, i. e. possessing nothing: (IAar, S, O:) Aboo-Haneefeh holds the opinion of ISk, (TA,) who cites the following verse from a poem of Er-Rá'ee in praise of 'Abd-El-Melik Ibn-Marwán; A^am~aA Alfaqiyru Al~a*iY kaAnato Haluwbatuhu wafoqa AlEiyaAli falamo yutorako lahu sabadu [ As to the fqyr whose milch camel was sufficient for his household, and nothing (more) was left to him: ] (S, O, TA:) As says that the mskyn is better in condition than the fqyr : and Yoo says that the fqyr is better in condition than the mskyn ; and adds, I asked an Arab of the desert, Art thou fqyr ? and he answered, No, by God, but rather mskyn : (S, O, TA:) or the former signifies needy, needing, or wanting; a needer; and the latter, one abased by need or want, or otherwise; sourceDefinition: sing. of fuwaTN , which signifies Cloths that are brought from Es-Sind, (Lth, O, K, TA,) thick, or coarse, and short, used as waistwrappers: (Lth, O, TA:) or striped waistwrappers: (K:) Az says, I have not heard this word in aught of the language of the Arabs, and I know not whether it be an Arabic word or of the language of the foreigners, but I have seen in El-Koofeh striped waist-wrappers, which are sold, and are bought by the camel-drivers and the Arabs of the desert and the servants and the people of the lowest sort, who use them as waist-wrappers, and call them thus; sing. fuwTapN : IDrd says that it is not an Arabic word: (O, TA:) it is added in the K, or it is a word of the language of Es-Sind: Sgh says, (TA,) fwTh is a word of the language of Es-Sind, arabicized, from Puwtah , with a dammeh not fully sounded: (O, TA:) [and SM adds,] it is called with us in El-Yemen, A^azohariy~ap : and by reason of frequency of usage, they have derived from it the verb above-mentioned. (TA.) The dim. of fuwTapN is ↓ fawayoTapN . (Har p. 294.) [See also De Sacy's Chrest. Arabe, see. ed., i. 195.] ― -b2- It (the pl.) is also applied to Short napkins, with striped extremities, woven at El-Mahalleh ElKubrà, in Egypt, which a man puts upon his knees to preserve himself therewith [ from being soiled ] at meals [ and with which the hands are wiped after washing ]. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. yafiySu , (S, O, K,) inf. n. fayoSN , (TA,) He went away into the country, or in the land. (S, O, K.) In the following verse of Imra-el-Keys, manaAbituhu mivolu Als~uduwsi walawonuhu ka$awoki Als~ayaAli fahowa Ea*obN yafiySu respecting which As said, I know not what is [the meaning of] yafiyDu , this word is said to be from fAS signifying as expl. above: (S, O:) [but I do not see what meaning that would be apposite in this case could be thence derived without straining:] but fAS signifies also it shone, or glistened; syn. baraqa ; (TA;) and some say that yfyS in this verse means yaboruqu ; (O, TA;) and the pronoun in manaAbituhu relates to the front teeth; (O, * TA;) by Ea*obN yafiyDu being meant the lustre ( maA=' ) thereof: (O:) [accordingly, the verse may be rendered, The places of growth thereof, i. e. their gums, were like the ( garment called ) suduws , and their colour was like the thorns of the sayaAl (q. v.), so that they were sweet and glistening: (see the context in “ the Divans of the six ancient Arabic poets, ” edited by Prof. Ahlwardt:) or, as some relate the verse, the last word is ↓ yufiySu , (IB, O, TA,) from maA A^afaASa bikalimapK [q. v.], (O,) so that it is a denotative of state, the meaning being Ea*obN fiy HaAli kalaAmihi [i. e. sweet when [displayed in] speaking; or rather, clearly uttering; but it will be seen below that yafiySu , as well as yufiySu , may, accord. to the M and K, be used in this sense:] (IB, TA:) see 4. ― -b2- maA A@sotaTaEotu A^ano A^afiySa minohu , meaning I was not able to turn aside, or away, from, or to avoid, him, or it. (S, O.) [See also mafiySN : and see 4.] ― -b3- And waA@ll~`h maA fiSotu , like as one says wAll~`h mA bariHotu [perhaps meaning By God I did not quit my place; as well as I did not cease: ] (S, O, K: *) mentioned on the authority of AHeyth: (TA:) [that it has the latter meaning is clear; for] one says, maA fiSotu A^afoEalu I did not cease ( maA bariHotu ) doing [such a thing]: (M:) and ↓ AstfAS , likewise, signifies bariHa . (IB, TA.)

definition: [ The lizard called Db~ escaped, or slipped, from his hand, is expl.
sourceDefinition: [ The lizard called Db~ escaped, or slipped, from his hand, is expl. as meaning] his fingers became unclosed ( Ainofarajat ) from [the grasp of] the Db~ , so that it escaped from him. (M, TA.) And one says, qabaDotu Ealayohi falamo yufiSo I grasped him and he did not escape, or get loose. (AHeyth, TA.) And qabaDotu EalaY *anabi AlD~ab~i faA^afaASa mino yadiY Hat~aY xal~aSa *anabahu [ I grasped the tail of the Db~ and it slipped from my hand so that it freed its tail ]: (Lth, S, O, TA:) [but in the O, mino is omitted before yadiY ; not intentionally, for the verb before mn is there masc., as above:]) this is when thy fingers become unclosed ( tatafar~aju ) from the grasp of its tail: (Lth, O:) and this [state of the fingers] is termed ↓ Alt~afaAwuSu . (TA.) [It is also said that] A^afaASati Alyadu signifies The fingers of the hand became unclosed ( tafar~ajato ) from the grasp of the thing. (K, TA. [But I doubt the correctness of this.]) ― -b2- And AlA_ifaASapu signifies The being clear, or perspicuous; syn. AlbayaAnu ; (O, K;) like AlmufaAwaSapu , expl. in art. fwS ;] and the being fluent. (O.) [And also The making speech clear, or perspicuous. ] One says, fulaAnN *uw A_ifaASapK A_i*aA takal~ama Such a one is a person endowed with clearness, or perspicuity, and fluency, when he speaks. (O.) And AfAS lisaAnuhu biAlkalaAmi His tongue made speech, or the speech, clear, or perspicuous; and so ↓ faASa , aor. yafiySu ; (M;) and maA yafiySu bihi lisaAnuhu , (K, TA,) inf. n. fayoSN , (TA,) his tongue does not make it clear, or perspicuous (K, TA.) And maA A^afaASa bikalimapK He did not make clear, or distinct, or perspicuous, a word, or a sentence. (Yaakoob, S, O, TA.) See also 4 in art. fwS : and see 1 in the present art. [And it is said that maA A^afaADa bikalimapK signifies the same. Or, accord. to Mtr, if he be correctly cited in Har p. 447, the verb in this sense, and app. as thus used in all the phrases mentioned above, is correctly with D , and not so with S : but this I greatly doubt.] ― -b3- One says also, AfAS bibawolihi He ejected his urine: (O, K:) or AfAD bh . (ElGhooree, in Har ubi suprà.)

[either as an inf. n., app. in an intensive sense, or as a simple subst.]; (O, K;) and so too is taqotiytN [as inf. n. of ↓ qt~t ], (K,) or so is taqotiytu AlHadiyvi ; (O;) and so is qatoqatapN [as inf. n. of ↓ qatofata ], (K,) or so is qatoqatapu AlHadiyvi ; (O;) i. q. nam~a , (M,) or nam~a AlHadiyva (S, O, K, * TA) or AlA^aHaAdiyva , (S, O, TA,) i. e. [ He uttered calumny; or] he made known, divulged, or told, discourse, or conversation, in a malicious, or mischievous, manner, so as to occasion discord, dissension, or the like; (TA;) or qat~a AlHadiyva signifies he falsified and embellished discourse, or conversation: (A:) it is said that Alqat~ , which signifies Aln~amiymapu [i. e. the uttering, or utterance, of calumny ], (M, L,) [and] so does ↓ Alqit~iytaY , (S,) is from AlHadiyva ↓ tqt~t , meaning he sought time after time to obtain a knowledge of discourse, or conversation, and listened thereto: (M, L:) and ↓ Alqit~iytaY signifies [also] the seeking time after time to obtain a knowledge of namaAy^im [i. e. calumnies, pl. of namiymapN ]. (M, TA.) ― -b2- And qat~N [app. as an inf. n.] signifies The lying, or uttering of falsehood: (K:) [or] a prepared lying. (M.) ― -b3- And qat~ahu , (K, TA,) inf. n. qat~N , (TA,) signifies qad~ahu [meaning He cut it out, or shaped it, in any manner, whether lengthwise or otherwise]. (K, TA.) One says, huwa Hasanu Alqat~i , meaning Hasanu Alqad~i [i. e. He is goodly, or beautiful, in conformation ]: and a poet says, kaA^an~a vadoyayohaA A_i*aA maA A@boranotaY Huq~aAni mino EaAjK A^ujiydaA qat~aA meaning qad~FA and xaroTFA [i. e. As though her two breasts, when they come forth unexpectedly (a meaning of AbrntY expl. in the L, in art. brt , on the authority of Lh, but it is here expl. in the TA as signifying AntSb , so that the phrase may be rendered either when appearing unexpectedly, or when standing out ), were two round boxes of ivory, excellently cut out, or shaped, and made smooth in their surfaces ]: (O, TA: *) regarding them as one member, he has made the verb singular. (O.) ― -b4- Also He prepared, disposed, or arranged, it; or put it into a right, or good, state. (M, K.) ― -b5- And He collected it together by little and little. (M, K.) ― -b6- And He made it, or made it to appear, to be little; syn. qal~alahu . (M, K.) And qat~a A^avarahu , (M, K,) aor. , inf. n. qat~N , (M,) He followed, or followed after, his track, or footsteps, in pursuit; or endeavoured to track him, or trace him. (M, K.) ― -b7- And qat~N signifies also The following the footsteps of a man secretly, in order to know what he desires [ to do ]. (O, K.) ― -b8- And A pastor's smelling the odour of a camel (O, K) that is mahoyuwm (K) [i. e.] that is smitten by the [ disease termed ] huyaAm . (O, TA. [Freytag, supposing mahoyuwm in this explanation in the K to be syn. with haAy^im , renders the verb as meaning He (a pastor) smelt the urine of a straying camel, that he might know its way. ]) -A2- See also the next paragraph.

sourceDefinition: , [aor. ,] inf. n. quroA=nN , He collected together the thing; put it, or drew it, together; (S, O, K, TA;) part to part, or portion to portion. (S, O, TA.) [This seems to be generally regarded as the primary signification.] ― -b2- Hence the saying of the Arabs, maA qaraA^ato h`*ihi Aln~aAqapu salFY qaT~u and maA qaraA^ato jiniynFA , meaning This she-camel has not contracted her womb upon a young one: (S, O, TA:) but most say that the meaning is, her womb has not comprised, or enclosed, a fœtus: or the former saying means she has not borne a fœtus: accord. to AHeyth, this same saying and maA qaraA^ato maloquwHFA are both said to mean, by some, she has not borne in her womb a young one ever: and by some, she has not let fall a young one, ever; i. e. she has not been pregnant: and accord. to ISh, one says, ↓ Daraba AlfaHolu Aln~aAqapa EalaY gayori qaro'K [which seems to mean The stallion covered the she-camel without her bringing forth, or becoming pregnant; for he adds that qr' AlnAqp means DEthA ; app. DaEatuhaA or DiEatuhaA ; but I have not found DaEapN nor DiEapN among the inf. ns. of waDaEato meaning “ she brought forth; ” and I rather think that the right reading is DaganuhaA or DigonuhaA , and that the meaning therefore is, without her inclining, or being desirous: see 10, third sentence; and see qaro'u Alfarasi ]: and there is another saying; that lamo taqoraA^o janiynFA means She has not, or did not, cast forth a fœtus, or a young one. (TA.) One says also, of the she-camel, (K, TA,) and of the ewe, or she-goat, (TA,) qaraA^ato , alone, meaning She became pregnant: (K, TA:) and likewise, of the pregnant [in general], or of the she-camel, accord. to different copies of the K, (TA,) meaning she brought forth: (K, TA:) ISh says that qaraA^ato is used in relation to a she-camel; and ↓ A^aqoraA^ato , in relation to a woman: [each, app., in the former sense and in the latter:] and that one says ↓ naAqapN qaAriy^N ; pl. nuwqN qawaAriy^u . (TA.) ― -b3- See also 4. -A2- qaraA^a AlkitaAbi , (S, O, Msb, * K, *) and bihi , (Msb, * K,) the verb being trans. by itself and by means of b , or this particle is redundant, (Msb,) and sometimes the ' is suppressed, so that one says [ qaraY and] qarayotu &c., (TA,) aor. and , (K,) the latter aor. on the authority of Ez-Zejjájee, as is said in the L, but generally ignored, (TA,) inf. n. qiraA='apN and quroA=nN (S, O, Msb, K) and qaro'N , (Msb, K,) this last mentioned by Az; (Msb;) and ↓ AqtrA^hu ; (K;) He read [ the book, or Scripture ], or recited [ it ]: (K, TA:) or qaraA^otu AlquroA=na means [properly, or etymologically, accord. to some,] I uttered [ the words of ] the Kur-án in a state of combination [or uninterruptedly ]; (O, TA;) as Ktr is related to have said: (O:) [or qaraA^a as used in a case of this kind app. signifies properly he read, or recited, the Scripture chanting; like as A^ano$ada properly signifies “ he recited ” poetry “ chanting with a high voice: ” (for Scripture and poetry are usually chanted:) then, he read, or recited, anything in any manner, without, or from, or in, a book.] It is said in a trad., mano A^araAda A^ano yaqoraA^a AlquroA=na gaD~FA kamaA A^unozila faloyaqoraA^ohu qiraA='apa A^um~i EabodK [He who desires to read, or recite, the Kur-án freshly, like as it was revealed, let him read, or recite, it in the manner of Ibn-Umm-'Abd ]; meaning faloyuran~ilo katarotiylihi [properly, let him read, or recite, in a leisurely manner, with distinct utterance, and with moderation; but conventionally, let him chant, in a peculiar, distinct, and leisurely, manner; like as he did ]: or yuHaz~ino kataHoziynihi [ let him read, or recite, with a slender and plaintive voice, like as he did ]: or yaHodurohu kaHadorihi [ let him read it, or recite it, quickly, like as he did ]. (O.) And in a trad. of I'Ab, it is said, kaAna laA yaqoraA^u fiY AlZ~uhori waAlEaSori , meaning He used not to recite [the Kur- án] aloud in the [prayers of the] noon and the [period of the afternoon called the] EoSr : or he used not to make himself to hear his reciting: as though he heard persons reciting and making themselves and those near them to hear. (TA.) The saying, in the Kur [lxxv. 17 and 18], A_in~a EalayonaA jamoEahu waquroA=nahu faA_i*aA qaraA^onaAhu faA@t~abiE quroA=nahu means Verily on us is the collecting thereof [i. e. of the Kur-án] and the reciting thereof; and when we recite it, then follow thou the reciting thereof: or, accord. to I'Ab, and when we explain it to thee, then do thou according to that which we have explained to thee: (S, O, TA:) or the meaning [signified and implied] is, verily on us is the collecting thereof in thy mind, and the fixing the recitation thereof on thy tongue; and when we recite it to thee by the tongue of Gabriel, then follow thou the reciting thereof, and often recur therein so that it may become firmly rooted in thy understanding: (Bd:) [therefore quroA=nahu in the former instance means the teaching thee to recite it; and thus we may explain the assertion that] qaraA^a and ↓ A^aqoraA^a are syn. in like manner as are EalaA qironahu and AstElAhu . (Sb, TA.) See 4. qaraA^a Ealayohi means He read, or recited, to him the Kur-án, &c., [ as a teacher, or an informant; (as is shown by phrases in the Kur xxvi. 199 and lxxxiv. 21;) like talaA Ealayohi : and also, as a conventional and post-classical phrase,] as a pupil, or learner, to his sheykh, or preceptor. (Msb.) ― -b2- See also 5. -A3- And see 4, first quarter.

definition: , said of a woman: see 1, former half.
sourceDefinition: , said of a woman: see 1, former half. Said of a she-camel, (K, TA,) and of a ewe, or she-goat, (TA,) She retained the seed of the male in her womb: (K, TA:) and when this is the case, one says that she is fY qirowatihaA , which is anomalous, for ↓ fY qiroA^atihaA ; (TA in the present art.;) meaning in the first period of her pregnancy, before its becoming apparent, or manifest. (TA in art. qrw .) [And accord. to Freytag, (app. in the phrase A^aqoraA^ato sam~FA ,) the verb is expl. in the Kitáb el-Addád as said of a serpent, meaning It retained poison for the space of a month. ] ― -b2- Also, said of a woman, She menstruated: and she became pure from the menstrual discharge: (S, O, * Msb, K, TA:) and so ↓ qaraA^ato , in both of these senses, (Msb, TA,) aor. , inf. n. qaro'N ; (Msb;) or in the former sense; (Akh, S, K;) and [accordingly] one says, qaraA^ato HayoDapF A^awo HayoDatayoni [so in copies of the S, agreeably with what immediately precedes, but in one of my copies of the S and in the O and TA, A^aqoraA^at , meaning, she menstruated once or twice ]; (S, O, * TA; *) and qaraA^ato signifies she saw the blood [ of the menses app. for the first time ]: (TA:) and A^aqoraA^ato signifies she became one who had the menstrual discharge. (Akh, S, O, TA.) [Accord. to Zj, as I gather from the TA, the second of the significations in the sentence immediately preceding is from the collection of the blood in the womb: in the opinion of IAth, it and the first signification are from relation to time: but I rather incline to think that the converse of this is the case, and that hence are deduced several other meanings here following.] ― -b3- AqrA^t Alr~iyaAHu (S, K) The winds blew, (K,) or began [ to blow ], (S,) in their time, or season. (S, K.) ― -b4- AqrA^ (said of a man, O, TA) He reverted, or turned back, (O, K, TA,) from his journey. (O, TA.) And He returned (K, TA) from his journey. (TA.) ― -b5- And He, or it, approached, or drew near. (K.) You say, A^aqoraA^otu mino A^aholiY I approached, or drew near to, my family. (O.) And A^aqoraA^ato HaAjatuka They object of want approached, or drew near; or has approached, &c. (S, O.) ― -b6- And It set, (K, TA,) said of a star: or the time of its setting came, or drew near. (TA.) A^aqoraA^ati Aln~ujuwmu signifies The stars set: (O:) ― -b7- and also (O) The stars delayed [ to bring ] their rain. (S, O.) ― -b8- And AqrA^ is also syn. with A^ax~ara , (K, TA,) in the phrase AqrA^ HaAjatahu [ He postponed, or delayed, the object of his want: ] (TA:) and, (K, TA,) as some say, (TA,) syn. with AisotaA^oxara [ He, or it, was, or became, behind, backward, late, &c.:] (K, TA:) [but it should be observed that A^ax~ara is often intrans., and syn. with AisotaA^oxara ; therefore one signification may possibly in this instance be meant by both: such, however, is not the case accord. to SM, as has been shown above, and as is further shown by his saying,] perhaps the saying of the author of the K, that it is syn. with A^ax~ara , may have been taken from the phrase A^aEat~amota qiraAka A^amo A^aqoraA^otahu i. e. Hast thou withheld thy entertainment for the guest, or guests, or hast thou postponed it? but his explanation is obviously loose and defective. (TA.) ― -b9- A^aqoraA^otu fiY Al$~iEori is from AlA^aqoraA='u [pl. of Alqaro'u or Alquro'u : hence it seems to mean I rhymed, or versified: compare A^arojaza from Alr~ajazu , and A^aromala from Alr~amalu , &c.]. (O. [See also 8.]) -A2- A^aqoraA^hu , (L, K, TA,) inf. n. A_iqoraA='N , (TA,) He (a sheykh, or preceptor, L, TA) made him, or taught him, to read, or recite; (L, K, TA;) [and so ↓ qaraA^ahu , inf. n. quroA=nN , as shown before:] see 1, last quarter. One says, A^aqoraA^ahu AlquroA=na (S, O, L, TA) and AlHadiyva (L, TA) He made him, or taught him, to read, or recite, the Kur-án and the tradition. (L, TA.) Hence A^aqoraA^ahu Als~alaAma : (AHát, TA:) see 1, near the end. ― -b2- See also what next follows.

definition: (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K, &c.
sourceDefinition: (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K, &c.) and ↓ quro'N , (Mgh, Msb, K,) or the latter is a simple subst. and the former is an inf. n., (Msb,) A menstruation: and a state of purity from the menstrual discharge: (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K, &c.:) thus having two contr. meanings: (S, O, K:) said by IAth to have the latter meaning accord. to Esh-Sháfi'ee and the people of El-Hijáz, and the former meaning accord. to Aboo-Haneefeh and the people of El-' Irák: (TA:) and a time; (AA, S, Mgh, O, K;) and so ↓ qaAriy^N ; (S, Mgh, O;) as in the sayings, hab~ati Alr~iyHu liqaroy^ihaA and ↓ liqaAriy^ihaA The wind blew at its time; (Kt, Mgh;) and this is the primary signification (IAth, Mgh, O) accord. to AA [and some others]; (Mgh;) whence [accord. to them] the first and second of the meanings mentioned above: (Kt, S, IAth, Mgh, O:) and qaro'N signifies also the termination of a menstruation: and some say, the period between two menstruations: (S:) accord. to Zj, it means the collecting of the blood in the womb; which is only in the case of becoming pure from menstruation: (TA:) the pl. is A^aqoraA='N and quruwo'N and A^aqoruw^N , (S, O, Msb, K,) the last of which [as also properly the first] is a pl. of pauc.; (S, O, Msb;) or when qaro'N or ↓ quro'N has the first of the meanings assigned to it above the pl. is A^aqoraA='N , and when it has the second thereof the pl. is quruwo'N : (K:) respecting the phrase val`vapa quruwo'K in the Kur [ii. 228], As says, it should by rule be val`vapa A^aqoruw^K : (Msb, TA:) the grammarians say that it is for val`vapF mina Alquruwo'i ; thus in the L: (TA:) or they say that it is for val`vapa A^aqoruw^K mina Alquruwo'i : but some of them say that it is allowable to use a pl. of mult. in relation to three and more as far as ten [inclusively] without [the necessity of] rendering the phrase otherwise in grammatical analysis. (Msb.) ― -b2- [Hence,] A rhyme: (Z, K, TA:) A^aqoraA='N (Z, O, TA) and quruwo'N (O) signifying the rhymes of verses; (Z, O, TA;) which terminate like as do the AqrA=' of the states of purity from menstruation; (Z, TA;) [i. e., they are thus called] because they terminate, and limit, the verses: (O:) and A^aqoraA='u Al$~iEori signifies also the several modes, or manners. or species, (IAth, O, K, TA,) and metres, (IAth, TA,) and scopes, (K, * TA,) of verse, or poetry: (IAth, O, K, TA:) the sing. is qaro'N (O, TA) and ↓ quro'N , and some say ↓ qiro'N also, and ↓ qariYo and qariY~N , and some say that it is qarowN [q. v.] with w : and the pl. of qariY~N is [also] A^aqoriyapN [a pl. of pauc.]. (TA.) One says, h`*aA Al$~iEoru EalaY qaro'i h`*aA Al$~iEori i. e. This poetry is according to the mode, or manner, &c., of this poetry. (O.) See also 10, first sentence. ― -b3- Also A periodical festival; syn. EiydN . (TA.) ― -b4- And A fever [app. an intermittent, or a periodically-recurrent, fever ]. (TA.) ― -b5- And i. q. gaAy^ibN [app. meaning A thing becoming absent, or unapparent, or setting, like a star: see 4]. (TA.) ― -b6- And quro'u Alfarasi means The days of the mare's desiring the stallion: or, of her being covered: one says hiYa fiY qaroy^ihaA and fiY A^aqoraAy^ihaA [ She is in her days of desiring &c.]. (TA.) See also 1, first quarter; and see 10, third sentence.

definition: is said by some of the erudite to be originally an inf.
sourceDefinition: is said by some of the erudite to be originally an inf. n. of qaraA^otu Al$~aYo'a meaning “ I collected together the thing, ” or of qaraA^otu AlkitaAba meaning “ I read, or recited, the book, or Scripture; ” and then conventionally applied to signify The Book of God that was revealed to Mo- hammad: (Kull:) it is [also expl. as signifying] the revelation, (K, TA,) meaning that which is termed AlEaziyz [ the mighty, or inimitable, &c.], which is read, or recited, and written in books, or volumes: (TA:) used as a subst., and unrestrictedly, it is applied in the language of the law to the substance itself [ whereof the Kur-án consists ], and lexically to the alphabetical letters [ in which it is written ] for these are what are read; as when one says, katabotu AlquroA=na [ I wrote the Kur-án ], and masisotuhu [ I touched it ]: (Msb:) [and without the article Al , it is applied to any portion of the Kur-án: ] accord. to AO, (S,) and Zj, (TA,) it is thus called because it collects and comprises the suwar [or chapters]: (S, O, TA:) and IAth says that the original meaning of the word is the collection; and that the quroA=n is so called because it has collected the histories [of the prophets &c.], and commands and prohibitions, and promises and threats, [and the like is said in the O,] and the A=yaAt [i. e. verses, or signs], and the suwar [or chapters]: but Ismá'eel Ibn-Kustan- teen, to whom, as a disciple to his preceptor, EshSháfi'ee read, or recited, the Kur-án, is related on the latter's authority to have said that AlquraAnu is a subst., and with hemz, and not taken from qaraA^otu , but is a name for the Book of God, like Alt~aworaApu [the Book of the Law revealed to Moses] and AlA_inojiylu [the Gospel]: and it is related that Aboo-'Amr Ibn-El-'Alà used to pronounce AlqrAn without hemz [like many others, but it is, and always has been, pronounced by most with hemz]. (TA.) ― -b2- It is also applied to The divinely appointed act of prayer ( AlS~alaApu ) because it comprises recitation [of words of the Kur-án]. (IAth, TA.)

sourceDefinition: A gut; syn. miEFY : (S, M, Mgh, O, K:) or all the A^amoEaA=' [or guts ]: or the guts [ AmEA=' ] that are in the lower part of the belly: TA:) pl. A^aqoSaAbN . (S. M, Mgh, O, K.) One says, huwa yajur~u quSobahu [expl. by what here follows]. (S, O.) The Prophet said, respecting 'Amr Ibn- 'Ámir El-Khurá'ee, who first set at liberty sawaAy^ib [pl. of saAy^ibapN , q. v.], (O,) or respecting 'Amr Ibn-Kamee-ah, who first changed the religion of Ishmael, (TA,) raA^ayotuhu yajur~u quSobahu fiY Aln~uAri [ I saw him dragging his guts in the fire of Hell]. (O, TA.) ― -b2- El-Aashà in his saying wa$aAhidunaA Aljul~a waAlyaAsamiY nu waAlmusomiEaAtu biA^aqoSaAbihaA means [ The rose being present with us, and the jasmine, and the songstresses ] with their chords of gut: or, as some relate it, (and as it is cited in the M,) he said ↓ biquS~aAbihaA , meaning with their musical reeds, or pipes. (S, O.) ― -b3- And (tropical:) The middle of the body; metaphorically applied thereto: so in the saying of Imra-el-Keys, (S, O, L,) or, accord. to the people of El-Koofeh and ElBasrah, it is falsely ascribed to him, (O,) wAlquSobu muDoTamirN waAlmatonu maloHuwbu [ And the middle of the body slender and lean, and the portion next the back-bone, on either side, smooth, and sloping downwards ]. (S, O, L.) ― -b4- And (assumed tropical:) The back. (O, K. [SM, not having found this in any lexicon but the K, supposed that AlZ~ahoru might be substituted in it for AlxaSoru , which is not therein mentioned as a meaning of AlquSobu .])

definition: [a coll. gen. n., signifying Reeds, or canes; and the like, as the culms of corn, &c.; and sometimes signifying a reed, or cane, and the like, as meaning a species thereof; ] any plant having (M, A,...
sourceDefinition: [a coll. gen. n., signifying Reeds, or canes; and the like, as the culms of corn, &c.; and sometimes signifying a reed, or cane, and the like, as meaning a species thereof; ] any plant having (M, A, Mgh, Msb, K) its stem composed of (Mgh, Msb) A^anaAbiyb [or internodial portions ] (M, A, Mgh, Msb, K) and [ their ] kuEuwb [or connecting knots, or joints ]; (Mgh, Msb;) [i. e. any kind, or species, of plant having a jointed stem; ] i. q. A^abaA='N [a word comparatively little known]; (S; [in the O AanA' , a mistranscription;]) and [it is said that] ↓ qaSobaA='u signifies the same: (S, O: [but see what follows:]) the n. un. of the former is ↓ qaSabapN (S, M, Mgh, Msb, K) and ↓ qaSobaApN or ↓ qaSabaApN : (K accord. to different copies; the former accord. to the TA: [but each of these I believe to be a mistake for ↓ qaSuboA='apN , which is said to be a n. un. of qaSobaA='u , and therefore held by some to be syn. with qaSabapN :]) ↓ qaSobaA='u [appears, however, to differ somewhat from qaSab , for it is said that it] signifies an assemblage of qaSab ; (M, K;) and its n. un. is ↓ qaSabapN and ↓ qaSobaA='apN [like HalafapN and HalofaA='apN which are both said to be ns. un. of HalofaA='N ; and TarafapN and TarofaA='apN , said to be ns. un. of TarofaA='N ; the former in each case anomalous]: (M: [see also Ham p. 201:]) or, accord. to Sb, ↓ qaSobaA='u is sing. and pl., (S, M, Mgh, O,) and so TarofaA='u , (S, M, O,) and HalofaA='u ; (S, O;) as pl. and as sing. also having the sign of the fem. gender; therefore, when they mean to express the sing. signification, they add the epithet waAHidapN ; thus, and thus only, distinguishing the sing. meaning from the pl., and making a difference between a word of this class and a noun that denotes a pl. meaning and has not the sign of the fem. gender such as tamorN and busorN , and such as A^aroTFY and EaloqFY of which the ns. un. are A^aroTaApN and EaloqaApN : (M:) or, as some say, ↓ qaSobaA='u signifies many qaSab growing in a place: (Mgh:) and it signifies also a place in which qaSab grow: (M, K:) [or] ↓ maqoSabapN has this last meaning; (Mgh, Msb;) or signifies, like ↓ A^aroDN qaSibapN , a land having qaSab . (M, K. *) ― -b2- A^aHoraza qaSaba Als~aboqi , (Msb,) or Als~aboqi ↓ qaSabapa , (TA,) [meaning (assumed tropical:) He won, or acquired, the canes, or cane, of victory in racing, ] is said of the winner in horseracing: they used to set up, in the horse-course, a cane ( qaSabap ,) and he who outstripped plucked it up and took it, in order that he might be known to be the one who outstripped, without contention: this was the origin of the phrase: then, in consequence of frequency of usage, it was applied also to the expeditious, quick, and light, or active: (Msb, * TA:) [accord. to the TA, it is a tropical phrase, but perhaps it is so only when used in the latter way:] it is said in a trad. of Sa'eed Ibn-El-Ás, that he measured the horse-course with the cane, making it to be a hundred canes in length, and the cane was stuck upright in the ground at the goal, and he who was first in arriving at it took it, and was entitled to the stake. (O, TA. [See also muqaS~ibN .]) ― -b3- [The ↓ qaSabap here mentioned as A certain measure of length, used in measuring race-courses, was also used in other cases, in measuring land, and differed in different countries and in different times: accord. to some, it was ten cubits; thus nearly agreeing with our “ rod: ” (see jariybN :) accord. to others, six cubits and a third of a cubit: (see fad~aAnN :) the modern Egyptian qaSabap , until it was reduced some years ago, was about twelve English feet and a half; its twentyfourth part, called qaboDapN , being the measure of a man's fist with the thumb erect, or about six inches and a quarter.] ― -b4- AlqaSabu AlfaArisiY~u [ The Persian reed ] is a kind whereof writing-reeds are made: (Mgh, Msb:) and another kind thereof is hard and thick; and of this kind are made musical reeds, or pipes; and with it houses, or chambers, are roofed. (Msb) One says, qaSabu AlxT~i A^anofa*u mino qaSabi AlxaT~i [meaning Writingreeds are more penetrating, or effective, than the canes of El-Khatt (which are spears); i. e., words wound more than spears]. (A, TA.) ― -b5- qaSabu Als~uk~ari is well-known [as meaning The sugar-cane ]: (Msb:) this is of three kinds; white and yellow and black: of the first and second, but not of the third, the juice [ of which sugar is made ] is expressed; and this expressed juice is called Easalu AlqaSabi . (Mgh.) ― -b6- qaSabu Al*~ariyrapi [is Calamus aromaticus; also called qaSabu AlT~iybi ]: a species thereof has the joints near together, and breaks into many fragments, or splinters, and the internodial portions thereof are filled with a substance like spiders' webs: when chewed, it has an acrid taste, and it is aromatic (Mgh, Msb) when brayed, or powdered; (Mgh;) and inclines to yellowness and whiteness. (Mgh, Msb. [See also *ariyrapN , in art. *r .]) ― -b7- qaSabN also signifies (assumed tropical:) Any round and hollow bone [or rather bones ]; (S, O;) it is pl. [or rather a coll. gen. n.] of which ↓ qaSabapN is the sing. [or n. un,], this latter signifying any bone containing marrow; (M, K;) thus called by way of comparison [to the reed, or cane]. (M.) ― -b8- And (tropical:) The bones of the yadaAni and rijolaAni [i. e. arms and legs, or hands and feet, but here app. meaning the latter], (A, Msb,) and the like: (Msb:) [or] (assumed tropical:) the [ phalanges, or] bones of the fingers and toes; (M, K, * TA;) (tropical:) the bones whereof there are three in each finger and two in the thumb [and the like in the feet ]; (A, TA;) and Zj says, the bones of the A^aSaAbiE [or fingers and toes ] which are also called sulaAmaY : (Msb in art. slm :) or, as some say, the portions between every two joints of the A^aSaAbiE : (M, TA:) and AlA^aSaAbiEi ↓ qaSabapu [or qaSabupu AlA_iSobaEi ] signifies the A^anomalap [here perhaps meaning the ungual phalanx ] of the finger or toe. (Msb, TA.) ― -b9- And (assumed tropical:) The bones and veins of a wing. (MF.) ― -b10- [And (assumed tropical:) Quills: thus in the phrase SaAra Alr~iy$u qaSabFA , in the K, voce A^anuwqN , meaning The feathers became quills: n. un. ↓ qaSabapN : see SanamapN .] ― -b11- And (tropical:) [The bronchi; ] the branches of the windpipe; (M, K;) and outlets of the breath; (K;) [i. e.] AlqaSabu , (S, M, O,) or faSabu Alr~iy^api , (A, Msb,) signifies the ducts ( Euruwq ) of the lungs; (S, A, O, Msb;) through which the breath passes forth. (S, M, A, O, Msb.) [See HaloqN .] ― -b12- And (assumed tropical:) Any things made of silver, and of other material, resembling [ in form ] the kind of round and hollow bone [or bones ] thus called: n. un. ↓ qaSabapN . (S, O.) And (assumed tropical:) Jewels (S, M, K) having the form of tubes ( A^anaAbiyb ), (S,) or oblong, (M, K,) and hollow. (M.) ― -b13- And (assumed tropical:) Brilliant pearls, and brilliant chrysolites, interset with jacinths. (IAar, O, K.) So in the saying, in a trad., (O, K,) related as uttered by Gabriel, (O,) [cited in the S app. as an ex. of the meaning next preceding this last,] ba$~iro xadiyjapa bibayoti fiY Aljan~api mino qaSabK (IAar, O, K) i. e. [ Rejoice thou Khadeejeh by the announcement of ] a pavilion [ in Paradise ] of brilliant pearls, &c.: (IAar, O:) or the meaning is, of hollow pearls [or pearl ], spacious, like the lofty palace: (IAth, TA:) or of emerald: (TA voce bayotN :) and it is said by some to convey an allusion to Khadeejeh's acquiring what is termed qaSabu Als~aboqi [expl. above], because she was the first person, or the first of women, who embraced El-Islám. (MF, TA.) ― -b14- And (tropical:) Fine, thin, or delicate, (S, O,) or soft, (M, Msb, K,) garments, or cloths, of linen: (S, M, O, Msb, K:) a single one thereof is called ↓ qaSabiY~N . (M, O, Msb, K.) One says, maEa fulaAnK qaSabu SanoEaA='a waqaSabu miSora (tropical:) [ In the possession of such a one are ] qaSab [meaning the cylindrical, or oblong, hollow pieces ] of carnelian [ of San'à ], and qaSab [meaning the fine, or soft, garments, or cloths, ] of linen [ of Egypt ]. (A.) ― -b15- Also (tropical:) The channels by which water flows from the springs, or sources: (S, M, A, O, K:) or the channels by which the water of a well flows from the springs, or sources: (As, T, TA:) n. un. ↓ qaSabapN . (M.) And qaSabu AlbaToHaA='i (assumed tropical:) The waters [ of the kind of water-course called bTHA=' (q. v.)] that run to the springs, or sources, of the wells. (As, S, O.) Aboo-Dhueyb says, A^aqaAmato bihi faA@botanato xayomapF EalaY qaSabK wafuraAtK naharo (As, S, M, O,) meaning She remained [ in it, and constructed for herself a booth, or a tent, ] amid wells and sweet water that flowed copiously. (As, S, O.) ― -b16- See also qaSabapN below, in the next paragraph. -A2- AlqaSabu is also a name for The ewe. (O.) ― -b2- And qaSabo qaSabo is A call to the ewe (O, K) to be milked. (O.)

definition: The most vehement, or intense, heat of summer;
sourceDefinition: The most vehement, or intense, heat of summer; (S, K;) from the [ auroral ] rising of the Pleiades, [ which, at the commencement of the era of the Flight, was about the 13th of May, O. S., ] to the [ auroral ] rising of Canopus, [ which, at the same period, was about the 4th of August, O. S.: ] (K:) or vehemence, or intenseness, of heat: (Msb:) pl. [of pauc.] A^aqoyaAZN and [of mult.] quyuwZN . (K.) ― -b2- Also, The quarter which people [ commonly ] call the Sayof ; (Msb;) the summerquarter, commencing when the sun enters the sign of Cancer; so termed by some, who called the spring-quarter the Sayof , and the autumnal-quarter the rabiyE ; others [in later times] calling the summer-quarter the Syof , the spring-quarter the rabiyE , and the autumnal-quarter the xariyf ; but agreeing with the former in calling the winterquarter the $itaA=' : (Mir-át ez-Zemán:) the Arabs say, that the year consists of four seasons, every one of these being three months; namely, the quarter called the Sayof , which is that called rabiyEu AlkalaA_i , consisting of [the Syrian months] Ádhár and Neysán and Eiyár [or March and April and May, O. S.]; then, the quarter called the qayoZ , consisting of Hazeerán and Temmooz and Áb [or June and July and August, O. S. ]; then, the quarter called the xariyf , consisting of Eylool and the two Tishreens [or September and October and November, O. S.]; and then, the quarter called the $itaA=' , consisting of the two Kánoons and Shubát [or December and January and February, O. S.]. (Az, TA.) ― -b3- laA taquwmu Als~aAEapu Hat~aY yakuwna Alwaladu gayoZFA wAlmaTaru qayoZFA , a saying of Mohammad, meaning [ The resurrection, or the time thereof, will not come to pass until the birth of a child be an occasion of wrath, or rage, and ] rain be accompanied by air like the qyZ [or most vehement heat of summer ]. (TA.) ― -b4- A_ijotamaEa AlqayoZu is an elliptical and abridged phrase, meaning The people, or company of men, assembled themselves in the qayoZ [or summer ]. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: See 1, in four places. ― -b2- AkfA^ fiY sayorihi Eani AlqaSodi , (TA,) or kafaA^a , (K,) He deviated, or turned aside, in his journey, from the object he had in view. A_ikofaA'N , (TA,) in poetry, accord. to a commentary on the Káfee, He used as the rawiY~ two letters having their places of utterance near to each other; as T with d : [such is the signification of the verb accord. to general usage in the present day:] or, accord. to the Ahkám el-Asás, he changed the rwY~ from r to l , or l to m : or he made a similar change of one letter to another having its place of utterance near to that of the former: or it has another signification, given below, accord. to the same authority: (TA:) or he used different letters in the rhymes; (S, K;) whether letters having their places of utterance near to each other, or the contrary; (TA;) or in some m and in some n and in some d , and in some T , and in some H , and in some x , &c.; as says AZ; and this is the meaning known to the Arabs: (S:) or he used different vowels in the rwY~ : (Fr, S:) or i. q. A^aqowaY : (S, K:) or, accord. to the Ahkám el-Asás, it signifies either as explained above on that authority, (TA,) or he used different final inflections in the rhymes: (K:) or he changed the final vowel in the rhyme; ending one verse with Dam~ap , and another with kasorap , [which are the two vowels that resemble each other]: (TA:) [see a verse cited in the first paragraph of art. gyb :] or he impaired the end of a verse in any way. (K.) Eloquent Arabs explained the meaning of the verb in this last manner to Akh, without defining any particular kind of impairment: but one made it to consist in the use of different letters. (TA.)
